News.title: French student's bleak warning as protesters march through Paris: 'We don't have a future'
News.content:
Holding a French flag, Matteo tells how young people in his country do not have a future. The student’s bleak verdict came as he was among thousands of demonstrators who marched through Paris.

After the country was rocked by its worst civil unrest in years, crowds took to the street on Saturday amid cost-of-living and school funding concerns. What started as a protest over staff shortages at a high school has sparked a national movement.

The Mirror joined a throng of protesters marching through the capital, with the crowd stretching as far as the eye could see.

To see more of the stories you value from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



View 9 Images Student Matteo told how young people in his country do not have a future (Image: Humphrey Nemar)

France protests live: Demonstrator reportedly loses fingers in violent clashes READ MORE :

France orders curfews amid violent riots across country as Emmanuel Macron begs for calm READ MORE :

“What we saw in the past two or three weeks is [Emmanuel] Macron, our President, is not understanding what we are protesting for,” Matteo said. “We can show all of the world through a strong movement that we are all together.”

France is not alone in its societal problems; many in Britain would no doubt share discontent over the cost of living. Indeed, Matteo points to other nations too. The political science student, in his 20s, explained: “I think we don’t have future and that’s clearly difficult.”

He added: “We don’t have future because of AI, we don’t have future because of ecology, we don’t have futures because our government doesn’t want to just let us have some good condition in our university.” On the lack of a future for French young people, he said: “That’s why there are a lot of people on the street. They are protesting.”

‌



9 View 9 Images Tech start-up worker Agathe, 33, with her sign in Paris on Saturday (Image: Humphrey Nemar) 9 View 9 Images Student Soline Malacarne said: 'Students are mobilised for bad studying conditions.' (Image: Humphrey Nemar)

Authorities confined the Paris march to the capital’s southeastern edge, away from the centre. Thousands of protesters marched from Porte d'Italie on Saturday afternoon. Trade unions led the procession, followed by protesters carrying flags and placards.

Agathe, 33, held a handmade sign saying “you’ve been served revolution”. The tech start-up worker told the Mirror: “We are protesting against government politics from years because it’s unfair. We are not listened [to]. And we when we try to manifest they try to forbid us to do it. So it’s a fundamental right and we are here for this to claim we have the right to not agree.”

‌



View 9 Images French authorities used water cannons and tear gas to disperse those protesting (Image: Humphrey Nemar)

She explained: “When you don’t listen [to] the people’s voice for years, you cannot ask people not to manifest and not to protest.” Agathe added: “I’m here for democracy, for liberty, I’m here for equality for everyone, for the less privileged and for equity.”

The Paris march began peacefully but near its endpoint at Porte de Vincennes, some protesters threw projectiles while police fired volleys of tear gas and used water cannons to disperse people. The Interior Ministry put nationwide turnout at 410,000, while the CGT union estimated nearly 800,000. The ministry's estimate included 110,000 in Paris.

View 9 Images Friends Mel and Leo in Paris on Saturday (Image: Humphrey Nemar)

‌



Earlier, we spoke to protesters gathered at Place d’Italie in Paris on Saturday afternoon. Art student Mel, 19, carried a banner reading “you are more shocked by ink on the wall than blood on the floor”. It is a reference to how she feels the protesting has been conveyed.

She told the Mirror: “I’m here because the state of France lately is so bad.” In reference to the government, police and far right, she explained: “I’m here today but I’m scared because they’re getting more violent every day.”

The teenager added: “It’s really terrifying to see my country like that. I’m proud to be French and the far right is trying to make it seem like people who are manifesting are not… But we don’t hate France, we do this because we love our country, we are proud of who we are.

“And, today, that’s why we’re here because I’m proud of who I am and I don’t want to leave my country in a way that I’ll be ashamed in the future.” She said the cost of living was “getting bad”, explaining: “Personally, I’m part of the lucky ones because I live with my family but I know friends who struggle every month to pay rent.”

‌



View 9 Images Students demanding better schools and workers seeking higher wages and pensions have brought anger over living standards into the final months of President Macron's presidency (Image: Humphrey Nemar)

Her friend, engineering student Leo, 18, said: “I think it’s really important to show that we are still going to protest, we are still going to go on the streets.” The teenager added: “I think it’s important that we can protest. It’s one of our rights.”

Meanwhile, Soline Malacarne said: “Students are mobilised for bad studying conditions.” The 23-year-old student, who also referenced the high cost of living, said direct democracy was “the best way to get heard”. She added: “I hope they will listen to the people.”

Elsewhere, police used tear gas in Lyon, where the rally had been banned, on Saturday morning. And in Clermont-Ferrand, officers reportedly used tear gas and stun grenades to push back demonstrators trying to reach the city centre. Authorities sought to prevent another weekend of looting, burned cars and attacks on public buildings. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said up to 70,000 officers would be deployed nationwide, backed by helicopters, armoured vehicles and water cannons.

‌



View 9 Images A scene during Saturday's protest in Paris (Image: Humphrey Nemar)

Thousands also marched on Saturday in Orleans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as Marine Le Pen's National Rally held a two-day congress in the city. Students demanding better schools and workers seeking higher wages and pensions have brought anger over living standards into the final months of President Macron 's presidency.

Energy prices in France were 21.3% higher in September than a year earlier, helping drive overall inflation to 3.1%, according to the national statistics agency, INSEE. Mr Macron met high school representatives Friday. They said he had promised to overhaul university admissions, but called for protests to continue until concrete measures are announced.

Over half a million people took to the streets last Saturday. Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted over the weekend. Gendarmes stood guard beneath the Arc de Triomphe as shops boarded up across Paris. Major museums, including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais were closed. Police changed the Paris route, replacing the planned Bastille-to-Nation march with a route between Porte d'Italie and Porte de Vincennes.

‌



View 9 Images Colleagues Lucile Toulgoat, left, and Rachel Basque (Image: Humphrey Nemar)

At Bastille, the original starting point, police used a megaphone to tell people to leave or face a 135-euro fine. We spoke to two protesters at Place de la Bastille who ended up being fined. Earlier, they had explained why they were there.

Rachel Basque normally sells fruit and veg but on Saturday she turned up for democracy. The 30-year-old, who was due at work later that day, said: “It’s our right and we shouldn’t have to be afraid to protest.” She added: “We are just fed up… we have to be here to support the kids and support ourselves.”

Her colleague Lucile Toulgoat, 25, added: “I’m tired of this police. I’m tired of the army coming.” Lucile said she felt “terrible” about the cost of living.

‌



For Matteo, the voice of young people is powerful. He said: “Gen Z is really strong at the moment to show the protest and to show that they want a better future.”

But whether they get it, sadly, remains to be seen.

News.title: Watch: BBC in Paris as police charge protesters and use tear gas during unrest
News.content:
Police have clashed with protesters in Paris as some demonstrations in France turned violent on Saturday.

A largely peaceful day of protests turned into unrest after nightfall, as protesters were seen throwing objects and fireworks at police.

Around 70,000 officers were deployed across France for a second consecutive weekend and used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds.

The Interior Ministry estimated around 400,000 people took part in Saturday's demonstrations, with nearly 1,000 arrests made.

Europe correspondent Nick Beake reports from Paris, where he says there are few signs the unrest will ease soon.

Follow live coverage here.

News.title: Met Police says letter with claims about Meghan's father not shared with other law enforcement
News.content:
Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes.

He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having a leg amputated in 2025.

Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home, the Sun reported.

He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the FBI in July.

In a statement released by Meghan on Friday she said that when she received the information of the claims against her father she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".

Meghan said she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

Authorities in the Philippines have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father.

The BBC was told on Friday the matter was being investigated by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force.

Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured his computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.

Meghan is the only daughter of Markle and her mother Doria Ragland.

He pulled out of attending Meghan and Harry's wedding in 2018 - citing ill health - and they became estranged.

The duke and duchess moved to the US in 2020 after stepping down as working royals.

They returned to the UK with their children this year after six years away.

News.title: Storm Boelo amber warnings kick in as parts of UK brace for 80mph gusts
News.content:
Amber weather warnings have come into force in northern parts of the UK as Storm Boelo continues to move across the country, with wind gusts up to 80mph forecast in the worst-hit areas.

Strong winds and heavy showers will intensify through Saturday night, with widespread gusts expected to hit Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England.

The amber warning for Scotland and England will stay in place until 21:00 on Sunday, bringing an increased risk of travel disruption and potential risk to life.

The second named storm in as many days comes as National Grid continues to restore power to thousands of properties in south-west England after the area was hit hardest by Storm Austen.

The National Grid said on Saturday that more than 124,000 properties had been restored with power supplies since the beginning of the storm. However, hundreds were still without power on Saturday evening.

In north-west England, more than 2,000 properties were without power on Saturday night due to the storm.

Strong winds could cause power cuts, flying debris, damage to buildings and trees, travel disruption and danger to life from large waves, the Met Office said.

The strongest winds will affect western Scotland first towards the end of Saturday, before spreading eastwards overnight and through Sunday.

By Saturday evening, wind gusts of 75mph had been reached at South Uist Range, Western Isles, Highland and Eilean Siar, Scotland, on Saturday, according to the Met Office.

News.title: Between quick wins and big dreams lies Burnham's biggest test
News.content:
But the widespread suggestion that you'll be able to blink and miss the Budget has got some hackles up in the Treasury. A budget, by its very nature, can never be a small event - it sets billions upon billions of taxes and spending decisions.

And there are likely to be extra taxes on banks, vows to sweep away some business regulation, particularly for small business, more powers passing to local leaders under the guise of devolution and more action on energy bills which are heading back up again.

John Healey has made it clear publicly and to staff, that he wants to encourage people with the guts and drive to start a business. One source said: "If you are taking on John's mantra about talking up Britain then you can't say, 'Nothing to see here'."

Whatever else the chancellor brings to Parliament in his red box, do not expect him to arrive with all the solutions to the country's very well-documented problems, whether that's getting the economy growing more convincingly, sorting out gaps in defence cash, welfare, social care, or new ways to pay off the country's groaning debts more quickly.

One former minister suggests even if Healey and Burnham had stumbled upon all the answers in a few months, it's just not possible to fix everything at the same time because of the constraints on the economy.

They wondered: "Is he going to invest in growth? Is he going to put everything he has into the challenges people will face this winter? Is he going to throw it at defence? There is just not enough to tackle all these problems simultaneously - ministers are going to be exposed to the cold light of day."

Burnham and Healey have to find a way of maintaining the balance in an unusually happy Labour Party.

MPs talk of ministers and Burnham himself being more visible and approachable in Parliament, knocking around with colleagues in the evening, fewer "golden slips" doled out when ministers were excused from voting alongside colleagues so they could get on with their important jobs.

One minister told me they'd had to tell their private office not to arrange for them to be "slipped" , from going to the Commons in the evening to see backbenchers.

It's paying off in the mood among MPs. One told me: "You're not feeling like the only way you can ever have a chat with a minister is by arranging an appointment for three months down the line â the soft touches really matter."

News.title: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep you and your home warmer for longer
News.content:
With the clocks going back this weekend, the nights will be drawing in.

So if you have a thicker duvet, now is the time to bring it out. Some supermarkets sell winter duvets for under Â£20 - look for 10.5 tog or higher.

But there's something to be said for a craftily placed blanket, too. When it gets cold, Rebecca, 44, from Hertfordshire, sleeps with a blanket underneath her mattress, which she says stops draughts. "This was passed to me by my nan, she swore by it," she says. Others swear by placing a blanket above the mattress but under the bedsheet.

You can heat your bed before getting in with a hot water bottle, but make sure you check the expiry date. A guide by NHS Scotland, external says to let the water from the kettle cool for a few minutes before filling, only fill it two-thirds full, squeeze air out of the top before putting the stopper on, and don't hold it directly against your skin.

Using an electric blanket - to heat your bed before you get in or to wrap around yourself on the sofa - is "one of the cheapest ways" to stay warm, says Emily Seymour, energy editor at consumer organisation Which?. Testing by Which?, external shows it typically costs between 2p and 8p an hour to run an electric blanket at its highest setting. The London Fire Brigade, external says to unplug your blanket before you get into bed unless it has a thermostat control, not to use a hot water bottle at the same time, and replace it every 10 years.

News.title: Strictly's new presenters - after mixed reviews have they found their feet?
News.content:
Strictly Come Dancing's new hosting trio received a very mixed reception when the latest series began a month ago. Ratings have dipped and the jury's still out, but critics say they are slowly getting into the groove.

Changing the hosting team on the BBC's flagship Saturday night entertainment show was never likely to be a waltz in the park.

And going from two presenters to three, and giving them slightly different roles, upset the show's rhythm even more.

Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman were always going to be a hard act to follow.

Into their sparkly shoes have stepped the safe and smooth Emma Willis; the flamboyant former professional dancer Johannes Radebe; and cheeky comedian Josh Widdicombe, a wildcard who was not hitherto associated with either the dance world or prime-time TV.

Willis and Widdicombe have been paired on the live shows, where he is tasked with injecting humour into the moments before and after each dance - with mixed results, say critics.

Radebe, meanwhile, has taken over from Winkleman upstairs on the mezzanine, bringing his warmth and dance expertise to the celebrity interviews following each routine.

News.title: California considers imposing 'world's first' tax on billionaires
News.content:
But the vote is also offering regular residents a voice on an issue that has roiled politics for decades.

"I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap.

The state has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the world. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps.

Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (Â£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system.

Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of US President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.

"If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she tells the BBC.

News.title: The artist dropping her debut album after a billion streams
News.content:
Jazzy is rooted in the Dublin club scene, starting her career as part of a group called Powerful Creative Minds in the city.

But as more and more clubs close, the DJ says there are fewer opportunities for artists to cut their teeth offline.

"When I first started going out, there was a lot more going on," she says.

"There was a lot more nightclubs to go to and it's very different when we look at it now, which is sad.

"There's definitely a home for dance music on the internet of course but club culture is very important and I think that's something that we need to keep going for sure."

Latest figures from the Night Time Industries Association, external suggest about 12 venues are closing across the UK every month, with almost 30% of the night time economy lost since the coronavirus pandemic.

"I hope to God that it doesn't disappear, the club scene altogether," says Jazzy, who describes a similar issue in Ireland.

"We all need to try and put a hand in to keep it going."

Jazzy's taking her new album on tour across the UK from next month, but first she has her biggest gig yet: Dublin's 3Arena in front of a home crowd.

Even after a Coachella set and supporting Calvin Harris, she describes this as the "biggest milestone of my career to date".

While she says fans can mostly expect her brand of uplifting records on the album, she says it's also more personal than her usual work.

She highlights one track in particular, Invisible, as a change from her more upbeat releases. It deals with a bad experience she had in the music industry, describing it as "like my first ever diss track".

"I hope [fans] learn a little bit more about me, because that was one of my goals with the album - to open up a little bit about experiences in life as well.

"So there's a little message from me in each song."

News.title: Plan for Northern Olympics to get £7m in Healey's Budget
News.content:
The report will look in closer detail at how hosting the games could work.

It will consider the kinds of venues and transport links required, how different cities could share the games, how communities could benefit.

Crucially it will also examine how much it could cost as well as assess the chances of a bid succeeding. The Conservative-Lib Dem coalition government said in 2013 it estimated hosting in London had cost Â£8.9bn.

A report in 2013 by the UK Trade and Investment, which has since been replaced by the Department for International Trade, said it had sparked a Â£9.9bn boost to the economy through new contracts, sales and foreign investments.

But the estimated amount was queried by some, including the Federation of Small Businesses and the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR).

Conservative shadow sports minister Louie French said that while hosting an Olympic Games would "likely provide a positive boost for the country", the cost of proposals would require "careful scrutiny".

He said the chancellor should use the Budget to bring down everyday costs before looking to "spend millions in taxpayer cash on reheated announcements made by his predecessor".

French added: "The irony is that Labour's new tourism tax will create a cost barrier for sports fans wanting to visit the North of England for an Olympic Games."

The new feasibility study for the Northern Games will be done by government, UK Sport, the Northern Mayors and include the British Olympic and Paralympic associations.

Healey said: "Olympic legacy lasts way beyond the celebration of sport over the summer. The North hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable.

"Britain's experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I'm picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious games. It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost."

News of the funding for the study was welcomed by the British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport.

"We welcome the government's continued support for exploring the potential of a future bid for the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the UK in the 2040s," they said in a joint statement.

"Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements."

News.title: Murder charge after body found in wheelie bin
News.content:
A man has been charged with murder after a body was found partially within a wheelie bin, police have said.

Devon and Cornwall Police said Mohamed Abotaka, 36, of Grand Parade, Plymouth, was charged with the murder of 52-year-old Ali Barzai. The force said Abotaka was due to appear in court on Monday.

Police said Barzai's body was found in a service lane off Grand Parade at about 06:40 BST on Wednesday.

Det Insp Chris Lithgow urged people not to speculate and said a heightened police presence would remain in the area in the coming days.

News.title: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of tour
News.content:
Sam Fender has called out the price of gig tickets ahead of his next tour, promising to lower the cost.

The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour earlier this week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester in summer 2027.

While tickets are yet to go on sale, Fender responded to a post on social media which claimed to outline the expected ticket prices.

The Geordie musician also said standing would not be split into a front and back tier and he had "no idea how this was normalised at gigs".

Tickets are due to go on general sale at 09:30 GMT on Friday, with a pre-sale at the same time on Wednesday.

But Fender said he was "not happy" with the reported prices.

"They're getting changed," he said on Instagram.

"It got inflated well more than I'd had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on."

The North Shields singer also said he did not want there to be an option for fans to pay more money to be closer to the front.

"The standing will not be split as well, I had no idea about it," Fender said.

"I have no idea how this was normalised in gigs... it won't be happening on this tour."

He is not the first musician to raise concerns over ticket pricing.

Zara Larsson agreed with fans earlier this year that her tickets were too expensive.

The Swedish singer said while she did not have control over the prices, she hoped she would in the future.

Follow BBC North East on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Newcastle on BBC Sounds.

News.title: Could Somerset pub be the oldest in England?
News.content:
But none of that helps to verify the claim to the title of England's oldest pub - so what does?

Wright said, put simply, none of the other pubs possessed the archaeological evidence, archival references or scientific data "to actually back up the claims".

He said: "It's all about carefully placing all of the evidence together and working out in what order the real claimants go - and The George came out with the crown."

Pub historian Charo Havermans agreed with that assertion.

"The strongest claims are when the history meets the science," she said.

"For example, tree ring dating can give us an idea of how old the timber or the wood used is.

"What we know about those times is that people wouldn't dilly dally so if they've cut down a tree, they're going to use it then," Havermans said.

"It's a pretty accurate way of knowing when the building materials were used to create that structure."

Havermans also said historical records such as licensing data, local maps, or the Domesday Book could help date a pub.

However, we may never truly know where the oldest boozers are - a sentiment reinforced by Guinness World Records which has "rested" the accolade for the oldest pub since 2000, "when it became clear that it was not possible to verify it in full".

A spokeswoman for Guinness World Records said it was "never able to state definitively which was the oldest pub in the country, since the age and historical usage of buildings is, in many cases, uncertain".

News.title: Thousands of people gather in support of Drumcree Orangemen
News.content:
Thousands of people have gathered in Portadown to show support for the Orange Order in the wake of the Drumcree dispute.

Hundreds of Orangemen paraded through the town centre, joined by bands and a crowd of supporters who were not deterred by the stormy weather.

The parade comes amid continuing tensions surrounding the long-running Drumcree dispute, whereby the Orange Order has been banned from walking down the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road in the County Armagh town.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has held talks with representatives from both sides in recent weeks.

Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) MP Carla Lockhart was there, while her party colleagues and assembly members Jonathan Buckley and Brian Kingston paraded with their lodges.

The Drumcree dispute has led to divisions within the unionist party, with Lockhart standing down as party officer on Thursday. She said the DUP had it "within its gift to remove" Michelle O'Neill as Northern Ireland's first minister.

This would mean removing DUP Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly from her role, as the two ministers share an office and cannot function without one another.

O'Neill had taken part in the Garvaghy Road protests which blocked the parade from taking place and earlier this week, the Sinn FÃ©in politician attended police interviews over her involvement.

News.title: Habitat destroyed by Cairngorms fire to be restored with government funding
News.content:
More than Â£1m is to be spent on nature recovery projects, including the restoration of habitats destroyed by a fire which ripped through a huge area of hillside in the Cairngorms.

The Scottish government funding will support habitat, species and river restoration, control of invasive non-native species and deer management across Scotland.

It includes Â£150,100 for recovery and nature restoration work following the Abernethy wildfire in the Cairngorms in July, to restore damaged habitats, help wildlife recover and reduce the risk of future wildfires.

Further funding will be provided to a range of other projects.

News.title: Reward offered over murder in flat used as brothel
News.content:
A Â£20,000 reward is being offered by Crimestoppers in connection with the murder of a man who was found dead in a Birmingham flat in 2022.

Jinming Zhang had been stabbed multiple times before he was found in the property, which police said was being used as a brothel, in Moseley Street in Digbeth.

West Midlands Police previously released CCTV of a suspect, while a DNA sample from the suspected killer found at the scene did not produce a match on the national database.

The case was featured in the BBC series of Forensics: The Real CSI last year, which revealed police believed the murder suspect may have sustained a hand injury in the frenzied attack.

Jenny Birch, who has been overseeing the investigation, urged anyone with information "no matter how small" to contact police.

"Someone out there knows something, and we won't give up until we have answers," she said.

News.title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
News.content:
The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.

As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit Â£100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.

The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.

"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.

"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.

"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."

The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.

But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.

"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.

"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."

The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing Â£200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.

News.title: Luke Littler hopes to be well-rested for quarter-final clash in Dortmund
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Luke Littler hopes an extra hour in bed will help fire him to the European Championship title.

The 19-year-old is looking to complete the set of major tournament wins in less than three years by coming out on top in Dortmund on Sunday.

And he is in ominous form after firing the second-highest average in the tournament’s history, with 114.47 in his 10-5 victory over Nathan Aspinall.

He will return on Sunday afternoon for a quarter-final against Krzyszstof Ratajski boosted by a later playing time and the clocks going back overnight ahead of a possible evening session consisting of a semi-final and final.

“I’ve just been told I am last on, so about 4pm,” he said. “The clocks go back, so an extra hour in bed as well.

“Tomorrow afternoon will be the tough one. Waking up, getting up, playing in the afternoon.

“I just want to get the afternoon game out of the way and then I can look forward to the evening.

“Hopefully I can complete the set.”

open image in gallery Littler beat his good friend Nathan Aspinall in Dortmund (Sebastian Doppstadt/PDC)

This is just the third time Littler is playing in Germany this year having received abuse from the crowds in the past.

There was a minor incident midway through the match, which required referee Huw Ware to step in, but Littler has opened the door to ending his boycott.

“That’s the first thing that has happened,” he said. “Just before I went for bull on the 126, the front table just decided to bang really loud on the table.

“The guy that did it looked up, I pointed at him and said, ‘That’s you’.

“Then he just picked up his pen, started writing on his little 180 card and didn’t look up. So, he knew what he’d done.

“But that’s the first thing about all weekend, the crowd’s been very good.

“I’ve not been to Germany this year, apart from Berlin and Frankfurt, so it’s only the third time they’ve seen me.

“Obviously I want a good reception because I want to be doing European Tours next year in Germany.

“Whereas if they’re not good to me, then I won’t go. But so far, so good, and with the way I’m playing, hopefully they like it and I can produce maybe a bit better tomorrow.”

Stephen Bunting celebrated his passage to the quarter-finals by watching Borussia Dortmund in Bundesliga action.

The Liverpudlian eased past Kim Huybrechts, firing four 100-plus checkouts in a 10-3 win to set up a last-eight showdown with Gerwyn Price on Sunday.

The Westfalenhalle arena is located next to Signal Iduna Park and Bunting made the short journey to watch Dortmund’s 1-0 win over Eintracht Frankfurt on Saturday evening.

open image in gallery Signal Iduna Park is opposite the Westfalenhalle in Dortmund (Nick Potts/PA) ( PA Archive )

Bunting, who supports Liverpool, has become a lucky mascot for the German giants and has never seen them lose.

“I think quite a few years ago now I went to the Bayern Munich and Dortmund game, and Dortmund won,” he said.

“Dortmund said, ‘Stephen Bunting’s been to our game, and we’ve never lost when Stephen Bunting’s there’.

“So yeah, I think they enjoy me going. I’ve been a few times now. I’ve got a great connection.”

Price made it through with a 10-4 victory over Cameron Menzies while defending champion Gian van Veen was dumped out by Luke Woodhouse, who was a 10-6 winner.

Ross Smith and Martin Schindler also made it through to the last eight.

News.title: 5 new podcasts to listen to this week
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Technology, conversations about grief and travelling to the wonderful Arizona, this week is full of new listens.

1. Designed in California

Streaming platform: All major streaming platforms and YouTube

Genre: Technology

open image in gallery Designed in California podcast cover (PA)

You don’t have to be a geek to enjoy this podcast, but it helps if you know your USB-C from your elbow.

The Designed in California podcast chronicles Apple’s 50-year history from its earliest days in Steve Jobs’ garage to the rise of the Mac, and all the nerdy bits in-between.

The five episodes in this first series are about the origin of Apple’s revolutionary MP3 player, the iPod. Listeners who owned a Walkman will be horrified to hear that the first iPod Classic was shipped 25 years ago. Younger listeners will be wondering what an iPod even was.

Hosts Jason Snell and Myke Hurley take us back to the “flannels and grunge” of the 90s to explain how the iPod “went from saving Apple to being discontinued in less than 25 years” when the iPhone killed the iPod star.

Journalist Snell takes us on a nostalgia trip from his first job on MacUser and his musical evolution from cassettes to CDs and even Sony’s MiniDisc, which he calls the “love child of a cassette and a CD”.

He tells how the way the world listened to music was forever changed when a technology that allowed you to “put every Beatles song ever recorded on a single CD” was unveiled – the MP3. We hear how audio scientist Karlheinz Brandenburg had to listen to Suzanne Vega’s Tom’s Diner a thousand times to improve compressed digital audio files, which must have been torture.

The podcast then goes into a lot of insider gossip and techie stuff before we get to how the iPod was finally released in 2001 delivering a “1,000 songs in your pocket”. Funny how quaint that sounds now.

(By Siobhan McNally)

2. All There Is with Anderson Cooper

Streaming platform: Spotify, YouTube and CNN

Genre: Life and wellbeing

open image in gallery All There Is with Anderson Cooper podcast (CNN Podcasts’/PA)

All There Is with Anderson Cooper follows the American broadcast journalist as he discusses the complexities of grief, while speaking with his guests.

This weeks episode features country music superstar, Wynonna Judd who lost her mother to suicide in 2022. Throughout the emotional but heart warming conversation, the pair go back to the start, speaking about Judd’s childhood.

She explains that growing up she was a highly sensitive kid and also shy, particularly when singing. “Around mom I could though,” she says, explaining that she had confidence around her mother. “I knew that she was proud of me when I would do the singing thing.”

They go on to talk about loosing a loved one to suicide – Anderson lost his brother too as he admits he was told, “I am the strong child’, growing up.

Judd then speaks of her relationship with her stepfather, admitting she only found out he wasn’t her biological one until the age of 30. This then inspired her hit song Girl Who Could Sing.

Overall, this would a highly emotional listen but also relatable to anyone who has lost a loved one and it give a sense of hope to opening up these difficult conversations around grief.

(By Sara Keenan)

3. The Tech Spill

Streaming Platform: Spotify and YouTube

Genre: Technology and business

open image in gallery The Tech Spill Podcast (The Tech Spill/PA)

“The safest bet is on yourself,” says The Tech Spill podcast creator Ama Owusu-Afriyie wisely. Her feisty attitude that “no job is safe – so I will make my own job” is an inspiring take, and one that is now sadly a reality for many young people for whom a “side hustle” is an actual career progression.

Podcast host Owusu-Afriyie can normally be found behind the mic interviewing business leaders and founders, but in this episode, she flips the script and is interviewed by her intern, Lulu.

Owusu-Afriyie says: “It’s the stories that make you connect with a founder,” like she did when she heard The Diary of a CEO Steven Bartlett talking about “finding £13.40 down the back of a chicken shop sofa”.

Let’s face it, you’ve got to be a bit special to be a founder of a start-up, and while Bartlett’s relentless self-optimisation gets a lot of stick, Owusu-Afriyie sounds like your normal run-of-the-mill child genius, “I would always get obsessed with things” and was a “four-year-old doing maths in Homebase”.

She recounts selling off chunks of her Galaxy Cookie Crumble chocolate bar in Year Seven to the highest bidder. Owusu-Afriyie says: “Everything clicked into place – that you can exchange value for money. If I just buy more chocolate, I make more money – I was making hundreds of pounds.”

While that just sounds like ripping off your mates, you have to laugh at Owusu-Afriyie’s cheek. Eventually she was told to stop because “my school blazer was heavy with coins”.

The podcast sound quality goes a bit in and out, but for someone who doesn’t like talking about herself, Owusu-Afriyie is fun and chatty about insights she’s gained along the way, especially from her Ghanian dad, and how being fired from her job pushed her to start her own successful company.

A must-listen for anyone who plans on becoming rich.

(By Siobhan McNally)

4. Radical

Streaming Platform: BBC and all major podcast platforms

Genre: Politics

open image in gallery Radical podcast cover (BBC/PA) ( BBC )

Award-winning journalist and podcaster Gabriel Gatehouse is the new host of Radical, a podcast exploring the people and ideas seeking to change the world.

Taking over from journalist Amol Rajan, who became the first murder victim on The Celebrity Traitors this year, Gatehouse brings a wealth of experience to the programme. As the former international editor of Newsnight, he has spent years reporting on major global events, covering foreign affairs, conflict and revolutions. His thoughtful questioning and impartial approach preserve the essence of Radical: a safe space where people can openly explore unconventional ideas.

One of the first guests to join Gatehouse for the Radio 4 podcast’s relaunch is author and activist Naomi Klein, renowned for her critical examination of corporate power, globalisation and capitalism.

Their conversation explores the ideas underpinning Klein’s influential books, including No Logo and The Shock Doctrine, as well as her latest release, End Times Fascism. They discuss her interpretation of the world, the origins of her political convictions and why her ideas are often regarded as radical.

The podcast gives its diverse range of guests, from all walks of life, a fair hearing, allowing their ideas to be examined through open and considered discussion.

Whether or not you agree with its guests’ bold ideas, this twice-weekly podcast offers an opportunity to question established assumptions, broaden your perspective and see the world through a more critical lens.

(By Camilla Foster)

5. Wonders of Arizona

Streaming Platform: Spotify, Apple Podcasts and Wonders of Arizona website

Genre: Travel

open image in gallery Wonders of Arizona (AZ/PA)

Wonders of Arizona takes listeners on an immersive road trip across the hidden gems and iconic landmarks of the diverse Southwestern state of the United States. Spanning seven episodes, the podcast is hosted by presenter and award-winning travel writer Aaron Millar and offers a fascinating exploration of the people, places and stories that make Arizona so unique.

Millar’s vivid storytelling brings Arizona to life. His rich, detailed descriptions of the people that he meets – down to the details of their tattoos and clothing – and the places he explores transports listeners straight into the heart of each destination.

The voices that accompany Millar on his journey are just as compelling. From local experts to people deeply rooted in their communities, each contributor offers valuable insight into Arizona’s culture, history, environment and everyday life, providing an authentic glimpse into what it truly means to call the state home.

Throughout the series, Millar takes listeners on an unforgettable journey through scorching deserts, the remarkable Sky Islands, the majestic Grand Canyon and many more fascinating destinations.

Millar’s infectious enthusiasm for travel, history and meeting new people shines through in every episode, and I could happily listen to his warm, captivating voice all day.

By capturing local voices and stories entirely on location, Millar uncovers the soul of Arizona in a way that feels both intimate and adventurous. Wonders of Arizona is travel journalism at its finest – beautifully narrated, thoughtfully researched and wonderfully immersive. After listening, I was left with an irresistible urge to add this glorious US state to my travel bucket list.

(By Camilla Foster)

News.title: Jamie Lee Curtis says honoring Rob and Michele Reiner at Emmys was ‘tougher’ than expected
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Jamie Lee Curtis has reflected on the emotional toll of honoring her late friends Rob and Michele Reiner at this year’s Emmy Awards.

Curtis, who had her wedding at the director’s house in 1984 and chose him as a godfather to her daughter, paid tribute to the couple during a memoriam segment at the ceremony in September.

In a new interview with The Hollywood Reporter, Curtis said that she wanted to honor her friends at the ceremony but found it “a little tougher than I anticipated.”

She added: “It’s been a little strange because it’s a very private grief, and yet I’m a public-facing person. I’m trying to walk that line a little bit.”

Next month, Curtis will become the inaugural recipient of the Michele and Rob Reiner Champion for Change Award during the Children’s Institute’s Cape & Gown Gala. The honor was created in partnership with the Children’s Institute, its president and CEO Martine Singer (Michele’s sister), and the couple’s children, Jake and Romy Reiner.

open image in gallery Jamie Lee Curtis has said it was ‘tougher than expected’ to honor her late friend Rob and Michele Reiner at the Emmy Awards ( Reuters )

Curtis explained: “I’m here for the Children’s Institute. I’m here to support their work. I’m going to be at the event to support the work that Rob and Michele did, and it shouldn’t be about me. And yet I’ve been the one talking a lot about them.”

Speaking at the Emmys in September, Curtis said onstage: “Last year we lost another cherished legend, our beloved ‘Meathead,’ Rob Reiner.”

“He was generous and kind and funny as hell and a friend to all.”

open image in gallery Jamie Lee Curtis was close friends with filmmaker Rob Reiner. She had her wedding at Reiner’s house in 1984 and chose him as a godfather to her daughter ( Getty Images )

Curtis said in the interview that when she attended the rehearsal, the Simon & Garfunkel song “Bridge Over Troubled Water” was playing.

“There’s an exercise in grief about desensitizing yourself, so I listened to that song for the next day, trying to get used to it,” she said. “It’s so moving to me naturally, and then it was sung live. It was very challenging because it was challenging enough to represent everyone and try to honor, in this case, particularly Rob’s passing, but I also have feelings of my own.”

Elsewhere in the interview, Curtis explained that she often admired the Reiners’ activism work.

“Every day with them was activism. They were enraged at the way the current administration had decimated progressive policies toward children, women, people of color, gay people and transgender people,” she said.

“I mean, don’t even get me started. Rob was a firebrand. I can talk a good game, and I’m a passionate advocate, but Rob had the acumen and the political savvy. I don’t have political savvy. He was able to find common ground with people he disagreed with and was a powerful leader,” she said.

The Reiners died in December 2025.

Their son Nick, 33, is due back in court next year in connection to the killing of his parents, who were found stabbed to death inside their Brentwood, Los Angeles, home on December 14.

News.title: Melania Trump faces backlash for not giving Pope Leo credit for Ukraine ceasefire
News.content:
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

First Lady Melania Trump faced backlash after taking credit for securing a ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Ukraine, while omitting Pope Leo XIV's earlier diplomatic efforts.

The White House announced that the Oleshky ceasefire will begin on October 29 to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and the evacuation of elderly residents.

According to the Vatican, Pope Leo XIV spoke directly with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy days before the White House announcement.

Ukrainian official Davyd Arakhamia and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed the ceasefire agreement, with Arakhamia noting contributions from both Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV.

The credit dispute underscores an escalating public feud between President Donald Trump and Pope Leo XIV over foreign policy and immigration issues.

News.title: Islam Makhachev makes huge UFC decision as unexpected title fight is confirmed
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Islam Makhachev will not be defending his welterweight belt anytime soon, with an interim-title fight announced for UFC 336 in January.

Saturday brought the unexpected news that Carlos Prates and Michael Morales will headline that event in Toronto, Canada, with the interim welterweight belt on the line.

Makhachev had been rumoured to headline the card at Scotiabank Arena on 30 January, with Prates standing out as his likeliest contender.

However, the Russian, 34, will seemingly take more time out before returning to the Octagon, leading the UFC to announce Prates vs Morales during UFC 333 on Saturday.

Makhachev is the UFC’s pound-for-pound No 1 fighter and last fought in August, outpointing Ireland’s Ian Machado Garry. With that, the former lightweight king retained the welterweight title for the first time and reached 17 straight wins, a UFC record. His win streak dates back to 2015.

Meanwhile, Prates is 7-1 in the UFC with seven KO wins, including against ex-champions Jack Della Maddalena and Leon Edwards. The Brazilian’s only UFC loss was a decision defeat by Machado Garry. The 33-year-old is 24-7 overall.

And Morales is 7-0 in the UFC with five KO wins. The Ecuadoran, 27, is 19-0 overall.

News.title: Sensational Spurs storm Stamford Bridge as Palmer loses his head
News.content:
Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has told Cole Palmer he must learn from his red card that contributed to his team’s London derby defeat by Tottenham Hotspur.

Tottenham head coach Roberto De Zerbi insisted Palmer should have seen red for shoving his pelvis into the face of Mateus Fernandes. But, having got off with a yellow card, the Chelsea midfielder then fouled substitute Conor Gallagher.

“I haven’t seen them [the yellow cards] on TV, but as far as I have been told, he probably got it right,” Alonso said. “So, for sure for Cole, but for everyone. We think [up until] now we haven’t received any red cards [this season] and we need to continue that way because we need to have this maturity to deal with difficult moments, when you have conceded 1-0, there was still 15-20 minutes to go, so we have to be calm. I need to check the action to talk with Cole, but it is one to learn for the future for sure.”

Asked if he thought Palmer should have been sent off for the first yellow card, De Zerbi, who was booked for his protests, replied: “Yep.”

Jordan Henderson had spoken to Palmer at the end of the previous week’s victory over Everton in which the forward could also have been booked for a second time and sent off.

But Alonso claimed he does not have any wider concerns about Palmer’s character. He said: “Today, for sure, yes, but it is not a [wider] concern. I think that Cole when he is focused on the game, when he is enjoying and today after the 1-0, it is a moment to keep calm, a moment to keep mature and for everyone.”

De Zerbi hailed his side’s character and claimed that Tottenham have “suffered enough” after two 17th-placed finishes and a slow start to the season until successive victories over Coventry City and Chelsea.

“We want to improve, improve and improve, to be better game by game, week by week. I think we have suffered enough,” De Zerbi said. “Changing the spirit of the group, changing the performance of the players, especially the more fragile players, maybe the younger players. We played very well. Great individual performances, great collective performance because we played very well. And then we put something different than Tottenham, I think, in the last period. Different attitude, different relationships with the players, different group.”

Chelsea were without João Pedro because of an injury and Alonso is waiting to find out how long the striker will be out.

“We don’t know yet because he has a lot of fluid,” Alonso said. “So he felt it yesterday [Friday] and we need to wait probably until tomorrow [Sunday] to do the test and to know the whole situation and the whole seriousness of the injury. We will know soon enough.”

News.title: Pollock at heart of scuffle that inspires Leicester to thumping win in feisty derby
News.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Leicester Tigers v Northampton Saints.

The Prem’s derby weekend continues today at Mattioli Woods Welford Road, where Geoff Parling’s side go head-to-head in with their East Midlands rivals.

Both Leicester and Northampton have two wins from the opening three rounds of the season and with both sides involved in a number of high-scoring encounters already in the new campaign, we could be in for a real treat.

Tigers started the season with a 38-40 loss at home to Saracens, but bounced back quickly with wins over Gloucester and Newcastle Red Bulls. They will be itching to right a few wrongs after suffering a chastening Champions Cup defeat in Pau last week.

Northampton, meanwhile, have notched up wins over Newcastle Red Bulls and Bath either side of loss to Bristol Bears.

A win today for Saints would be their first on the road since defeating Exeter Chiefs at Sandy Park in April.

“It (the East Midlands derby) means a lot to everyone, we know it will be a great atmosphere at Mattioli Woods Welford Road,” said Parling.

“I don’t think with this sort of game either team has to build it up too much emotionally because that just comes, so I think it’s actually about being really really calm in the moment.”

“Hopefully we can put the best of ourselves out there and I’m sure Saints will be able to do exactly the same.”

Saints are without a victory in Leicester since January 2023, when a single point decided the 18-19 result.

Since then, the last five meetings between the sides have been won by the hosts on the day – with Saints last taking home the bragging rights when a Tom Litchfield hat-trick helped Northampton to a 45-31 win on home soil in last season’s league play-off.

Kick-off gets underway at 3.05pm. Stay with us here for all the latest updates.

News.title: Saliba has fight on his hands to usurp ‘unbelievable’ Konsa
News.content:
Hello and welcome to coverage from the Emirates as Premier League champions Arsenal host Everton.

Mikel Arteta’s men produced a good performance in midweek to draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League while David Moyes’s squad have had the week off following their 2-0 defeat by Chelsea last weekend.

Arteta said: “We’re having three games in six days so we know what’s happening, especially when the games are so demanding and the necessity is to win. We know that, so we prepare the players for those scenarios and do the best we possibly can.

“I know David so well and how he sets the team, the quality they have in their organisation and individually. It’s no coincidence they didn’t lose before their last game. They have a really good team, which we know because in recent clashes, it’s always been a really difficult game for us.”

Both teams enter this game having been beaten just once this season but eight points separate them with Arsenal in second and Everton in eighth.

Moyes said: “It’s not an easy game and never has been over many years. We look forward to it; they had a game in midweek, and we have to try and capitalise on that. I thought we did really well last year against them; we played really well down at Arsenal, and I hope we can do the same.

“When I look back at the team we had out, we were pretty threadbare at that time, but we did a good job, and I hope we can do it again. Obviously Arsenal have some many different tools in their bag and people they can use in different positions, so we’re fully aware of the team we’re up against and the level.”

Former Arsenal players Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Christian Norgaard could feature for Everton this afternoon.

News.title: ‘Tactical genius’ Emery outsmarts Maresca as City crash to first league defeat
News.content:
It was four years ago to the day that Emery grabbed this famous club by the shirt and collar and gave them an almighty shake. After a summer of much instability including many player sales, he appears to have already struck a formula with his newly assembled team.

There were a number of fine individual performances from many of the summer arrivals, such as Jackson, goalkeeper Zion Suzuki and Johan Manzambi.

Emery said: “We were very motivated and Manchester City is the best team in the world so this is the level. This year we started so poorly and we needed time to understand how we improve. The players showed the capacity to retrieve the level we’ve had over the last few years.

“Nicolas is more mature and very demanding of himself to improve. Earlier this season he was shooting over the crossbar but he is now finding the corners. There is still work to do and 11 points is not enough but we are feeling better.”

Villa were fierce from the start and ahead after six minutes. Guéhi’s mistake was punished by John McGinn, with the ball dropping to Jackson who crashed a shot into the roof of the net.

The home team did require Suzuki to produce saves to stop efforts from Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Abdukodir Khusanov as City responded. Ndiaye also struck the outside of the post and City were level seven minutes into the second half with Erling Haaland nodding in Ndiaye’s cross at the far post. Haaland had touched the ball just eight times in the opening 45 minutes but invariably only needs one chance.

News.title: England hammer France to keep Rugby League World Cup hopes alive
News.content:
With Samoa beating Papua New Guinea 64-6 earlier on Saturday, England’s task was put into stark and imposing focus. The Pacific Islanders have a points difference of plus-132. Courtesy of this mauling, England’s is plus-64. So they must see off Papua New Guinea by a big number next Friday and then pray that Tonga defeat Samoa two days later. That is their only route through.

In truth, that is as much as McDermott could hope after their initial shortcomings, as they seek to avoid missing out on the last four for the first time in the World Cup’s 72-year history.

“What we’ve done today, given the context, is just enormous,” McDermott said. “We had to win big but, as any coach will tell you, nobody thinks like that. You think, ‘we’ve got to win’.

“We had some real good, candid conversations this week about what that actually means and we’ve been able to do that without getting distracted in chasing points.”

It should be remembered that this was only McDermott’s second game in charge and, even allowing for the poor opposition, they were dramatically improved.

“We’ve been together for five field sessions only,” he said. “We’re building something here and there was a little bit of that on show today.

“Certainly the six tries we scored in the last 17 minutes or so before half-time are what we’ve been chasing. We can see how good that’s going to be.

“If this group’s together for a process or a long build-up to a tournament, we could achieve some special things but, over a short space of time, it’s been remarkable really.”

It is incredible to think that England took 22 minutes to break the deadlock, when the ever-excellent Dom Young burst through. From there, they averaged a try every four or so minutes, with France looking increasingly forlorn and fatigued.

News.title: How an aid initiative maimed thousands of children in war-torn Africa
News.content:
Tormented by pain from severe internal burns, Amza Kebbie is one of thousands of children in Sierra Leone damaged for life by an aid intervention which went horribly wrong.

It has been five days since the four-year-old boy drank caustic soda, one of the two main ingredients for making soap, after mistaking it for drinking water. The highly corrosive liquid, also known as sodium hydroxide, has stripped the lining of his oesophagus and part of his stomach, causing life changing damage.

He’s now in intensive care, clinging precariously to life. An intravenous drip provides fluids and there’s a nasal cannula that enables him to breathe. Medics and relatives look over him around the clock.

If he can gather enough strength (which the nurses say is by no means guaranteed) the dangerously sick child will undergo a gastrostomy, an operation that will see a tube directly inserted into his stomach so that he can be fed long term.

Amza drank caustic soda while being looked after by a neighbour who was making soap at home Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

He can no longer swallow properly and may never be able to do so again, say his doctors.

This is not an isolated tragedy. Across Sierra Leone, there are thousands of children like Amza, and their number is growing every year.

At the Goderich Surgical Centre in the capital Freetown, around 200 children are admitted annually with caustic soda poisoning. Many more are thought to die in remote regions where emergency medical treatment is unavailable.

Behind the calamity is a humanitarian initiative that has spectacularly backfired. It’s a prime example of the law of unintended consequences; of a seemingly sensible and undoubtedly well meaning public health intervention doing more harm than good.

Fatmata Kamara accidentally drank caustic soda at her grandmother’s house in 2014 and has had a feeding tube ever since Credit : SImon Townsley

The story starts in the aftermath of Sierra Leone’s vicious civil war, which ran between 1991 and 2002.

Fought between the government and the Revolutionary United Front – backed by Liberian warlord Charles Taylor – the war claimed an estimated 50,000 to 70,000 lives, displaced 2.5 million people and left the country brutalised and in ruins.

In its aftermath, international aid agencies and NGOs desperately sought ways to revive the country and alighted on DIY soap making as a way of killing two birds with one stone.

Siblings Aminata Fofana and Salieu Bangura help out with the family soap-making business Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Organisations including UNHCR, UNICEF and World Vision thought the practice would both improve sanitation in the country’s disease-ridden shanty towns and provide home-bound women with the means to earn a sustainable income.

It seemed like an obvious “win-win”, and schemes to help women set up in the soap making business rapidly proliferated.

An annual report by the International Federation of the Red Cross, published in May 2002, promoted a micro-finance scheme to fund small-scale soapmaking.

Saieu Bangura, 13, with a tub of soap flakes Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

In 2005, the Centre for War Affected Women in Sierra Leone’s Kono district, backed by the UNHCR, listed soap making as one of the main training courses for war widows and female amputees.

And at about the same time, the Freetown-based Safer Future Youth Development Programme, supported by UNICEF and the charity War Child, provided “a tool kit for soap production” at its training workshops.

As recently as 2020, Action Aid ran a promotional article on its Sierra Leone website showing how soap making had enabled women to become financially independent of their husbands.

The article ran under the headline: “With Soap Making Skills – I'm Empowered!”

Mabinty Bangura is taken to theatre for an endoscopy Credit : Simon Townsley

It is for good reason that the ancient Greek physician Hippocrates urged doctors “first, do no harm”.

To follow the rule literally is not possible as all health interventions entail some risk but it's a reminder never to underestimate the capacity of a new intervention to backfire.

There are plenty of examples from history to choose from.

During the British Raj in India, the government offered a cash bounty for every dead cobra as a way of reducing the danger of venomous snakes.

The surgical team examine the internal damage via an endoscopy Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But rather than leading to a decline in snake numbers, the plan resulted in entrepreneurial individuals breeding cobras just so they could kill them and then claim the reward.

Once officials realised what was happening and the scheme was stopped, thousands of the then worthless cobras were released into the wild, greatly increasing the risk of snakebite.

In the late 1950s, the Chinese Communist regime introduced an equally calamitous public health campaign involving sparrows.

They issued a directive ordering the birds to be destroyed because they were thought to spread disease and destroy crops.

A child’s gastrostomy scar with a feeding tube in place Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

What those behind the idea failed to consider was that sparrows are natural predators. As their numbers declined, the locust population exploded, decimating agriculture and contributing to the Great Chinese Famine in which millions died.

So what went wrong in Sierra Leone? What did those behind the soap making scheme fail to foresee?

Experts say the initiative simply failed to consider the danger inherent in encouraging people to use toxic chemicals in their homes.

The brightly coloured buckets in which caustic soda is made, and then mixed with oil and scent to make soap, are the same buckets used across the country to fetch and hold drinking water. And just like drinking water, the lethal solution is cool, clear and inviting.

Just a drop is enough to cause the most horrific burns. So when a thirsty young child like Amza runs in from play and mistakenly scoops up a cup of it to quench their thirst they will lose their oesophagus, if not their lives.

Giuseppe Meucci, chief surgeon at the Goderich Surgical Centre Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Giuseppe Meucci, chief surgeon at the 56-bed Goderich hospital in Freetown where four year old Amza is being cared for, has been treating patients burned by sodium hydroxide nearly every day since arriving in Freetown in 2019.

Three quarters of patients seen by the hospital’s specialist programme for oesophageal burns, set up in response to the crisis and run by the Italian medical charity Emergency, are under five.

“It’s a struggle in this country,” says Dr Meucci. “Almost every family knows someone who has suffered because of this problem. But they just keep coming.”

Hospital director Jasna Sundic Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“In most countries you remove the source of danger for the child, but here that doesn’t seem to happen,” he says.

“It’s one of the main health problems of this country. Soda is there with malaria, malnutrition and typhoid complications. It’s one of the reasons why so many children die before they reach five years old.”

Hospital director Jasna Sundic agrees.

“This is a very severe issue but one which is very preventable,” she tells the Telegraph. “[But] however much we do here, we have not been able to decrease the overall number of soda patients being admitted.

“We cannot stop mothers who have no other source of income except making soap.”

Ibrahim Kerah is fed by his father Mohamed Credit : SImon Townsley

In a handful of rare cases, burns victims are sent abroad for complex oesophageal reconstruction surgery but this is not an option for the vast majority of children injured in Sierra Leone.

More than 60 per cent require surgery, but for these children, like Amza, a feeding tube that bypasses the oesophagus is the only option.

The hospital has many of these gastrostomy patients.

Critically underweight Mabinty Bangura Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

In a ward dedicated to soda burns, four-year-old Ibrahim Kerah is being fed through his stomach tube by his father Mohamed.

They travelled together on the back of a motorbike taxi for nearly 10 hours to get here for his third check-up appointment.

The Telegraph watches as Mohamed carefully prepares his son’s meal, adding spinach leaves to the porridge-like mix which is fed into a syringe at the end of the tube.

At an adjoining bed two-year-old Mabinty Bangura is critically underweight after ingesting soda about six months ago. Nurses have put her on a high protein drip so she can regain enough strength to undergo the same bypass surgery.

In the courtyard outside, mothers whose children have just had a gastrostomy are being taught how to prepare the liquid food.

Ibrahim and his father Mohamed endured a 10-hour motorbike journey to attend his hospital check-up Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Isatu Alie, 24, has been living with a stomach tube for 12 years, and now works for Emergency as a patient ambassador.

She is eight months pregnant with her second child and proud to have overcome her injury and the stigma of having to feed through a tube.

“I remember what happened so well,” she says. “I had just got back from school. I took my cup and dunked it into the water bucket. My aunt made soap and, on that day, I didn’t ask about the liquid in the bucket. The pain was incredible”.

More than a decade has passed since her surgery, and Isatu has adjusted well.

“I’m okay with it now. I feel like a normal human being; I’m blessed to be here,” she says.

“Now I speak to children and their parents who have just experienced the same thing and tell them not to lose hope.”

Pregnant Isatu Alie now works as a patient ambassador Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

A small proportion of the patients needing treatment following caustic soda burns are adults.

Among them is 21-year-old Junisa Bundeh, who is on a follow-up visit to check his stomach tube. He explains that he gulped down what he thought was a cup of water from a basin while eating at his grandmother’s house three months ago.

“It was so painful,” recalls Junisa. “I realised what it was straight away because it was so harsh. I tried to spit it all out but the liquid was already going down my throat.”

Mothers are taught how to prepare liquid food; Junisa Bundeh shows his feeding tube Credit : SImon Townsley

In the muddy lanes of Freetown’s Waterloo district there are makeshift soap making operations all over.

The coloured plastic buckets full of either soda or water are everywhere.

Against the backdrop of the rainy season’s persistent gloom, the containers symbolise a measure of cleanliness for families sheltering from torrential downpours under mouldy concrete awnings.

As the Telegraph watches Yabom Kapro, a village elder, making soap, the risks involved are immediately obvious.

Chief Yabom Kapro makes soap at her Waterloo town home, near Freetown Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

As she tips a purple bucket of caustic soda solution into a large basin and then adds palm oil from a plastic jerrycan, local children hover round the cluster of colourful containers.

Yabom uses a wooden paddle to stir the mixture into a creamy paste and then pours it into a mould held in place by an old motorcycle tyre.

Buckets containing caustic soda dissolving, top. Caustic soda crystals, below Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Once set, the beige-coloured cake of soap is cut into blocks which are then grated on a wire mesh contraption to be sold at the local market.

“When you dilute the caustic soda, it is completely clear like water at first,” says another soap maker, 43-year-old Cilina Bangura.

“Afterwards a white scum forms on the top, but you cannot be watching all of the time, [even] with all of these children around.”

Cilina knows the risks but says she can't afford to stop making soap. It has, as the NGOs intended, become an economic lifeline for her and her family.

“I want my children to continue making soap when I stop working,” she says. “I took out a loan to buy everything I needed, and now it is the only way I can make a living.

“Of course, I know how dangerous soda is – it has burned my skin many times – but I don’t have another option.”

Home-made soap, in Waterloo Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Maimunatu Sankoh, three, whose family lives in a nearby tin-roof shack, is sadly too well aware of that danger from her own bitter experience of soda poisoning.

As she feeds her daughter through a stomach tube, Maimunatu’s mum Iyesatu complains: “I have never seen any public information about soda.

“There are warnings on the packets but that is no use once the product is dissolved in water. They need to tell people to keep buckets out of the way.”

Iyesatu Kamara feeds her daughter Maimunatu Sankoh at their home Credit : SImon Townsley

Incidents of children consuming harmful chemicals are not confined to developing countries and were once common in the west.

In the US, the Poison Prevention Packaging Act was introduced in 1970, mandating childproof containers and the labelling of harmful household products.

The UK followed suit in 1975 with the introduction of child-resistant safety caps on containers of caustic soda and most other noxious household substances.

Despite the risks, Cilina says she can't afford to stop making soap Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Such legislation is still a long way off in Sierra Leone and is anyway far too late for four-year-old Amza.

Under heavy sedation in the intensive care unit, his glazed eyes open only occasionally.

The only visible evidence of his injuries is some scarring on his lips, but the doctors say his throat, oesophagus and stomach have all been seared by several large gulps of soda.

The boy’s mother, Mamie Kebbie, 30, keeps a watchful vigil, stroking his listless head tenderly. She says he used to be a playful and vivacious child.

If they are taken to hospital quickly, children with soda burns are normally given an oesophageal dilation endoscopy – a procedure which aims to keep the oesophagus open – but for Amza this has not been possible.

Freetown, Sierra Leone Credit : Simon Townsley

“This is a very severe case,” explains nurse Annette Turay, who heads the hospital’s intensive care unit. “When he was brought in, about 10 hours after he had ingested the soda, we were unable to conduct an endoscopy because he already had respiratory problems.

“He has pneumonia and he cannot feed through his mouth. He cannot even swallow his own saliva.

Mamie Kebbie keeps a vigil at her son's bedside Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“It will be a week before he is strong enough for us to be able to operate. We will insert a gastric tube into his stomach. He will have to keep this as his main way of being fed for a long time, potentially forever.”

But nurse Turay has seen worse.

“I have seen so many children suffering a lot after ingesting soda, so many dying too.

“A few weeks ago, we had a child in the ward who died because his stomach was completely gone”.

The Telegraph contacted all the NGOs involved in the setting up of and promotion of soap making schemes in Sierra Leone that are mentioned in this story for comment.
