The siege of Taiz — a strategic gateway to southern Yemen — isn't only constricting water supplies. Shortages of groceries have sent food prices soaring. Fuel is also in short supply, making it difficult to maintain basic services such as hospitals and sanitation, which compounds the public health risks.

Amnesty International has called on the Houthis to immediately open roads into the city, saying Taiz is being pushed to "the brink of a severe humanitarian disaster."

Houthis strangle Taiz, cut off residents' access to wells

Yemen descended into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis seized much of the country's north, including the capital of Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognized government into exile. Taiz has been a focal point of fighting ever since.

War-related damage to Taiz's aging water infrastructure magnified the pressures of population growth and frequent droughts that led to shrinking supplies of groundwater. Residents began paying for water delivered by trucks, a mostly reliable alternative — until recently.

Sponsor Message

By August, Yemen had become a widening front in the Iran war. The Houthis ramped up their advance on Taiz last month, after a lightning-fast capture of the port city of Mokha, an area about 130 kilometers (80 miles) away that is vital to controlling shipping through the Red Sea.

As Houthi forces took control of more land and roads surrounding Taiz, residents' access to nearby wells was cut off and deliveries of water from outside the city declined.

The truckers that have managed to ferry water into Taiz have in some cases tripled their rates to make the perilous journey.

As Taiz's fuel supplies dwindle, its water utility is struggling to maintain limited operations and desalination plants are running well below capacity.

The city is also enduring shortages of fuel and food

Since August, Taiz province, which includes the city and surrounding areas, has taken in roughly half of those displaced from other parts of Yemen because of the fighting — an estimated 124,000 people, according to the United Nations' migration experts. That is only compounding the pressure on Taiz's limited supply of water and other necessities.

Some displaced families are now living in makeshift shelters or tents and surviving on one meal a day, said Jens Laerke, a spokesperson for a division of the United Nations that focuses on emergency aid.

Fuel for cooking and transportation has also become scarce — and more expensive. The price of cooking gas has more than quadrupled, according to Hani Bafaqih, a water, sanitation and hygiene expert at the aid organization CARE in Yemen. To get by, some families are cooking over fires made by burning wood, charcoal or cardboard.

These fuel shortages have made it harder for community kitchens to provide free hot meals to families and have also forced waste-collection services to shut down.

"The shortages feed into each other. Without fuel, water pumps, hospital generators and solid-waste collection stop. With less clean water and waste piling up, the risk of disease, including cholera, rises," Laerke said. The health risks are exacerbated by thirsty families tapping into unprotected wells that could be contaminated with waterborne diseases, he said.

Sponsor Message

Food prices are also soaring. Flour and rice are about 50% more expensive than they were over the summer, according to aid groups, and fruits and vegetables are hard to find.

Ahmed Abdel Gaber is living with nine other family members in the ruins of another building after being displaced from their home by the fighting. He used to earn money hauling construction material, but that income is no longer steady and his family is barely scraping by.

"We heavily rely on assistance and donations from people to get food," he said in a phone interview.

Al-Shahid, a hair salon owner, said her income also dried up a few weeks ago. The salon was forced to close as former customers began to prioritize their spending on food and water. Her 10-year-old daughter and 5-year-old son now eat mostly rice, bread and cheese, she said.

Why Taiz matters to the Houthis

While the Yemeni government still controls the center of Taiz, the siege is making it difficult to deliver supplies to its forces there. In the hills surrounding Taiz, the government forces are trying to repel the Houthis but face stiff resistance, especially east of the city.

Gaining control of Taiz city is vital to the Houthis if they seek to advance south toward Aden and Lahj, analysts say, but that won't be easy.

"Any Houthi attempt to seize parts of the city, let alone take it entirely, would likely require a prolonged and costly battle, with significant casualties among Houthi fighters," said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.

Three Houthi officials said the rebel group controls roughly 80% of the countryside surrounding Taiz and several key neighborhoods inside the city. The Associated Press couldn't independently verify the claims by these officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to brief the media, but Yemen's foreign minister, Afrah al-Zouba, has acknowledged the rebel group's tightening grip on the city.

Sponsor Message

The Houthis' fight for control of the city is made significantly more difficult because of its large civilian population, the officials said.

Earlier this week, missiles fired by the Houthis struck a residential area in Taiz, killing two teenage girls and renewing attention on the dangers faced by civilians.

Abdel Gaber said he can hear loud explosions every day from fighting that is happening roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) away. The family isn't returning to their home in a mountain village out of concern for their safety.

Leaving Taiz is not an option for al-Shahid because the costs of travel and renting a home in another province are prohibitive.

"Staying in our home is inevitable — whether it be a matter of life or death," al-Shahid said.

World.title: Flooding in Four Corners region displaces residents, as storms move southeast
World.content:
Flooding in Four Corners region displaces residents, as storms move southeast

toggle caption i Aaron Schenk/Aaron Schenk

On Thursday morning in Hurricane, Utah, Juana Puga stood in ankle-deep brownish water asking herself: "Why again?"

Just a couple hours earlier, at around 8:30am, Puga went out to run some errands. It wasn't raining outside, she says. But when she returned to her house, rainwater had flooded her whole yard.

"It was just coming in so fast that it was just hard to even understand," Puga says. "Within five minutes most of my house was underwater."

Rare, heavy rainfall started to hit New Mexico, Colorado, Utah and Arizona on Wednesday. Since then, brown-colored floodwaters have led to road closures, mandatory evacuations and emergency declarations across the four states. The southern Utah city of Hurricane issued an emergency declaration on Thursday after flooding damaged more than 100 homes and RVs.

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i Juana Puga/Juana Puga

Puga, her husband, and five young boys just moved back into their house on Oct. 1. A flood in August forced them to renovate and rebuild. Less than a month after her sons fixed up their new rooms, Puga says she's living through a "nightmare" again.

"We were literally in our house for only 22 days," she says. The family is staying with Puga's in-laws in one room, but are hoping to move to a rental next week.

"It's just devastating," Puga says. "So much work we put into our house and I just thought, 'why again?' "

In response to a post on X that showed brownish-red floodwaters in Hurricane, Gov. Spencer Cox, wrote on Thursday: "Our hearts are with the families whose homes and livelihoods have been impacted."

toggle caption i Juana Puga/Juana Puga

Thick, brown floodwaters

Over the weekend, the flood watch extended to central and southern New Mexico and far west Texas.

As of Saturday, areas of southern Utah, southwest Colorado, and the northern parts of Arizona and New Mexico had been hit the hardest. The intense rain led to rapidly rising floodwaters, Thursday and Friday.

In San Juan County, N.M., looking out a window on Friday afternoon, Devin Neeley saw light, puffy clouds and a blue sky. The county's public information officer for emergency management called the stark contrast to the brown rainwaters "surreal."

"[The sky] belies really the danger that is coming down the river in historic levels," Neeley says. "We have not seen flooding like this in generations."

Neeley says emergency responders rescued people on their roofs after floodwater inundated their homes. The county was put under an emergency declaration and residents in susceptible areas were told to evacuate Thursday afternoon.

"These are communities that have beautiful riverfront places to live," Neeley says. "And unfortunately, that's a problem today."

In Farmington, N.M., located in the center of the hard-hit regions, Police Chief Steve Hebbe said at a press conference on Friday that "this is singular and this is real."

"So far, we have not had any deaths that is very fortunate, but this is not something that should be played with," Hebbe said.

Sponsor Message

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis declared disaster emergencies in 12 counties. Polis also authorized the use of National Guard members to assist with rescue efforts in southwest Colorado.

toggle caption i South Fork Fire Rescue/AP

On Friday morning, La Plata County sheriff closed parts of the Animas River in Durango, Colo. to recreation, KSUT reported.

Aaron Schenk took out a 14-foot cataraft to glide down 26 miles of the Animas River that weren't closed.

"There were real big waves, fast currents, lots of water flooding," Schenk says. "The river in spots was half a mile wide when normally it's a couple hundred feet at most."

Schenk, who owns a sewage disposal company called Mountain Septic, expects to see an uptick in repairs across La Plata County.

"This is definitely not normal," he says, adding that the region has "received more moisture in the last, 6 or 8 weeks than we have in the entire 12 months prior."

The flooding comes after extreme weather hit the Southwest throughout the week. Arizona saw baseball-sized hail and a possible tornado that injured at least one person Wednesday evening.

A record amount of rainfall

The region's mountainous and desert terrain is conducive to flooding. In August, intense flash flooding in the Grand Canyon led to multiple deaths.

Severe thunderstorm warnings started earlier in the week, says Kris Sanders, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Grand Junction, Colo. The remnants of Hurricane Trudy, which was active from Oct. 15 to Oct. 18, in the Pacific Ocean formed into a slow-moving low-pressure system that worked its way southwest.

Sanders says a lot of the storms weakened as they came through the region, but the heavy rain did not. Portions of southwest Colorado and southeast Utah saw two to four inches, whereas areas with higher elevations, like the San Juan Mountains, got up to six inches. This caused small creeks and streams and rivers to flood.

Sponsor Message

"Those rainfall amounts are records in themselves," Sanders says.

While the amount of rainfall is rare, he says, these storms typically happen in the region at this time of year. An event last year caused major flooding in the same spots, "like a carbon copy" of this year, Sanders says.

The threat is not over, he says, and thunderstorm watches are active in many of the same areas through Sunday.

Daniel Swain, a climate scientist with the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, says the severe thunderstorms are fueled by the large amount of moisture in the air. He says that moisture comes from the record-warm waters off parts of the West Coast, which are driven by an ongoing strong El Niño event and a recent marine heat wave (which he attributes largely to human-caused climate change).

The flooding isn't a surprise, he says, pointing to a prediction he and others made in the spring – that if El Niño materialized according to forecasts, southwestern U.S. could see extreme precipitation events through October.

Now, "that is exactly what we've seen," he says, "because this isn't even the first event this fall."

Puga, whose home flooded in Hurricane, Utah, says she and her neighbors have been cleaning up their properties and are trying to "see the light." She doesn't want to move and leave the community she loves, she says.

"We already did this. We can do it again," Puga says. "But it's just hard."

World.title: Duelling petitions highlight rift over paroled murderer at McGill law school
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Students at McGill University's law faculty remain divided over the presence of a convicted murderer in the classroom, with a new counter-petition outlining why some students feel unsafe and don't want him in their presence.

The anonymous open letter, dated Oct. 19 and put forward by a group of students, accuses the university of failing in its duty to protect female students.

It outlines concerns about Jeffrey George Ewert, who was convicted of second-degree murder and attempted murder for attacks against two women in B.C. in 1984.

The authors argue that attempting to rehabilitate a convicted murderer without adequate safety frameworks goes against the university's core values and breaches its duty of care to the student body.

"McGill’s failure to do so unduly and disproportionately harms the young women of our community," the document reads.

The students want the university to form a committee that would include both students and experts on the rehabilitation of violent offenders in order to develop guidelines for next steps.

"Any decision to resume Ewert's in-person studies must be made only after the committee has developed this framework," the letter goes on to say.

The authors say they chose to withhold their names because signing the document raises safety concerns for them.

Earlier petition calls for Ewert's return to university

Ewert is serving a life sentence and was granted day parole in 2025.

He sexually assaulted and killed one woman and, less than six weeks later, beat and choked a 15-year-old so severely that she was paralyzed and disabled for life, according to a summary of his case in his parole board file.

While various clinical assessments ranked Ewert’s risk of reoffending as moderate to high, official parole documents say with close supervision at a halfway house and clinical follow-up, that risk “seems to fall more into the moderate risk category.” He has not been on campus since early October.

The letter follows an earlier petition arguing Ewert should be allowed to return to university.

That document argues the exclusion undermines Ewert's access to education and rehabilitation as an Indigenous man and a survivor of the Sixties Scoop.

Annica Dickens, one of the authors of the petition and a third-year law student, said she was troubled that Ewert was removed from campus without being given the chance to address the concerns first.

"People cannot meaningfully rebuild their lives if their opportunities can be withdrawn so readily," said Dickens in an email.

Meanwhile, a second letter supporting Ewert, addressed to the university's leadership, has been signed by hundreds of academics, students and citizens.

It reiterates many of the concerns raised by Dickens and asks that the university restore Ewert's full access to the Faculty of Law and "review how decisions concerning Indigenous, racialized and formerly incarcerated students are made."

Security of students 'paramount,' McGill says

McGill University did not provide an update on Ewert's status, or answer questions about allegations raised in the counter-petition.



A spokesperson told CBC News that the "safety and security of our students is paramount. Full stop."

Citing privacy laws, the university declined to comment on the specific case, but said "McGill would act quickly and decisively should concerning information be brought forward about a student’s background or behaviour on campus."

WATCH | A debate at McGill law: Convicted killer attending McGill law school divides students over safety, 2nd chances | Duration closed caption 5:35 A convicted murderer’s presence at McGill University's law school while on day parole has sparked debate over public safety and rehabilitation. Several students say they feel vulnerable and frustrated by a lack of transparency regarding Jeffrey George Ewert's violent past against women, while his lawyer and student supporters argue he deserves a second chance.

The controversy has sparked debate within the broader legal community in Canada.

In an op-ed in the Montreal Gazette, one lawyer wrote there is a "bitter irony in asking women entering a profession that demands confidence, advocacy and strength to share their education with a man whose own file describes a need to dominate and control women."

Lisa Kerr, an associate professor and director of the Criminal Law Group at Queen's University, cautioned that "we should be very hesitant about any measures that could result in the exclusion of people with criminal records from accessing education.

"Canada's incarcerated population is in desperate need of education and job training," she wrote in an email to CBC.

"We want people with criminal records and experiences of incarceration to access education and gain the skills for successful reintegration."

Lisa Kerr is an associate professor and director of the Criminal Law Group at Queen's University. (Queen's University)

CBC Montreal contacted other law faculties in the province, including Université de Sherbrooke, Université Laval, Université du Québec à Montréal and Université de Montréal, to ask what measures they have in place to manage or mitigate risks when admitting students with past violent criminal convictions.

All four universities said they are not permitted to ask applicants about their criminal history.

“This violates the Charter of Rights and Freedoms,” said Geneviève O’Meara, a spokesperson at Université de Montréal.

Simon La Terreur, a spokesperson at Université Laval, said the university does not intend "to take the place of the competent authorities in assessing the risk a person may pose for the purposes of parole, but the safety of our university community remains a priority nonetheless."

World.title: Toronto police seeking mother, 22, for allegedly abducting her 3 children
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Toronto police are seeking the public’s help in locating three missing children, allegedly abducted by their mother from the Midland Avenue and Eglinton Avenue East area.

Daniel, 6, Irina, 3, and four-month-old Anastasia were having a semi-supervised visit with a relative on Friday, when their mother took them and fled the premises, police said Saturday.

Their mother, Somerda Miclescu, 22, is believed to be driving a 2017 White Ford Expedition SUV with Ontario licence plate DJJS 875, according to police.

From left, Daniel, 6, Irina, 3, and four-month-old Anastasia were having a semi-supervised visit with a relative on Friday, when their mother took them and fled the premises, police say. (Toronto Police Service)

The mother does not have legal custody of the children and her location is unknown, police said.

Police described her as 5-7, around 180 pounds, with long, dark black hair. Police say she was last seen wearing a long black skirt and a dark-coloured top.

Police had first responded to a call on Friday at around 11:30 a.m. for an abduction in the Midland Avenue and Eglinton Avenue East area.

Ionut Stroe, 25, is also wanted as a person of interest for owning the vehicle Miclescu fled in.

Unrelated to the alleged abduction, police say Stroe is currently wanted for four counts of failing to comply with a release order.

Police described him as being around 5-11, 235 pounds, with a tattoo on his right forearm.

Ionut Stroe, 25, is also wanted by police as a person of interest for owning the vehicle Somerda Miclescu fled in. (Toronto Police Service)

No Amber Alerts are being issued at this point, according to Insp. Jeff Allington at a news conference Saturday.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police directly at 416-808-4100.

World.title: Tens of thousands march in France as protests continue over schools and living costs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Clashes erupted in Paris as a mass march drew to a close on Saturday, with more than 400,000 people rallying across France over school funding and soaring living costs in a fresh challenge to President Emmanuel Macron's government.

The Paris march began peacefully, a week after widespread rioting and looting during protests across the country. Near its end point at Porte de Vincennes, some protesters threw projectiles while police fired volleys of tear gas and used water cannons to disperse people.

The Interior Ministry put nationwide turnout at 410,000, while the CGT union estimated nearly 800,000. The ministry's estimate included 110,000 in Paris, where authorities had confined the march to the city's southeastern edge, away from the centre.

Elsewhere in France, police used tear gas in several other cities, including Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand and Strasbourg, as well as water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported. In Marseille, officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march's end point.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said police made nearly 1,000 arrests but added that the number is expected to increase significantly as more are counted.

Nuñez said beefed-up policing, with 70,000 officers backed by helicopters, armoured vehicles and other support, helped prevent a repeat of widespread looting and damage to shops that occurred during the previous weekend.

A police officer throws a tear gas canister during a demonstration against rising living costs in Rennes, France, on Saturday. (Jeremias Gonzalez/The Associated Press)

The unrest is shaking Macron's authority in the final months of his presidency before voters choose his successor in May. The stakes are high: the far-right National Rally has accused his government of failing to protect the public and urged people to channel their anger into votes.

In Paris, an Associated Press journalist saw tens of thousands of people marching from Porte d'Italie early in the afternoon, but it appeared to be a smaller crowd than a week earlier. Trade unions led the procession, followed by protesters in raincoats carrying flags and handmade placards.

More than half a million people took to the streets last Saturday. Around 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted over that weekend amid street violence not seen in years.

Museums closed, shopkeepers worried

Gendarmes stood guard beneath the Arc de Triomphe as shopkeepers boarded up storefronts across Paris on Saturday. Near the Saint-Lazare train station Saturday, Akram Ahmed, a 34-year-old contractor, was boarding up an optician's shop.

"I got the call last night," he said. "The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life."

Just Asking wants to know: What questions do you have about the wave of youth-led protests across Europe? Send us your questions before our Oct. 24 show

Major museums, including the Louvre, Musée d'Orsay, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais — where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display — were shuttered Saturday.

Art Basel, one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.

WATCH | Here's why student in France started protesting this month: Why thousands of high school students in France are protesting | Duration 1:43 Police fired tear gas and water cannons at protesters blockading French high schools — as students, teachers, parents and unions took to the streets against what they say is underfunding of the education system. Rights groups and students have accused authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government ‌has responded to the demonstrations with riot police and says the movement has been hijacked by outsiders and morphed into urban violence.

Following the unrest, Paris police prefect Patrice Faure urged Parisian shopkeepers to hire security guards. He later clarified that protecting business owners and their establishments is the responsibility of the government.

Some protests have been banned

Police changed the Paris protest route Friday. At Bastille, the original starting point, police used a megaphone to tell people to leave or face a 135 euro (around $210 Cdn) fine.

Soumaya Abed, a 58-year-old nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, said she had been joining protests for more than 30 years but had never seen a march start at Porte d'Italie.

"They are using what happened last week as an excuse to quiet protesters," she said. "But it won't stop the movement. It won't stop students from demanding better conditions in schools."

WATCH | Police used tear gas, water cannons during first round of protests: ‘It’s utter chaos': Protests in France evolve into anger over broader economy | Duration closed caption 2:21 Police in France used tear gas and arrested hundreds as widespread demonstrations over underfunding in schools evolved into scenes of anger and unrest over the cost of living.

A protest march was also scheduled in Marseille, but in cities including Nice and Montpellier, as well as Lyon, rallies were banned by the local authorities.

Thousands also marched Saturday in Orléans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as the National Rally held a two-day congress in the city.

Trade unions have criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.

Macron, a centrist, has entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.

Nuñez acknowledged Monday that police had lost control in some cities during last weekend's unrest. He offered to resign, but Macron refused the offer.

Students and workers are angry

Student groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system. Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.

They are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros (around $310) a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.

High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods. Some also called for a reform of the university admissions system, seen by many as unfair.

With the government seemingly unable to respond to students' demands, the movement has morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, just months before the vote to choose Macron's successor.

"The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people," said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University. "And it's not possible anymore."

Macron met high school representatives Friday. They said he had promised to overhaul university admissions, but they called for protests to continue until concrete measures are announced.

Organizers from the "yellow vest" protest movement called for another day of rallies Oct. 31 to defend the right to demonstrate.

WATCH | France deployed riot police as students marched: Students in France clash with riot police amid weekslong education protests | Duration closed caption 3:26 Teachers formed a line to shield students from police in Paris, as countrywide protests over education reform have reached their fourth week.

Other protests rock major European cities

While protests in France have claimed most international attention, large demonstrations are also rocking many European cities Saturday from Madrid to Milan, Lisbon and Tirana, Albania.

The protests encompass a broad range of issues from pensions and housing to anti-war movements, education and corruption.

People march through the streets of Milan on Saturday to protest against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services during one of several protests in Italy organized by groups across the political spectrum. (Antonio Calanni/The Associated Press)

In Milan, luxury boutiques were boarded up in the Italian fashion and finance capital as protesters launched fresh demonstrations on Saturday, one week after looting and clashes with police.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters last week.

Security was also heightened in Rome, where authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up controls around the Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo.

A separate anti-war march took off in central Rome, and there are concerns over possible infiltration by violent groups.

Organizers sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and hands visible.

Aside from Rome and Milan, demonstrations have been called in at least seven other cities. The newly formed "Oct. 17 Movement" has been the main driver alongside student federations, grassroots trade unions, and anti-war coalitions.

In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police used water cannons on large groups of protesters, some of whom threw projectiles at police. Authorities said 2,500 police officers are patrolling the streets Saturday.

World.title: Can millions of people live on the moon? These scientists say yes — but not for very long
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Humans have long dreamed about reaching out and exploring space. Most science fiction, more often than not, portrays cities on the dusty lunar surface and Mars.

And if you listen to some billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, cities on the moon are coming soon.

In fact, in February, SpaceX CEO Musk posted on social media that the company was shifting its focus away from settling on Mars — something Musk has been passionate about for the past decade.

“For those unaware, SpaceX has already shifted focus to building a self-growing city on the moon, as we can potentially achieve that in less than 10 years, whereas Mars would take 20+ years,” he wrote.

For those unaware, SpaceX has already shifted focus to building a self-growing city on the Moon, as we can potentially achieve that in less than 10 years, whereas Mars would take 20+ years. The mission of SpaceX remains the same: extend consciousness and life as we know it to the stars. It is only possible to travel to Mars when the planets align every 26 months (six month trip time), whereas we can launch to the Moon every 10 days (2 day trip time). This means we can iterate much faster to complete a Moon city than a Mars city. That said, SpaceX will also strive to build a Mars city and begin doing so in about 5 to 7 years, but the overriding priority is securing the future of civilization and the Moon is faster. —elonmusk

This statement — and those of Blue Origin CEO Bezos, who has claimed “millions of people” will be living in space by 2045 — intrigued Martin Elvis, senior astrophysicist at Harvard University’s Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory.

He, along with astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell, honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre in England, decided to take a look at the numbers.

But their findings, it turns out, aren't great for a lunar civilization, so don’t start packing just yet.

In their paper , published in the journal Frontiers in Space Technologies, the pair decided to examine power and water needed to sustain humans on the moon.

When it comes to power, they found that solar and nuclear would be enough to sustain one million people on the lunar surface.

But then there's water.

It may be surprising to some, but there is water on the moon. It’s believed that most of it is contained in permanently shadowed regions (PSR), areas at the poles that never see sunlight.

But in this study, they found that there’s not enough on the moon to sustain a large human presence on the lunar surface.

WATCH | NASA shares plans for Moon Base: NASA shares plans for moon base | Duration closed caption 2:04 NASA has outlined its plans to build a base on the moon that will first be occupied by rovers and drones, but the longer-term goal is human habitation.

“Our work shows that, yeah, if you want to have an Antarctic base on the moon for the next few hundred years, no problem. If you want to have a small town, that's doable. If you want to cover the face of the moon with cities, like in the best science fiction, then you have to find a way to get the water there, because it's not there right now,” McDowell said.

Assuming that there is roughly one billion tonnes of water on the moon, which is in line with current estimates, they found that a civilization of one million people would only be able to live on the moon for roughly 100 years. And that’s only if we can recycle 98 per cent of the water, which is what is done on the International Space Station.

'A small lake'

Elvis said that while one billion tonnes of water sounds like a lot, you have to put it in perspective.

“If you had a huge aquarium the size of Central Park in Manhattan, you could fill it up to where the Statue of Liberty was just underwater and that's the amount of water you've got. So it's huge in one way, but … it's a small lake. And a small lake is not going to supply a big city for very long.”

That’s not to say that humans can’t ever live on the moon. If it were a town of 10,000, they found that would be sustainable for centuries.

However, that's assuming that the one billion tonnes of water is an accurate estimate.

"Very likely a billion is way overestimating. It's probably 20 or 30 times too big," Elvis said.

WATCH | How Artemis II is setting up the next stage of space exploration: How Artemis II is setting up the next stage of space exploration | Duration closed caption 4:42 Jacob Bleacher, NASA's chief exploration scientist, says the first two Artemis missions have set the stage for the next moon landing, a moon base and eventually, human exploration of Mars, missions so challenging that only international co-operation makes them possible.

He also said that it's unlikely that we'd be able to recover all the water that's available. Instead, it would be more like one-third to half of what is present.

"So my best guess is the real amount of water available that we can be fairly confident about is one per cent of what we said before. So instead of 100 years, it's one year."

And there's one other thing: We don't know in what form that water exists. And we need to figure that out.

"It's one thing to detect it from satellites, but ... there are uncertainties in those measurements," said Gordon Osinski, a professor in planetary geology at Western University in London, Ont.

" I think it is there, but let's go and ground-truth that and confirm it. And then there's the bigger unknowns of what form it's in…. Is it more like the permafrost up in the Arctic, where it's basically soil with, you know, sub-millimetre size ice crystals, which are hard to get out of?"

While this may sound like pessimistic news for humanity's plans to explore the cosmos, McDowell said it's best to know what you're dealing with.

"The truth is never negative," he said. "What's negative is to actually go and try and do something that isn't going to work."

World.title: Q&A: Premier Danielle Smith says she doesn’t need Alberta separatists’ support
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says the matter of separatism is settled within her party and she doesn’t need the support of those who want the province to leave Canada.

Smith says she told members of her United Conservative Party on Wednesday that they should support the will of the majority of Albertans who have voted to stay in Canada, or leave the party.

But some prominent separatists like Mitch Slyvestre, the president of the UCP's Bonnyville-Cold Lake-St. Paul constituency association, have long argued that they helped oust former premier Jason Kenney and get Smith in as leader of the UCP.

CBC Radio’s West of Centre host Kathleen Petty interviewed the premier on Friday.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Jared Wesley from the University of Alberta had observed “a referendum does not just reveal your strength — it can also reveal your weakness.” Did it here?

It showed to me that certainly on the constitutional questions, there just is not the appetite to pursue it. And I think there's a couple of reasons for that.

On constitutional change, I think people are still a little fatigued from all of the different realms that were unsuccessful in previous years. So I think it's a question of how much success we could have on them. But they're also not top of mind for people.

I think what we saw is the immigration questions are certainly more important than the other ones. And so those will be the ones we'll prioritize.

But not hugely more important, because that number is still pretty skinny. So what guidance do you believe that's giving you for the legislation that you're planning for this spring?

Well, it seems to me people are very enthusiastic about the idea of having to show citizenship in order to be able to vote. So I think people need to be prepared that that is very likely going to be the first thing that we act on with enabling legislation. And our next provincial election is next October.

We're making it as easy as possible because we now have a citizenship marker on your driver's licence. So you can go through and get all of that process done. So you can just have one piece of ID.

Hear full referendum debrief with Danielle Smith here:

When it comes to waiting periods for temporary workers or what the fees might be to access some of the programs, we're going to have to take a bit more time with that.

But I think we can solve a lot of the problems by focusing our newcomer population on the jobs that are available. Because when somebody comes with a high-paying job, they probably don't need to rely on social services. And when somebody makes a commitment to being a permanent taxpayer as a permanent resident, they'll get the same programs as everyone else.

So if we can fix that part, then I think it will reduce some of the stress on our health care and education and other systems.

Question 10, you say it’s settled — 75 per cent of Albertans said we want to stay in Canada. It seems it isn't settled in your party though. So how do you deal with that?

Well, it is settled in my party.

How’s it settled?

I am the leader not only of government but also of my party. I'm the chief communicator for our party, and I have said that anyone who wants to run as a candidate for us, anyone who wants to be on our provincial board, has to align with what Albertans told us.

If you're going to be in a political party and show faithfully that you're going to represent the people, then you have to listen to the message they gave you and the message that Albertans gave us — 75 per cent — that they're proud Canadians and want to stay a part of Canada.

So how will you enforce it?

Right now, I am allowing people some time to reflect on what democracy means.

And when they’re finished reflecting?

If you don't want to agree to follow the will of the people, you don't have to be a candidate for us. Don't put your name forward. You don't have to run for our provincial board.

And if they do, you don't sign their nomination papers?

Well, I guess we'll see whether or not people will rise to the occasion. I think most people do.

Most people. But I'm curious about what you do with the people who don't.

They have lots of options to continue. They can be in advocacy groups. They can set up podcasts. They can continue to be involved in other political parties.

But in our political party, we respect democracy and we respect Albertans. If you had candidates running for you who said, “You know what, vote for me and I may or may not do what you ask me to do,” it's not a very strong selling feature. I think for us to have the credibility with Albertans, that we're going to listen to them and faithfully implement what they ask us to do, we have to sign that pledge.

UCP MLA Jason Stephan announced that he would not be running for re-election. Had you told him you would not sign his nomination papers, given that he publicly said he was voting for Option 2, which is to have another referendum?

He made his own decision. He had told me last year that he wasn't sure whether or not he was going to run again, and he wanted to take some time to reflect on that. And so he obviously did that over the course of the last week or so, and he made the decision not to run again.

So you didn't influence that decision by saying anything?

He announced that, I believe, before the results came in. So he had made that decision.

I'm curious how you feel about how separatists will continue with their advocacy, because they argue you won the leadership and the election, in part because of them. Can you keep your leadership and election without them?

[Laughs] Well, that's not who was supporting me.

The people who were supporting me were the ones who were really concerned about the COVID response. The people who were supporting me were the ones who were concerned about some of the DEI ideology that was in classrooms. They were the ones who were concerned about young children being transgender … behind their parents’ backs. Those are the people who voted for me.

This new movement is actually brand new. I mean, some of the leaders of it just woke up one day in April of last year and decided to join the separatist movement.

But some of them you had relationships with. It’s not like you didn’t know them, like Mitch Sylvestre and David Parker.

But to be clear, you run your campaign on areas of common interest and common policies, and the areas of common interest and common policies were the ones I described — but also talking about autonomy within Canada.

Our position as a party and my position in running was: let's try to make Canada work by getting Canada to focus on its areas of jurisdiction so we can focus on ours. That's always been my pitch. Others think that there's another way, but that's not been my position.

World.title: 82 days later, no repairs started on washed-out road dividing small Quebec town
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Mayor Jacques Allard stands in front of the 70-foot gap that now divides his town of L’Ascension.

Spray painted white lines on the ground track the ongoing erosion that continues with every rainfall.

It's been 82 days since heavy rain washed away parts of Principale Street and de L’Ascension Road that connects the small municipality to the city of Rivière-Rouge on Aug. 3.

The mayor says on its end, L’Ascension is ready to start work to repair the road.

They have their contractor, the engineer plans are in place and the replacement culvert — twice the diameter of the previous one — is sitting idly by the protective fencing that surrounds the giant crater.

So what's the delay?

The municipality says it's waiting for the green light from the Quebec government to begin the repair, which their contractor expects to take five weeks and cost roughly $3 million.

A report of the required work also had to be sent to Fisheries and Oceans Canada for approval — a report that took 70 days to be approved and was then sent to the government.

The washout is directly in front of the fire hall, impacting emergency services. (Andie Bennett/CBC)

L’Ascension is now awaiting confirmation that they will receive the subsidy from the program that provides financial support to municipalities affected by natural disasters.

Allard says the bureaucracy slowing down this work is unacceptable.

“Normally they have a protocol to fast track. Now it is a very slow track," he said.

300 people cut off

The crater left behind by the rushing water that ripped up sections of asphalt and collapsed culverts is 45 feet deep and 70 feet wide.

Thirty per cent of the small population lives on the other side of the gap, meaning around 300 people are cut off from their community.

Nicolas Côté owns a small grocery store in town. He says business is already down 15 per cent compared to last year due to its inaccessibility.

Residents on the other side of the gap must either take their business to the nearby town of Rivière-Rouge or make a detour of more than an hour to reach their local grocery store.

The gap is 45 feet deep and 70 feet wide and sits where the road used to connect in L’Ascension. (Andie Bennett/CBC)

Côté says when you live in a small town where the population is just shy of 1,000 people, it's more like a family.

He says many people have sent him messages saying they hope the repairs happen soon so they will see him again and be able to shop at their local store.

“Maybe it's tough to fix, but to wait so much time … and we still don't know what will happen," Côté said.

The local grocery store in L’Ascension has already seen a 15 per cent drop in business compared to last year due to the lack of access for residents. (Andie Bennett/CBC)

With winter coming, Allard says there is a lot of anxiety within the community. He is also concerned about the financial impact if the repairs are not completed as soon as possible.

“On the other side, it takes five minutes to get here. Now it's 50 minutes. How will we pay to remove the snow in the winter? The trucks will have to make this detour. We will have a big expense for fuel," he said.

CBC News reached out to the Domestic Security Ministry for comment. It said it is currently reviewing the file and will confirm, as soon as possible, whether the work is eligible for financial assistance.

World.title: Why a new round in the U.S.-Iran conflict could be the most devastating yet
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The warning signs are flashing red with indications that once the ballots are counted in the U.S. midterm elections, the United States and Israel will relaunch their war with Iran.

The next round of attacks could be more devastating than the first, warn analysts.

"A renewed war seems almost inevitable," said Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli Middle East and Iran analyst whose earlier warnings and cautions about the risks of a direct conflict with Iran were largely borne out by events.

Citrinowicz, who worked for Israel's military as an intelligence official for more than two decades, had initially warned that any U.S. and Israeli attack on the Islamic regime would not likely lead to regime change but would instead end up engulfing the entire region in a wider conflict — an assessment that proved true.

In an interview with CBC News, he said that assessment still holds.

"The problem is there is no silver bullet solution to the impasse we are now at in the Persian Gulf and in front of Trump he has only bad and worse options."

Under U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, their countries broke with decades of restraint and shadow warfare and launched two distinct wars with Iran over the past 18 months.

Iranian women look at a building, which was damaged in a U.S. and Israeli strike in March, in Tehran on Aug. 22. (Reuters)

The first in June 2025 began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, lasted 12 days and ended with a fragile ceasefire.

The conflict roared back to life in February of this year following a massive U.S. military buildup in the region. It began with Israel's strikes against Iran's senior leadership, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Worst round yet

Citrinowicz, who's with Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, said a third round of war could be the worst yet, based on what Iranian officials are telegraphing.

"They will attack the energy facilities in the Gulf. But more than that, they will cause significant damage to civilian infrastructure, communications, as well as cutting off the internet lines going under [the] Hormuz Strait," he said.

He said there is even a possibility that Iran could push some of its massive land army into the fight with limited assaults against Gulf countries that house U.S. bases, such as Kuwait and Bahrain.

"We'll see a regional war with Iran investing a lot in attacking the U.S. presence in the region to cause maximum economical damage to the U.S. international economy."

Smoke rises from a burning vessel, following what the U.S. Central Command said was a strike on an Iranian-affiliated dhow, at a location given as the Gulf of Oman, in this still image taken from a video released on Oct. 14. (U.S. Central Command/Reuters)

Midterm dynamics

While both sides have largely avoided fresh strikes against each other's bases or territory since the summer truce collapsed, the conflict remains active. The U.S. imposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports and Iran has continued to target commercial shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, driving up global energy costs.

Posting on Truth Social Thursday, Trump blamed Iran for trying to artificially drive up oil prices ahead of the midterms on Nov. 3, elections that many pollsters believe will see Trump's Republicans lose control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate as well.

"They are even making up fake hits, mines and everything else," said Trump, implying that Iran is exaggerating the extent of the damage it's causing.

A report published this week by the Washington, D.C.,-based Critical Threats Project alongside the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) also suggested Iran is trying to use strikes on shipping to weaken Trump's position heading into the elections.

"The increase in Iranian attacks on vessels is part of the ongoing Iranian campaign to pressure the United States to meet Iranian demands, including control over the Strait, by driving up global prices," the report said.

People walk on the beach, with vessels in the Strait of Hormuz visible near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Oct. 13. (Razieh Poudat West Asia News Agency/Reuters)

Iran's demands

Iran's government wants relief from punishing sanctions, reparations for the damage caused by earlier U.S.-Israel strikes, the release of billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets and the right to keep its supplies of enriched uranium.

Mediators with Pakistan and Qatar have spent weeks trying to push diplomatic solutions to get the two sides talking again, but to no avail.

For both Netanyahu and Trump, the war with Iran remains unfinished business.

The Islamic regime not only remains in power, but its leadership has also proven remarkably adept at adapting to both the military strikes and the economic blockade imposed by the West.

"The war in some respects has probably persuaded Iran's leadership to double down on their commitment to the revolutionary ideology that has really forged this regime," said Suzanne Maloney, a vice-president and director of the foreign policy program at the Washington, D.C.,-based Brookings Institution.

Like Citroniwicz, she said if war resumes, Trump won't be able to easily contain it.

"The retaliation as we've seen will come not just from Iran, but from its proxies and partners in the region," she said, referring to the Houthi militias in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon.

Iran's goal won't just be to hit back at U.S. military targets but also soft economic targets, such as airports, that could undermine Gulf countries for years to come, she said.

WATCH | How one conflict plays into another: How the Houthi-Saudi Arabia conflict plays into broader Middle East war | Duration closed caption 8:02 Saudi Arabia has recently been rocked by attacks from Yemen's Houthi rebels. The weekend strikes came in response to Saudi's own ongoing attacks on Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen, which resumed in July amid the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran. Analyst Sina Toossi explains how the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis plays into the broader war in West Asia.

Maloney and Karim Sadjadpour, a prominent Iran expert with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, were speaking on an online Carnegie panel about the future of the war in Iran.

"I genuinely don't think that President Trump has a clear idea in his head what he's trying to achieve," said Sadjadpour.

"I don't see any possibility of what Trump is looking for — which is like a knockout punch, a military strike — which will essentially force the Iranians into a compromise or capitulation."

Nuclear timeline?

Trump claimed his justification for the initial attacks on Iran was to ensure the country doesn't get a nuclear weapon.

At the time, while Iran possessed enough enriched uranium to theoretically pursue a weapon, many independent experts and U.S. intelligence sources believed it was still likely months away from doing so — and perhaps more importantly, that the regime's supreme leader had not yet made the definitive political decision to cross the nuclear threshold.

Since those initial June 2025 strikes, the human cost of the war has been severe.

Western NGOs claim the death toll in Iran is well over 7,000, including civilians and government figures who have been killed in the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes.

Lebanon has also suffered an especially heavy toll, with local media reporting more than 4,000 fatalities.

Twenty-one U.S. service members were killed, mostly by Iranian strikes on U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf, while more than 70 Israelis have died.

People drive near a billboard depicting U.S. President Donald Trump on a building in Tehran on Sept. 16. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA/Reuters)

There have also been deaths throughout the Gulf countries, including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, as well as in Iraq and Yemen.

The New York Times and other U.S. media are reporting the Pentagon is working on a new battle plan for the possible next round of attacks — but whether Trump will ultimately authorize it is unknown.

'Finishing the job'

Israel's leadership, on the other hand, has made no secret of its push to restart the conflict, with Netanyahu explicitly stating his desire to bring down the Iran regime by "finishing the job."

Netanyahu faces Israeli voters in the coming days, and whether he hangs onto his job could end up in a photo finish.

Relaunching the war with Iran could offer him a tactical way to stay in power; even if his party loses seats, a widening security crisis could lead to the creation of an emergency unity government with members of the opposition, said Citrinowicz.

"The real risk is that Netanyahu will involve his political considerations together with some other operational development in Iran that he is going to not necessarily invent, but probably [inflate]," he said.

A shopkeeper works at his shop in a local market in Tehran on Sept. 26. (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency/Reuters)

"And this combination will lead to an unnecessary attack against Iran."

Sadjadpour from the Carnegie panel said there is no obvious military way out of the impasse and says Trump's maximalist goals have closed down diplomatic options as well.

"I believe there's a pretty clear formula under which it [Iran's government] compromises," said Sadjadpour. "It's when it faces what I would describe as existential economic pressure, coupled with a clear, limited diplomatic exit.

"If you're asking them to change their identity, that's not going to succeed."

World.title: Black Sea sailors thought a rescue boat was racing toward them. Instead, it was a drone that sank their ship
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the early hours of Oct. 13, the crew from the HS Dignity gathered on the deck of the cargo ship and put on life jackets as the vessel rocked in the churning waves of the Black Sea. The captain had given the order to abandon the vessel because it was sinking after a sea drone struck its hull.

As the 16-man crew, made up of Syrian and Egyptian nationals, peered into the darkness, they spotted the outline of a boat moving quickly toward them. They shone their flashlights, thinking rescuers might have already responded to their distress call.

But what they saw alarmed them.

No one was driving the boat.

“We realized that this boat was also part of the group that was attacking us. Of course, we all ran,” said Ashraf Mamdouh, the vessel's 42-year-old chief officer.

The sea drone rammed directly into the ship.

“The vessel began sinking rapidly into the water. The whole crew was falling to the deck; nobody could stand properly because of the impact and the chaos,” he said.

“We didn't have time to finish launching the lifeboats.”

WATCH | How the dramatic rescue happened: Inside dramatic rescue as drones hit hundreds of ships in Black Sea | Duration closed caption 4:58 The Black Sea is a key shipping corridor in the escalating war between Russia and Ukraine. Maritime analysts believe there have been more than 500 attacks on commercial ships in the region in the past year, killing mariners and leading to dramatic rescues at sea. Briar Stewart and CBC’s visual investigations team take you inside a strike and speak with one of the survivors.

The Dignity is one of nearly 50 commercial vessels that maritime analysts say have been attacked in the Black Sea this month as the conflict between Russia and Ukraine escalates at sea.

The strikes have brought much of the traffic through the key shipping corridor to a halt and prompted NATO to step up maritime security , including by deploying more patrol boats and radar.

More than 30 killed or missing

At least 31 seafarers have been killed or are missing in the attacks.

Many of the vessels that were recently attacked were travelling through the western Black Sea, including some that were struck off the coasts of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania.

On Friday, a search-and-rescue operation was underway after a ship flagged to Comoros, a small archipelago off the coast of East Africa, was struck by drones just outside Romania's territorial waters.

The crew of 13 included Ukrainian and Azerbaijani sailors. One body has been recovered, while officials say three people remain missing.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan blamed Russia for the attacks.

Data shared with CBC News by maritime risk management firm Ambrey suggest there have been more than 500 attacks on commercial vessels this year in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, which are connected by the narrow Kerch Strait.

Of the 45 attacks recorded in October, Ambrey believes Russia was responsible for 40.

Russia's Ministry of Defence has acknowledged striking dozens of ships this month alone in social media posts, almost always claiming the vessels were supporting Ukraine's military.

But Mamdouh, who spoke to CBC News from a hotel in Varna, Bulgaria, said the Dignity had sailed from Algeria and was headed for Romania, where it was scheduled to pick up grain.

Ashraf Mamdouh, the chief officer aboard the HS Dignity, arrives in Varna, Bulgaria, on Oct. 13 after his ship sank when it was hit by two sea drones. (Nikolay Doychinov/AFP/Getty Images)

Adrift in the Black Sea

The Dignity had already been at sea for more than a month when the drones struck at about 1:30 a.m.

Mamdouh and other experienced crew members urged everyone aboard to get as far away from the ship as possible to avoid being pulled under as the 123-metre vessel sank beneath the churning waves.

“We tried to gather together to reduce everyone's fear and panic. We wanted to remain in one group so that, if a rescue team arrived, it would be easier for them to rescue as many people as possible,” Mamdouh said.

This undated image of the HS Dignity shows the ship before it sank in the Black Sea on Oct. 13. (Submitted by Ashraf Mamdouh)

He began calling out to other crew members, but the strong winds drowned out their voices.

“I started asking everyone, ‘Why are you moving away from each other?’ I hadn't realized that I was drifting away, too. The sea currents were separating us.”

At one point, a life raft suddenly appeared beside him. He climbed aboard and lay there for four hours, until another commercial vessel appeared nearby.

Still clutching his cellphone, he switched on its flashlight to attract the attention of the crew aboard the Azov Concord.

Cargo ships are seen in the Black Sea from Port Varna, in Varna, eastern Bulgaria on October 13. (Nikolay Doychinov/AFP/Getty Images)

18-year-old among the missing

Mamdouh was pulled from the water and is one of five crew members who survived. Eleven remain officially listed as missing, including 18-year-old Hamza Suleiman, a Syrian who was on his first voyage aboard a ship.

“The last phone call between Hamza and me was on the night of Oct. 12,” said his father, Basel, who spoke to CBC News via Zoom from Tartus, Syria.

“Hamza contacted us and said hi to his mother and reassured us. He said, ‘Dad, we're in Bulgaria now.’”

Basel said his son had taken the job aboard the Syrian-owned ship because he expected to work in the engine room, where he hoped to learn more about engineering.

Hamza Suleiman, 18, boarded the HS Dignity in August for his first job as a seafarer. He has been missing since the vessel sank on Oct. 13 off the coast of Bulgaria. (Submitted by Basel Suleiman)

But he became disillusioned when he was assigned to work on the deck. He grew increasingly fearful after learning that another vessel, the Alfa Watan, had been struck by drones on Oct. 6.

Ten crew members aboard that ship, most of them Syrian, have yet to be recovered.

After the Alfa Watan attack, Suleiman spoke with his son, who said he wanted to leave the vessel.

Basel Suleiman told CBC News he tried contacting the ship's owners to arrange for his son to disembark in Turkey, but the young man remained aboard.

Mamdouh, who spoke with Suleiman's father, told him that the last time he saw his son, the young man was aboard the ship wearing a life jacket. That detail has helped sustain his father's hope that he might still be alive.

Basel agreed to speak publicly about his son despite the uncertainty surrounding his fate.

“We don't have the ability to reach the [Bulgarian] authorities or to go and look for our children with our own hands,” he said.

Khaldoun Nabelsi, head of the Syrian Seafarers Association of the U.K., said he had been in contact with several families whose relatives had been killed in strikes on commercial vessels. He said he had counted at least 18 Syrian seafarers killed.

“Nobody is forced to take these jobs, but in other ways you are forced. If you want to work, you have to go,” Nabelsi said.

“They have to find a deal to stop this. But from our side, as a seaman or as a shipping company, we can do nothing.”

The deteriorating security situation has prompted the Philippine government to issue a directive prohibiting its citizens from boarding vessels navigating the northern stretches of the Black Sea.

In an image supplied by the Romanian government, the fire-damaged Royad Mammadov ship sits in the Black Sea on Oct. 5 after a suspected drone strike that killed two people. (Romanian Interior Ministry/Handout/Reuters)

Shipping companies scale back operations

Some shipping companies that normally operate in the region are avoiding it altogether or have sharply reduced the number of vessels they deploy there.

Turkey-based ED Shipping has a fleet of 26 vessels, but 19 are currently “laid up,” meaning they are temporarily out of service and not operating at sea, said the company's chief financial officer, Demre İşcen.

One of the company's ships, the Circon, was struck on June 5 while transiting the Sea of Azov. Two crew members were killed.

Ukraine carried out the attack, acknowledging that it had targeted five vessels that night, including ships stationed at occupied Ukrainian ports. Ukraine said the vessels were involved in transporting stolen Ukrainian grain, as well as military cargo and fuel .

İşcen disputes that account, saying the Circon was on its way to a port in the Sea of Azov near Rostov-on-Don, Russia, where he said the company had a contract to load Russian grain.

“Our crew members are Azeri and Turkish nationals. We didn't have anything to do with Ukraine. We didn't have anything to do with occupied-area grain … stolen grain, whatever,” he told CBC News in an interview from Istanbul.

“Ninety per cent of the time, we carry grain cargo from Russia to Turkey, Bulgaria, Romania, Moldova, Georgia, Greece, all around the Mediterranean, Aegean Sea, Red Sea, Black Sea. This is our main trading area.”

İşcen said the company was losing millions of dollars every month and that some of its seafarers were out of work because its ships were no longer travelling to Black Sea ports.

Other mariners say they will refuse any work in the region.

Mamdouh remains in Bulgaria with the other surviving members of the Dignity's crew. They are waiting for new documents so they can leave Europe and fly home.

“I will not go back to the Black Sea again. Never,” he said.

“This situation is too dangerous.”
