World.title: 'Eyes moving west': Sydney's new airport opens to passengers today
World.content:
Western Sydney International Airport (WSI) is officially open to passengers, with the new terminal being described as "a generational change to aviation".

The first commercial passenger flight from WSI departs for the Gold Coast at 11am.

Jetstar flight JQ362 is sold out and will be the first service from a major new Australian airport in more than 50 years, with JQ363 from the Gold Coast then landing back at WSI at 3pm.

The first departure to Melbourne then occurs at 6pm from WSI.

JQ362 will be the first service from a major new Australian airport in more than 50 years. (ABC News: Therese Banna)

Located 45 kilometres from Sydney's CBD and 18km from Penrith's city centre, the Badgerys Creek aviation hub is a 24/7 operation, unlike Sydney's Mascot terminals.

WSI officially opened for cargo operations back in July.

"We've been in the final sprint of the marathon, so the legs are feeling a bit wobbly, but we're really happy that we're here," WSI CEO Simon Hickey said.

" This is a massive milestone; this is a generational change to aviation. "

What the future holds for WSI

The new airport has been designed with growth front of mind. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

According to Mr Hickey, "eyes are moving west" when it comes to forward-planning for the future growth of Western Sydney and its new airport.

"We're designed for growth. We've built an airport terminal that is about the same size as Adelaide Airport, which is about 10 million annual passengers a year," he said.

"We're not going to start at 10 million passengers a year, but we're going to grow into that … [by] the early to mid 2030s, we'll start to get closer to that."

WSI projects it could reach its full 82 million passenger capacity per year by the 2060s. (Supplied: WSI)

Into the 2060s and with the addition of more terminals and another runway, WSI could reach its full 82 million passenger capacity per year.

In comparison, London's Heathrow Airport in 2025 welcomed over 84 million passengers.

"Destinations will continue to grow," Mr Hickey added.

"What I can say is that in just over 12 months from now … we'll have over 250 destinations that people can connect to … [it's] a magnificent start and we'll continue to go from there."

There are hopes further airlines will come on board as well.

Simon Hickey says he is happy that the commercial opening day has arrived. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

About 10,000 workers helped build WSI, with approximately half of that workforce from Western Sydney, Mr Hickey said.

"Up to 8,500 jobs will be required to support operations across the precinct by the time WSI reaches 10 million annual passengers in the 2030s," he said of the projected job growth opportunities.

Weighing up if a trip from Sydney's new airport is for you The doors to Western Sydney International Airport are set to soon welcome commercial passengers.

Indigenous artists from Western Sydney were also commissioned for their artworks to decorate the new terminal.

One of those featured, Dharug and Darkinjung artist Adam Laws, said he tried to map the local floral and fauna in his sculptures called Barayabinyang or Songbirds, which is featured in the external forecourt.

"To have Dharug culture represented there for all those visitors, it's just so good to get us on the map and get our stories and traditions out there. Let people know we are still here, still resilient," he said.

Adam Laws is delighted to have his artwork showcased at the new airport. (Supplied: WSI)

Ultimately, Mr Hickey said WSI wanted to "provide choice" to all greater Sydneysiders and those coming to Australia from around the world.

"We can't wait to welcome passengers to this beautiful airport."

World.title: Labor pitches $1.5 billion plan to slash emergency wait times
World.content:
Premier Ben Carroll is promising to expand a dozen emergency departments by 25 per cent in a re-election commitment to launch Victorian Labor's campaign.

Labor will on Sunday kickstart its pitch to win a fourth term with its red campaign bus and $1.5 billion worth of announcements focused on health.

The premier has not yet put a timeline on delivering the full policy, which also includes hiring another 1,500 health workers and rolling out an extra 150 hospital beds. The government said most beds will open next year.

Of the extra health workers hired, 750 would be nurses.

Mr Carroll addressed the media alongside his wife at Melbourne's Royal Children's Hospital earlier this month. (ABC News)

Victorian Labor said the emergency department expansions would slash waits by up to 20 per cent at five hospitals in Melbourne, including the Alfred, Austin and Royal Children's, as well as 10 regional hospitals, including Bendigo and Ballarat Base Hospital.

Labor views health as one of its remaining advantages; Mr Carroll brought his wife Fiona to a press conference at the Royal Children's Hospital earlier this month.

"We've waited in an ED with our daughter many times — nothing's more stressful," Mr Carroll said in a statement.

Labor promises expanded emergency departments at: Alfred Hospital

Austin Hospital

Ballarat Base Hospital

Bendigo Hospital

Footscray Hospital

Latrobe Regional Hospital

Royal Children's Hospital

Shepparton Hospital

Swan Hill Hospital

Werribee Mercy Hospital

Wonthaggi Hospital

University Hospital Geelong

But Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has also made a flurry of announcements in the space.

The Coalition has promised 10 new or expanded "exit lounges" at hospitals to free up beds, cut wait times at emergency departments and stop ambulance ramping.

Ms Wilson has also committed to funding 25,000 extra planned surgeries a year through private hospitals, which exposed Ms Wilson to attacks from Labor that she would "Americanise" the health system.

She also promised to expand the Bairnsdale emergency department.

Jess Wilson has also pledged extra Protective Services Officers to work across seven hospitals. (ABC News)

One Nation leader Warren Pickering on Friday said a government he led would clear the HECS debt of health graduates who spend five years in regional Victoria to relieve significant workforce shortages.

The Coalition has offered a $10,000 incentive and a further $10,000 for every year a health worker lives regionally.

The Victorian government said it had existing programs in place to boost the regional health workforce.

World.title: Some regions still climbing as nation sees record drop in house prices
World.content:
Australia's last holdout against a cooling house market is still on the way up, but years of rapid growth are expected to come to an end soon.

Earlier this year Helen Burns sold her "little cottage" in the Adelaide Hills for about $800,000, venturing 350 kilometres south-east to a new home in the small town of Penola in South Australia's South East.

The move was motivated by family factors but deemed a "no-brainer" when she crunched the numbers.

"[I] pretty much tripled the land size and doubled the house size for only $20,000 [more]," Ms Burns said.

This kind of calculation saw regional prices rise in Victoria, the Northern Territory and South Australia, with regional SA the steepest of the bunch.

Helen and Geoff Burns moved to Penola in April with their dog Raven. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

On the ground in the lagging state

The latest Domain property report showed prices outside of Adelaide rose 19 per cent in the past 12 months, with the median price at $595,000.

Housing data for the September 2026 quarter. (Supplied: Domain)

A report from Proptrack earlier this year outlined how regional SA house prices had almost doubled in the past five years.

Naracoorte real estate agent Margot Shortt described the past year as "nothing short of crazy" with many people getting into the market thinking it would keep rising.

Margot Shortt says an interest rate rise in November would be "another level of pain" for buyers. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

While prices have continued to rise, Domain's data only runs to September 30; and two days earlier, the RBA lifted interest rates to a 15-year high.

Ms Shortt said this, along with broader economic factors, meant calls and messages to the agency had "absolutely fallen off a cliff".

"We have seen probably a 99 per cent decline in enquiries."

She said it was hard to actually know if the local market was dropping given the lack of recent sales.

"Is the market terrible? We haven't really seen too many transactions transpire so we can't compare," she said.

All capital cities down

The latest Domain property report showed Australia's housing market fell 4.7 per cent, the steepest quarterly drop on record.

Every capital city has seen the median house price head south for the first time in 15 years.

But outside the capitals, data were more varied.

Adelaide University housing economist Chris Leishman said Sydney and Melbourne were generally the first to witness shifts and Adelaide was "always a fairly slower responder".

He said you would expect regional SA to be the last housing market still growing as the rest of the country started to plateau or drop.

"Look at any state and compare it to its metropolitan city … the regional areas tend to perform strongly later in the cycle," he said.

Professor Leishman said Australia is at the tail end of one of the longest and most pronounced housing booms ever seen.

Across all regional areas, the media house price fell 1.1 per cent in the last quarter. (ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara)

Across Australia, he failed to see strong growth over the next couple of years and believed there "has to be a correction".

"Markets tend not to crash though, particularly in Australia," he said.

He expected six to 12 months of prices going down further, before starting to rise again in the long term.

World.title: Kim Jong Un crosses new bridge into China as trade ties warm
World.content:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has visited the Chinese border city of Dandong, crossing a newly opened bridge in a symbolic move seen as highlighting Beijing and Pyongyang's push to expand trade ties.

During his visit, Mr Kim was accompanied by China's fourth-highest-ranked official Wang Huning, who conveyed greetings from President Xi Jinping, its official Xinhua news agency said.

Mr Kim arrived in Dandong via the New Yalu River Bridge connecting North Korea and China, a South Korean government official said on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak publicly.

The bridge connects China's Dandong New Zone and North Korea's Sinuiju, as seen from the Chinese side. (REUTERS: Florence Lo)

The new bridge is expected to help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products that North Korea needs for development.

Its official opening this month is the latest sign of warming ties between Beijing and Pyongyang, after two summits between their leaders in the past 13 months.

China, which fought alongside North Korea in the 1950–53 Korean War, remains Pyongyang's main economic and diplomatic backer and accounts for most of its official trade.

Kim walking on bridge

But North Korea's deepening military ties with Russia since Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine have led analysts to question whether Pyongyang is becoming less reliant on Beijing.

Mr Kim's trip nevertheless points to a renewed push by China and North Korea to bolster their economic relationship.

South Korea's Yonhap news agency had earlier reported that Mr Kim was expected to return to North Korea after Saturday's visit.

North Korean flags adorn the New Yalu River Bridge during its opening ceremony. (Reuters: Florence Lo)

Footage from Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed Mr Kim walking on the bridge, lined by people waving flags, towards North Korea.

Mr Wang accompanied Mr Kim to a Korean War memorial in Dandong, where the North Korean leader paid tribute to Chinese People's Volunteer Army soldiers who fought alongside North Korea during the three-year conflict, Xinhua reported.

Mr Kim also toured a Dandong automobile factory, it said.

New bridge boosts bilateral ties

The countries opened the three-kilometre New Yalu River Bridge, their most significant land border crossing, this month after a long delay, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce after years of strained ties and ‌pandemic-related disruptions.

"Kim has given his imprimatur to bilateral trade by crossing the New Yalu River Bridge to enter China," said Christopher Green, a Korea specialist at Leiden University in the Netherlands.

The delayed opening had shown how dysfunctional the relationship had become, he added.

A North Korean customs building at the end of the newly opened bridge. (Reuters: Florence Lo/File Photo)

During a meeting on Saturday, Mr Wang told Mr Kim that China was ready to use the bridge's opening to expand personnel exchanges and economic and trade cooperation, Xinhua said.

A visit by Mr Kim now is consistent with the current phase of closer economic ties and more frequent high-level exchanges between China and North Korea, said Lu Chao, an expert in China-North Korea relations at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, a Chinese government think-tank in Shenyang.

"The opening of the bridge has resolved a major bottleneck in China-North Korea trade logistics," Mr Lu said.

"With the logistics constraint eased, bilateral trade is likely to increase further."

Trump waits for Kim to engage

Mr Kim's last known visit to China was in September 2025, to attend the 80th Victory Day celebrations in Beijing, when he held a summit with Xi Jinping.

Mr Xi made a state visit to North Korea in June.

Donald Trump is hoping to re-establish connections with Kim Jong Un. (Reuters: Leah Millis/File Photo)

US President Donald Trump has been eager to jump-start talks with North Korea, but US and South Korean officials see fading chances of him meeting Mr Kim this year, Reuters reported on Friday.

China hosts a summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum next month in Shenzhen, which Mr Trump is expected to attend.

Reuters

World.title: Italian police wield batons, French fire tear gas at latest protests
World.content:
WorldEuropeParis protests Italian police wield batons, French fire tear gas at latest protests David Crowe October 25, 2026 — 7:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. London: Police have clashed with protesters in France and Italy during massive rallies one week after similar gatherings descended into riots and looting in major cities. Officers wielded batons against some of the protesters in Turin to prevent crowds coming close to stores, highlighting anxiety about a repeat of the destruction witnessed on city streets one week earlier. A man lies on the ground as police in Turin take on demonstrators during protest against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services during one of several protests across Italy. Mauro Ujetto/LaPresse via AP Protesters tried to force their way into the Colosseum in Rome but were escorted out by the police, while others held a peaceful protest in the Italian capital. The protests in France, meanwhile, were smaller and less violent than those seen on the previous weekend, when authorities estimated that 3000 stores were damaged or looted.



The French government estimated that about 440,000 people joined the protests in various cities on Saturday, down from an estimated 550,000 who took to the streets across the country the previous Saturday. In Paris, students and union members joined a demonstration along a route agreed with authorities from Porte d’Italie to Porte de Vincennes, east of the city centre and distant from areas looted the previous weekend. A group of protesters shield themselves from a water cannon during a protest on the streets of Paris. Getty Images Protesters dressed as Spider-Man attend a demonstration against rising living costs in Rennes, France. AP Photo/Jeremias Gonzalez Most of the protest was peaceful, but some vandals tried to break into a car dealership, the Parisian police said in a statement.



About 110,000 people joined the Paris march, according to the police, who released photographs of home-made weapons such as blocks of timber with nails attached, which they confiscated from some of those in the crowd. While authorities sought to ban rallies in cities including Marseilles and Lyon, some protesters gathered there and elsewhere to declare support for freedom of speech and freedom to demonstrate. Police used tear gas against protesters in Paris, Lyon and other cities. View post on X Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said at least 1000 people were arrested at the events across the country on Saturday, speaking at about 8pm on Saturday night (5am on Sunday, AEST). He said the number was likely to increase. There were more than 2700 arrests during the riots and looting on the previous weekend.



While attention has focused on France over the past week because of the scale of the looting and violence, similar protests in Italy led to looting in Milan and clashes with police in several cities. Police named a freelance journalist, Youssef Siher, as a key organiser of a new October 17 movement that aimed to continue the protests and confront authorities, according to reports in national newspaper La Repubblica and other media outlets. Siher was described as a 30-year-old second-generation Italian from Brescia who was a pro-Palestine activist and coordinator of the protests. While progressive activists dominated many protests, a right-wing rally assembled in Rome with a call to “unblock everything” and oppose those who were bringing city streets to a standstill or looting shops. “We reject the permanent, fruitless and ideological confrontation of the youth left,” said the rally organised by student members of Azione, a centrist party whose name translates as “Action”.



Related Article Protests Just what do France’s angry youth want? It’s complicated Protesters gathered in cities ranging from Brussels to Madrid and Lisbon to demand government action on the cost of living, with housing costs a particular concern in Spain and Portugal. While police in Lisbon and Porto cleared protest encampments in recent days, many protesters returned to continue campaigning for policies to ease the cost of housing. In Madrid, the scene of massive rallies over housing in recent weeks, people gathered on Saturday to call for more protection for pensions. Spanish unions are planning a general strike on November 11 to galvanise protest over living conditions ahead of the country’s parliamentary elections on November 29 to decide whether Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez holds power.

World.title: Sydney to host Super Netball grand final for first time
World.content:
Breaking SportNetballSuper Netball Sydney to host Super Netball grand final for first time Frances Howe October 25, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The last time Sydney netball fans had the chance to support a home team in a league grand final was 18 years ago in the former ANZ Championship. The Super Netball league was nearly a decade away from foundation when a six-year-old Amy Sligar, who now plays for the Sydney Sirens, watched the NSW Swifts defeat the Waikato Bay of Plenty Magic 65-56 in July 2008. Sydney will host the Super League netball grand final next year, much to the delight of Amy Sligar from the Sydney Sirens, Grace Whyte from the Swifts and Netball Australia boss Mark Falvo. James Brickwood “I would have watched that game with stars in my eyes and probably my heroes were playing in that game,” she said. Though the Swifts would appear in two more grand finals of the ANZ Championship and go on to play in three of the Super Netball grand finals since the league began in 2017 none were in Sydney. Neither were the two other grand finals a Sydney team featured in.



But Sligar, now 24, has the chance to play a final at home in 2027. On Sunday, Netball Australia and the NSW government will announce that the 2027 grand final will be held on July 31 at Afterpay Arena at Sydney Olympic Park, the same venue will then host the Netball World Cup a month later. The Adelaide Thunderbirds celebrate their 2026 Super Netball title win in Melbourne. Getty Images “Netball is one of the biggest participation sports in NSW, with thousands of kids and adults taking to the court every week, and it deserves the same attention and support we give our other major sport,” NSW Premier Chris Minns said on Sunday. “For too long, we haven’t invested enough in netball and we’re working to change that – from grassroots facilities and participation right through to bringing the biggest events in the sport to NSW.”



The state government expects the grand final will bring 8000 spectators to Sydney to watch at the 18,000-capacity arena, adding what they estimate to be more than $4 million to the economy. The World Cup in August will see a target of 200,000 attendees to watch Australia’s Diamonds defend their 2023 title. The state government has also set up a $1.5 million World Cup legacy program for players, coaches and officials. Minister for Sport Steve Kamper said the events would make the city the centre of the netball world next year. Netball Australia chief executive Mark Falvo said 2027 will be huge for netball fans in Sydney. Sligar said knowing the grand final will be held at home provides extra motivation for the season ahead, especially over local rivals the Swifts.



“My first reaction is that it makes me want to make the grand final even more to have a home grand final,” she said. “You almost couldn’t write a better script to have a new Sydney team [the Sirens] and then Sydney hosting the grand final, Sydney hosting the World Cup this year.” “I think for young boys and girls and men and women to be able to come and see the world’s best netball, it just builds excitement on the sport.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Friday.

World.title: ‘National suicide’: The election issue tearing Israelis apart
World.content:
A row over whether a Jerusalem coffee shop could open on the Sabbath escalated into an epic culture war. For modern Israel, it could be the shape of things to come.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Jerusalem/ Bnei Brak: Almost anywhere else in the world, a cafe opening for business on Saturday would not be an inflammatory act. But in downtown Jerusalem, Cafe Basimta’s decision to sell coffee and pastries on the Sabbath ignited an almighty culture war between the Holy City’s ultra-Orthodox and secular residents. Soon after the coffee shop opened in a quiet alley in May, dozens of ultra-Orthodox teenage boys wearing black suits and fedoras showed up to block its entrance while chanting “Whoever breaks the Sabbath has no part in the world to come”. A young ultra-Orthodox protester stands his ground outside Cafe Basimta while counter-protesters make their point. The cafe has now decided to stay shut on Saturdays. AFP Ultra-Orthodox Jews believe in resting on the Sabbath, the frequent study of religious texts, strict gender segregation and eating kosher, pitting them against the less devout, who favour a more relaxed approach. As the demonstrations grew each week, so did counter-protests. Hundreds of non-religious activists locked arms to protect the entrance to the café, and prominent politicians from the right and left joined in. The fact that the cafe’s owners – the messianic and controversial Jews for Jesus organisation – were hardly secular was a wrinkle in the narrative. But it didn’t deter most of the counter-protesters, who believed they were fighting for an important principle. The argument raging over whether coffee and pastries could be sold on the Jewish sabbath became a microcosm for wider debate on modern Israeli society. AFP



“We see it as our right to be able to drink coffee on the Sabbath in the centre of Jerusalem,” says deputy Jerusalem mayor Adir Schwarz, a champion of the city’s secular population. “Our capital is supposed to unite all Israelis, and if any Jew is being pushed out of Jerusalem, that is a bad forewarning for the rest of the state of Israel.” While the havoc was a boon for business, the owners ultimately decided it wasn’t worth the pain. In September, the cafe announced it would no longer open on Saturdays. “The cafe has become, over the past several months, a focal point of friction and danger,” Jews for Jesus chief executive Eli Birnbaum said. Strict ultra-Orthodox modesty laws have brought the community into conflict with the 21st century. Disappointed by the decision, secular activists mostly abandoned the cafe and business plummeted. When we visited last week, the coffee was excellent, but only a handful of customers were there. Schwarz says the backdown was just the latest blow to secular Jerusalemites, who feel increasingly marginalised and disempowered. Ultra-Orthodox residents are rising in number and moving into secular suburbs, sparking heated battles over resources and cultural norms. ‘We live in separate worlds, and those worlds are getting further apart’ Rabbi Yisrael Goldwasser “A territorial battle is playing out in certain neighbourhoods as their identity changes and becomes more religious,” Schwarz says.



Schwarz cites strict ultra-Orthodox modesty laws which can expose female pedestrians to harassment and intimidation for wearing jeans. “The fact a secular woman cannot walk in pants through the neighbourhood she grew up in is a big problem,” Schwarz argues. Children in Bnei Brak. The birthrate for ultra-Orthodox Jews now vastly exceeds that of other groups. Israel’s ultra-Orthodox community – known as the Haredim – makes up 14 per cent of the national population. That figure is exploding, reflecting the fact that the birth rate for ultra-Orthodox women (6.5 children per woman) is vastly higher than for other Jewish women (2.2 children). By 2065, the Haredim are projected to comprise a third of Israeli society, a figure unimaginable when Israel was founded in 1948. Such rapid growth equals more political power but also greater scrutiny about ultra-Orthodox Jews’ contribution to Israeli society. Twenty minutes from central Tel Aviv, Bnei Brak is a world away from modern Israel. The fight over Cafe Basimta is emblematic of a deeper battle being waged in Israel ahead of national elections on Tuesday. Topics that foreigners may expect to be front-of-centre – like how Israel waged its war on Gaza or the possibility of a two-state solution with the Palestinians – are almost entirely absent from the public discourse. Meanwhile, the concessions provided to ultra-Orthodox Israelis are tearing the nation apart and dominating the campaign. Bnei Brak is a mere 20-minute drive from the gay bars and non-kosher restaurants of Tel Aviv, but it might as well be on a different planet. “We live in separate worlds, and those worlds are getting further apart,” Rabbi Yisrael Goldwasser says of the two cities, which serve as avatars for Israel’s ultra-Orthodox and secular tribes. Here there is none of the clashing and intermingling you find in more integrated Jerusalem. Bnei Brak Rabbi Yisrael Goldwasser says he is alarmed by the push for compulsory military service for the ultra-Orthodox community, who are currently exempt. Vered Adir



Bnei Brak is one of the world’s most densely populated cities: 230,000 people, almost all of them Haredi, crammed into just seven square kilometres of land. “It’s a terrible city, it’s dirty, it’s more crowded than Gaza,” Goldwasser says as he slurps a bowl of matzo ball soup. His kosher phone, which blocks internet access, sits on the table. On the plus side, he says it is a self-contained society packed with restaurants, yeshivas, shops and medical facilities where the streets remain lively until the early hours of the morning. In Hebrew, the Haredim means those who tremble before God. To be ultra-Orthodox is to be on edge. But Goldwasser says the community’s naturally high anxiety has spiked to intolerable levels because of an all-out campaign to force them to serve in the military. The dilemma of ultra-Orthodox army service has existed before the founding of Israel in 1948. To ensure as broad support as possible for the creation of a Jewish state, founding prime minister David Ben-Gurion granted 400 yeshiva students exemptions from compulsory military service. This reflected the ultra-Orthodox community’s fraught relationship with Zionism (many believe establishing a sovereign Jewish state before the arrival of the Messiah violates divine law). Related Article Exclusive

Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘Like a wounded animal’: Netanyahu will do whatever it takes to stay in power, former PM warns A decade later, with thousands of students now exempt, Ben-Gurion questioned his decision. Today, court filings by Israel’s attorney-general estimate that about 80,000 are avoiding military service. This became a source of fury as Israel fought a multi-front war against its enemies after the October 7 attacks of 2023. The burdens of service – time spent away from family and the risk of dying on the battlefield – have not been distributed evenly across society. Reflecting the new era Israel entered after October 7, the Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that the longstanding blanket exemption for yeshiva students was unlawful. Fierce resistance has followed. Last year, chief rabbi Yitzhak Yosef used his weekly sermon to warn that the ultra-Orthodox community “will all board planes and leave Israel” if they are forced to serve in the army.



Attempts to force Haredi men to enlist, including through arrests, have sparked riots and blockades of major highways. In June, ultra-Orthodox rioters smashed windows, damaged flowerpots, and vandalised a car parked at the home of the Supreme Court’s deputy president. Elchanan Wasserman says his story proves you can be ultra-Orthodox and serve in the Israeli military. “As far as they’re concerned, it’s life or death. Religion comes first,” Wasserman says, explaining why the issue arouses such passion. Bnei Brak yeshiva student Yakov, 20, says he has no intention of enlisting. “Prison, sanctions, nothing can break us,” he declares. His dream is to be a rabbi. Protests and arrests have accelerated in the lead-up to the October 27 election, raising the temperature. The military arrested 40 ultra-Orthodox men returning from the United States on Tuesday at Tel Aviv airport on suspicion of draft dodging. An ultra-Orthodox Jew burns an Israeli flag as anti-government amid protests against their military service exemptions. Getty Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose conservative coalition is reliant on ultra-Orthodox parties, criticised the arrests. “We need to preserve the world of Torah study because it has preserved us,” he said in a radio interview. On the other side of the debate, the four main Jewish parties running against Netanyahu are all campaigning to end sweeping exemptions from military service. They are convinced they are onto a vote winner. An overwhelming 72 per cent of Israelis want to see the Haredim drafted alongside other Israelis eligible for military service, according to a September poll by the Israel Democracy Institute.

World.title: ‘Without you the union is gone’: Mick Gatto’s secret support for John Setka
World.content:
Leaked texts reveal how John Setka raged, survived and stayed at the top of the CFMEU through a domestic violence scandal, with unwavering support from his gangland friend and some Labor insiders.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The sky was a blanket of unrelenting grey and large droplets clung to the leaves of the red flowering gums lining the road in Melbourne’s west as a thickset man with thinning hair scrolled through his mobile phone. Australia’s most powerful union leader wanted advice. If anyone knew how to navigate bad press and criminal allegations it was Domenic “Mick” Gatto. Any other union or political leader facing criminal accusations of stalking and terrorising their wife would have been penning their resignation letter. But not the towering trade union chief now focused on his phone. As usual, the boss of Australia’s construction union, a division of the CFMEU, was defiant. And why wouldn’t he be? He was John Setka, son of a blue-collar worker who in 1970, when John was only six, had survived one of Australia’s worst industrial accidents. John’s dad had ridden a slab of the West Gate Bridge as it plummeted through nearly 50 metres of icy Melbourne air. The same slab of concrete and iron had claimed the lives of 35 others. Forty years after his father’s escape from death, John Setka had led tens of thousands of chanting protesters through Melbourne’s CBD, unfazed by the cops on horseback or those sweating on foot in their riot gear. Setka at the 2018 ALP conference in Adelaide, two days before he stormed out. Alex Ellinghausen In 2018, he had stormed out of the national conference of Australia’s oldest political party having labelled its former leader Kevin Rudd a “f---ing dog” and a “maggot” as the ex-prime minister was awarded his Labor Party life membership. The rain was still falling, the sky growing ever greyer. Setka knew his so-called union comrades were now judging him. F--- ’em. Setka tapped furiously on his phone. “F--- these prim and proper people have never done it hard in the [sic] whole lives,” Setka texted his mate. “I’m sick of all these squareheads trying to micro manage me and tell me who I can be seen with or who I can talk to. Yet when the shit hits the fan they’re nowhere to be seen.”





And yet, behind the scenes, it wasn’t all bad for Setka. He was also fielding support, and not only from Mick Gatto. It said something of Setka’s power and reach that it wasn’t just several of his male comrades offering him backroom support, but women too. Even when Albanese was the newly installed opposition leader and moved to turf Setka from the party, Setka’s phone had lit up with text messages from female federal and state Labor politicians and union figures. Victorian MP Bronwyn Halfpenny had assured Setka she was “thinking of you and hope everything will be OK”. She had texted: “You are a great comrade to working people so the establishment will always want to bring u down. Hope to see you soon. Xxx.” Rail, Tram and Bus Union secretary Luba Grigorovitch (now a state Labor MP and minister) had repeatedly sent messages of support, vowing to direct her union to back Setka. “We will get through this John xx,” she had promised. From left: former CFMEU official Derek Christopher, state Labor MP Luba Grigorovitch, an unidentified supporter and Setka at a 2024 CFMEU event. Instagram Grigorovitch advised Setka to rely on the behind-the-scenes advice of communications expert and Labor political adviser Tanja Kovac, who also headed EMILY’s List, a group devoted to promoting ALP women into parliament. Kovac had also texted Setka, telling him to craft his public messaging carefully. Setka had decided to plead guilty to a charge of harassment and breaching a family violence order, but Kovac warned Setka that he not only had to survive the Magistrates’ Court but the court of public opinion as well. It was vital that Setka be seen to publicly champion “the need to talk about family and gendered violence”, texted Kovac. “Be strong, genuine, sorry & the leader I know you are,” she had advised, finishing her text with the words: “Thinking of you.” Kovac also suggested that Setka find supporters willing to support him publicly. Mick Gatto required no cajoling. Of all Setka’s backers, he had been the most unflinching. Gatto was, in underworld parlance, staunch. Where Kovac urged Setka to display contrition, Gatto urged him to fight. “Sorry you are going through all this nonsense. If I was you I would reconsider pleading guilty,” Gatto advised.



Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad ‘Trading drugs for weapons’: Police charge CFMEU delegate over union HQ deals Governments and the “establishment” had also come after him, Gatto told Setka. They had changed the law to stop him from running his boxing promotion company. Now they were coming after Setka because of all he had done for the hundreds of thousands of building workers around the country. Gatto wasn’t having any of it. “Thanks john for publicly defending our friendship,” he texted. “I do love ya. Without you the union is gone.” Setka hadn’t bothered to respond to some of his other supporters, but for Gatto he had only love. “Thanks brother. I really appreciate the support and I’ll never forget it,” he told his ally. Setka’s union would also not forget Gatto’s support. A month after Setka took to the steps of the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court, with Emma by his side, to publicly “take responsibility” for the criminal harassment and intimidation of his wife, another man appeared on the steps of the neighbouring Supreme Court. Gangland identity Faruk Orman had just been released from prison, his murder conviction quashed after a court had found he’d been denied a fair trial because his lawyer engaged in serious misconduct. Nick McKenzie and Ben Schneiders’ book. Before being jailed for 12 years, Orman had worked as Mick Gatto’s driver. But it was the accusation that he had acted as the wheelman for an underworld hitman that had landed Orman in prison. Orman had entered prison with a boyish face and a skinny frame; he’d left with jowls, a slight paunch, and no desire to drive any more gangland figures around town.

World.title: ‘Fourteen-year-olds are watching it’: Think Love Island is grown-up entertainment? Think again
World.content:
CultureTV & radioReality TV ‘Fourteen-year-olds are watching it’: Think Love Island is grown-up entertainment? Think again Bridget McManus October 25, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Sophie Monk, flaunting the ironic bombshell bogan persona on which she so endearingly trades in Andy Lee’s survey quiz show The Hundred, declares that this eighth season of Love Island Australia, has “hit its actual peak of brilliance”. In the trailer, which rivals Sam Kekovich’s Australia Day lamb ads for its lavish parody of patriotism, our Sophie, the host since its inception, is tossed the keys to the US series’ villa in Fiji. Here, 10 young Australian “hotties” will this time try to fall in love, refrain from cheating and win over viewers for a $50,000 prize. Love Island Australia host Sophie Monk says young teenagers are now the biggest audience for the reality show. Announcing that the set “just needs a bit of Aussification”, Monk winks at two shirtless tradies hanging a Vegemite poster and cracks a MAGA gag from a pink inflatable in the pool. There is nothing not to love about Monk. But there are increasingly uncomfortable aspects to this raunchy matchmaking show. For starters, the audience is getting younger.



“I’ve noticed that, now, it’s a lot of daughters and mums – they watch together,” says Monk. “Fourteen-year-olds are watching it. That’s the majority, I’d say, of people that come up to me with their mum, and they both want a photo. Because we all want love, don’t we?” Related Article Streaming Everything we should (and shouldn’t) expect from the Girls reboot Monk’s joke in the trailer that “a few red flags have slipped in, but it’s too late now!” doesn’t seem so funny about 20 minutes into the first episode. Encouraged by Monk, the women take turns walking up to a man on a heart-shaped podium to perform a passionate kiss, before the man makes his selection. The camera zooms in as one man puts his hand around a woman’s throat, seemingly inferring the controversial “sex choking” trend. Monk says she didn’t notice this during filming, and likens the spectacle to a party game. “I’m definitely not perving!” says Monk. “I guess it’s just that age group where they do spin-the-bottle … I’m so protective of them all. I wish I had had a show like this when I was a teenager.”



Some of the new crop of Love Island Australia contestants dressed up as squirrels. Monk came of age on reality TV, with Popstars Australia in 2000, and a decade later, while continuing to forge an acting career at home and in the US, appearing on The Bachelorette and Celebrity Apprentice – so she well knows the perils of the game. She has not seen the Binge documentary The Curse of Love Island, which covers the deaths by suicide of four people associated with the original UK series, including host Caroline Flack, and airs the mortified reflections of former contestants. Related Article Australian TV SBS debate ‘brings together’ childfree advocates and anti-abortion campaigners She insists the Australian cast are in safer hands, even in the very villa where the previous US series was marred by allegations of racial slurs and bullying. “It’s changed so much. When I started, no one knew how big [reality TV] was going to be. It was wild. There were zero rules. And when it was over, it was like, ‘Bye!’ ” she recalls. “We didn’t know what to do when the fame stopped. Now, there are psychologists for that. [This cast] is looked after through the show, before the show and after the show. I just wish that was around when I was younger.”



In the first episode, a British expat cast as a temptress waits in a “hideaway villa” to test the loyalties of paired-up male contestants, though Monk says there is no emotional manipulation on this series. “Producers were out to get you a bit more back then, and they’re not now. Love Island’s not that. We don’t need villains.” Instead, Monk says there is a “psychological study” behind the bikini-clad glamour. “It’s the conversation points,” she says. “Like Married At First Sight, people come away and discuss things. I know they’re in bathers, but once you pull all that away, within a day, you forget that they’re even hot, and you just learn so much by watching. Well, I do.” Love Island Australia airs Monday-Thursday at 10am on 9Now; and 8.30pm on Nine (the owner of this masthead).

World.title: The answer to the meaning of life
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsReligion The answer to the meaning of life Nomi Kaltmann October 25, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

What is my purpose in this world? It is one of the oldest questions we ask ourselves. Across cultures and faiths, people spend their lives searching for the answer. Judaism offers a beautiful response to this eternal question: every person enters this world carrying a soul that is divine in origin, and every soul has something unique that only it can contribute to the world. Jewish mysticism takes this idea one step further. It teaches that no soul arrives on Earth by accident. Each soul is sent with a mission that belongs to it alone. There is a children’s song taught in Jewish kindergartens that captures this beautiful idea: “For 70 or 80 years, a soul descends to this world just to do a favour for another.” Judaism teaches that if your calling is to be a teacher, be a teacher. Imagine that. A lifetime of joys and disappointments, triumphs and heartbreaks, all for one act of kindness, one conversation, one moment of compassion. While humans might measure our lives by our achievements, in Judaism we believe that God measures us by our acts of chosen kindness.



This understanding also means that our callings are not meant to look the same. Judaism has never imagined that holiness belongs only to those who stand behind a pulpit or devote their lives to studying Torah. The artist who awakens beauty through their creativity, the doctor who heals the sick, the teacher who inspires their students, the parent who nurtures their children with love and patience, the lawyer who pursues justice for their clients – each of these careers can fulfil a sacred purpose by offering their gifts in service of others. Related Article Faith

Religion In the small things, hope floats There is a story told about a university professor who embraced Orthodox Judaism and wrote to a renowned Hasidic rabbi asking whether he should now leave academia to become a rabbi. The reply he received was unexpected: “Absolutely not.” The Hasidic rabbi explained that for this professor, his classroom was already his sanctuary. His gift was teaching, and by living his faith with integrity before generations of searching students, he could inspire far more people than he ever would from behind a lectern as a rabbi in a synagogue.



Finding one’s purpose in life is rarely immediate or easy. For many people it unfolds slowly, through unexpected turns and abandoned plans. It may take decades before we recognise the work that only we can do. In my own life, I explored many different paths before discovering that writing was my gift. I find joy in taking ideas that are complex and making them accessible to others through my prose. In Jewish thought, our talents are never simply possessions for personal enjoyment; rather, they are entrusted to us, and they become sacred when we use them to bring a little more wisdom, kindness and hope into the world. Perhaps that is what a life full of purpose really looks like. Not becoming someone else, but fully embracing the person your soul was always meant to be. Nomi Kaltmann is an Orthodox rabbi.

World.title: You’re an NRL star thinking about joining the Chiefs? This is what your life in PNG will be like
World.content:
Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 You’re an NRL star thinking about joining the Chiefs? This is what your life in PNG will be like Adrian Proszenko October 25, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Can I really see myself living in PNG? It’s a question NRL players, coaches and officials, intrigued by the prospect of banking tax-free dollars, are asking themselves as the PNG Chiefs prepare to enter their first free-agency period on the player market. It’s an impossible question to answer without travelling to the Pacific nation and experiencing the lifestyle first-hand. Trent Hodkinson in Port Moresby with Chiefs fans. Adrian Proszenko Which is why former Manly and Bulldogs half Trent Hodkinson and his wife, Chantelle, decided to tour the facilities before they committed to the sea change. Hodkinson, who had previously spent time in Port Moresby during his playing days, had been earmarked to become one of coach Willie Peters’ assistants. The couple, who have lived in NSW and Queensland, share a spirit of adventure. They were keen to experience life in England, before injuries prematurely cut short the former NSW halfback’s playing career. Now a unique opportunity had presented itself in PNG ahead of the Chiefs entry into the NRL in 2028, but they first wanted to double-check if relocating would work for them and their two children, aged six and three.



After just a few days in PNG, they had their answer. “It’s a great, unique opportunity to be part of something special, to live here, and to bring the family over,” Hodkinson said. “I think that’s exciting – not many people get to do that. Loading “That’s the type of people Chantelle and I are, we want our kids to embrace and experience different countries and cultures. What better place to do it than Papua New Guinea, where rugby league is life?” On Wednesday, the Chiefs revealed their inaugural jersey. Which players are prepared to fill them when their campaign kicks off in 2028 is the biggest story in rugby league as a raft of superstars prepare to hit the open market on November 1.



While the Hodkinsons decided it would suit them, the fit may not work for other members of the Australian league community. “This is not going to be for everyone,” Chiefs coach Willie Peters conceded. Inaugural PNG Chiefs NRL coach Willie Peters. NRL Photos “Some people might prefer where they are, while others will look at this and see it as where they want to play, get better, and do something for something bigger than themselves – a club doing something for a country. “For me, I was no different than anyone else. You need to make sure it works for your family, but it needs to be bigger than that. A lot of people will be making sacrifices to be here. My wife is coming over, my youngest son is coming over, and everyone’s situation will be different.”



The living arrangements will be very different from what the game’s stars are used to in Sydney or Brisbane. Chiefs players will be seeing a lot of the airport, and it’s not just because they are travelling to away games every second week. Their vista will be the tarmac of the adjoining Jacksons International Airport. They will reside at Airways, described on their website as an “oasis of understated luxury”. “Understated” being the key word. This is not Hayman Island. There are two primary restaurants, one swimming pool, a children’s playground and adjoining green space, although it currently looks more brown than green due to a lack of rain. The view of the airport at Port Moresby from the Airways Hotel where NRL players will call home from 2028. Adrian Proszenko They will live in one of the new residences under construction, in the hope they will be ready for the arrival of players in 12 months’ time. The facility – descriptions alternate between “five-star resort” and “compound” – will be their home for the length of their stay. The prices for food, for the most part, are on par with those in Sydney. A 250g Black Angus Steak Diane at the Airways’ Bacchus restaurant costs the equivalent of $56.



Then there’s the immaculately presented Waterfront Supermarket in town, where the label of every single product is turned to face the consumer. There you can do a weekly shop and pick up fresh produce at reasonable prices; a loaf of bread for $2.25 (Australian), bananas are $3 per kg, a pack of thin beef sausages are just $A3.80 a pack, double smoked ham is $14.50 per kg. However, imported goods are more expensive – for instance, a two-litre bottle of Biozet Attack laundry liquid is $40. For the most part, the players will live in a bubble, as they did during COVID-19, far removed from the fans who so adore them. Living in close proximity during the lockdowns brought some teams – most notably Penrith – closer together. Others felt like the walls were closing in. A local ground in Port Moresby. NRL Images “We have to be realistic, we can’t pretend we’re like any other football club. We’re not, we’re unique,” said Chiefs general manager Michael Chammas. “I’ve done a lot of homework on teams that succeeded during the Covid bubble. When you talk to the Penrith players, the best time of their lives was the covid bubble.



“They loved it, their families loved it, they wish they could go back to Twin Waters. A big part of that was they lived in an open space, the kids could run about. They had a great team environment and they had success. “I’ve spent some time with the Warriors, they had a lot of time on the road during that period. [Warriors CEO] Cameron George said the biggest single challenge is keeping the families happy. That’s our biggest challenge. We know that. PNG pathways manager Joey Grima at a local ground in Port Moresby. NRL Photos “Even if we have good players, we’re only as good as the environment that’s being created where we live. If the partners and kids aren’t happy, then players we sign won’t be happy.” Life in PNG will be very different to what players are accustomed to. Things they take for granted – being able to drink the tap water, reliable Wi-Fi or moving through the community without security – will be sacrificed.



The adjustment is likely to be easiest for the footballers. They will be given a routine and purpose that will help them fill their days. If you’re a player who wants to knuckle down and focus on your career, it can be done in Port Moresby without distraction. However, the transition is likely to be harder for partners and kids. In the case of Hodkinson’s wife Chantelle, her employer will afford her an opportunity to continue her interior design work remotely. Whether other wives and girlfriends receive the same flexibility to pursue their careers, or enjoy an active social life, remains to be seen. If left behind on away footy trips, boredom could become an issue. Local getaway in Papua New Guinea, Loloata Island resort. NRL Photos Peters, Chammas and recruiter Liam Ayoub have opted not to pursue several potential signings in the belief they wouldn’t handle the unique environment in PNG. There will be chances to experience a change of scenery. There are several private getaways, such as Loloata Island, where families can swim, snorkel and be pampered. However, the majority of their time will be spent at Airways.



“We need to find downtime, because everyone is different,” Peters said. “You can’t be with each other 24/7 and then play on the weekend through the roller coaster of a season. We need to work out ways for players to get away, and there are some beautiful places here to go.” Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Broncos’ Chief concern over Carrigan partner’s PNG trip Danny Weidler Sport columnist Papua New Guineans are friendly, but most live in abject poverty. If you see a footballer playing a game with just one shoe, you know that it will be worn on his kicking foot. Given Port Moresby is regularly ranked among the top-five most dangerous cities in the world, there are few opportunities to mix with the locals without a security detail. There’s a reason why tax-free dollars are being offered. “We’re going to have challenges, no doubt,” Peters said. “The first thing is to try and bring in as many great people as possible who want to be here; that’s the key. You’ve got to want to go on this journey, because if you’re doing it just for tax-free dollars, it’s going to be difficult.” Adrian Proszenko travelled to Port Moresby as a guest of the PNG Chiefs. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Italian police wield batons, French fire tear gas at latest protests
World.content:
WorldEuropeParis protests Italian police wield batons, French fire tear gas at latest protests David Crowe October 25, 2026 — 7:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. London: Police have clashed with protesters in France and Italy during massive rallies one week after similar gatherings descended into riots and looting in major cities. Officers wielded batons against some of the protesters in Turin to prevent crowds coming close to stores, highlighting anxiety about a repeat of the destruction witnessed on city streets one week earlier. A man lies on the ground as police in Turin take on demonstrators during protest against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services during one of several protests across Italy. Mauro Ujetto/LaPresse via AP Protesters tried to force their way into the Colosseum in Rome but were escorted out by the police, while others held a peaceful protest in the Italian capital. The protests in France, meanwhile, were smaller and less violent than those seen on the previous weekend, when authorities estimated that 3000 stores were damaged or looted.



The French government estimated that about 440,000 people joined the protests in various cities on Saturday, down from an estimated 550,000 who took to the streets across the country the previous Saturday. In Paris, students and union members joined a demonstration along a route agreed with authorities from Porte d’Italie to Porte de Vincennes, east of the city centre and distant from areas looted the previous weekend. A group of protesters shield themselves from a water cannon during a protest on the streets of Paris. Getty Images Protesters dressed as Spider-Man attend a demonstration against rising living costs in Rennes, France. AP Photo/Jeremias Gonzalez Most of the protest was peaceful, but some vandals tried to break into a car dealership, the Parisian police said in a statement.



About 110,000 people joined the Paris march, according to the police, who released photographs of home-made weapons such as blocks of timber with nails attached, which they confiscated from some of those in the crowd. While authorities sought to ban rallies in cities including Marseilles and Lyon, some protesters gathered there and elsewhere to declare support for freedom of speech and freedom to demonstrate. Police used tear gas against protesters in Paris, Lyon and other cities. View post on X Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said at least 1000 people were arrested at the events across the country on Saturday, speaking at about 8pm on Saturday night (5am on Sunday, AEST). He said the number was likely to increase. There were more than 2700 arrests during the riots and looting on the previous weekend.



While attention has focused on France over the past week because of the scale of the looting and violence, similar protests in Italy led to looting in Milan and clashes with police in several cities. Police named a freelance journalist, Youssef Siher, as a key organiser of a new October 17 movement that aimed to continue the protests and confront authorities, according to reports in national newspaper La Repubblica and other media outlets. Siher was described as a 30-year-old second-generation Italian from Brescia who was a pro-Palestine activist and coordinator of the protests. While progressive activists dominated many protests, a right-wing rally assembled in Rome with a call to “unblock everything” and oppose those who were bringing city streets to a standstill or looting shops. “We reject the permanent, fruitless and ideological confrontation of the youth left,” said the rally organised by student members of Azione, a centrist party whose name translates as “Action”.



Related Article Protests Just what do France’s angry youth want? It’s complicated Protesters gathered in cities ranging from Brussels to Madrid and Lisbon to demand government action on the cost of living, with housing costs a particular concern in Spain and Portugal. While police in Lisbon and Porto cleared protest encampments in recent days, many protesters returned to continue campaigning for policies to ease the cost of housing. In Madrid, the scene of massive rallies over housing in recent weeks, people gathered on Saturday to call for more protection for pensions. Spanish unions are planning a general strike on November 11 to galvanise protest over living conditions ahead of the country’s parliamentary elections on November 29 to decide whether Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez holds power.
