World.title: Usman Khawaja reveals illness he kept secret his entire Test cricket career
World.content:
Usman Khawaja was just 22 and revelling in being part of the New South Wales cricket team when he was diagnosed with a potentially crippling disease that he would keep secret his whole career.

Only now, having retired from international cricket after Australia's Ashes win in January, is Usman revealing that he lived with rheumatoid arthritis while playing 88 Tests for Australia.

Usman Khawaja in hospital with his mother Fozia Khawaja by his side when he was first diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. (Supplied: Usman Khawaja)

Even good friends such as his childhood cricket buddy David Warner and Test teammate Michael Hussey were unaware of the diagnosis that Usman thought would end his cricket dream before it really took off.

In fact, Usman says that when doctors initially battled to diagnose the cause of debilitating pain in his left knee, he feared he had a terminal illness.

"I genuinely thought I was going to die," Usman, 39, tells Australian Story. "I went from this athlete who was playing professional cricket to not being able to walk 10 metres to the bathroom."

Left out of the Australian team eight times, Usman Kahwaja was one of the most dropped players in Australian Test cricket history. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

It's another remarkable story to add to Usman's eventful career that saw him score 6,229 Test runs, including 16 centuries, as well as two one-day international tons for Australia.

He was the first Pakistani-born person to play Test cricket for Australia, and the first Muslim.

He was one of the most dropped players in Australian Test history, losing his place in the team eight times but always finding his way back, most notably in Sydney in 2022 when he scored twin centuries at the age of 35.

His experience of racial and religious vilification would lead him to speak out about discrimination, in cricket and more broadly, contributing to a greater cultural awareness within the Australian squad.

Says Todd Greenberg, Cricket Australia's CEO: "He's broken the mould in so many different ways. He'll leave the culture of Australian cricket in far better shape than what he found it."

Loading...

Now, Usman is keen to give hope to those living with an autoimmune disease, detailing his health battle in his soon-to-be-released autobiography, Sabr.

"If a person can play at the top level … as a professional cricketer with rheumatoid arthritis, then I think a lot of other people can achieve a lot, too," he says.

Given the cricket rumour mill, Usman admits it's surprising the secret he's kept since the 2009 off-season never got out. He told medical and coaching staff and cricket administrators but not a single player because he did not want special treatment, or for the disease to be used against him.

Usman manages his condition with regular injections of a drug which he calls a "godsend" and credits with getting him back to the crease about six months later.

"Without that drug," Usman says, "I would never have played cricket ever again or even lived a normal life again."

By January 2011, he had become the 419th Test player to be handed a baggy green, and the tumultuous and influential international career of Usman Khawaja was on its way.

Usman Khawaja had an emotion-filled final Test match at the Sydney Cricket Ground on January 8, 2026. (Getty Images: Ayush Kumar/Eurasia Sport Images)

Breaking the 'typical' cricket player mould

As a cricket-mad immigrant boy growing up in Sydney, Usman found it hard to relate to the Australian cricket team.

Its beer-drinking and larrikin culture felt foreign to the way he was being brought up by his parents, Tariq and Fozia Khawaja, who had immigrated from Pakistan when Usman was four.

A young Usman Khawaja (left) plays cricket in the park. (Supplied: Usman Khawaja)

He wasn't keen on the sledging, either, having copped racial abuse on the sporting field — mostly from parents.

"As great cricketers as they were," Usman says of the Australian team of the early 1990s, "it kind of felt like that bogan vibe, that same vibe [from those] parents."

Usman Khawaja, pictured with his father Tariq Khawaja, was cricket-obsessed from a young age. (Supplied: Usman Khawaja)

That vibe changed for Usman in 1999, when players he could relate to — Adam Gilchrist, a left-handed batsman like him, and fast bowler Brett Lee — arrived on the scene.

"They're the ones that dragged me over to the Australian cricket team … I started supporting Australia way more and then eventually after that it was just Australia, Australia, Australia."

Usman and Tariq Khawaja hanging out at the cricket fields. (Supplied: Usman Khawaja)

But despite his obvious skills, the Pakistani/Indian community told him he would never make the Australian team.

"They're like, 'Oh yeah, you're good but you'll never play for Australia because they don't pick our kind, they don't pick brown people to play for Australia, there's too much racism. You'll never get there.'"

But then, Ricky Ponting broke his finger in December 2010.

And Usman got his big break.

"I was a Pakistani boy debuting for the Australian cricket team," Usman says. "It's a big deal."

The crowd applauded as the debutante made his way onto the Sydney Cricket Ground in January 2011. Usman was nervous, hoping not to get a duck. His father Tariq recalls sitting in the SCG stands with Fozia, praying.

Usman Khawaja chats with Ricky Ponting at an Australia training session just before his debut. (Getty Images: Hamish Blair)

Usman scored two off his first ball. The second ball? A four from a well-timed pull shot.

Michael Hussey remembers team members jumping out of their seats, applauding. "You could see he had the talent, had the ability, and also had the courage to go out and play his way," he says.

Usman scored 37 that day. But by September, he was dropped for the first time. He made it back in November to play South Africa, scoring 65 in one innings, his first half century, but after a December series against New Zealand, he was dropped again.

Usman Khawaja runs between wickets during his innings of 37 during his Ashes debut in January 2011. (Paul Miller: AAP)

Usman says that early in his Test career, he was on the wrong end of "fifty-fifty" selection decisions.

He believes unfair stereotypes that subcontinent players "don't work as hard as Aussies" were at play.

"I wasn't your typical Australian cricketer … I didn't drink alcohol. I prayed. I did Ramadan. My name was Usman Khawaja," he says.

Usman decided he needed a fresh start. He moved to Brisbane in 2012, taking a big pay cut to play for Queensland.

"It was the hardest but the best decision I've made in my life," he says.

Usman Khawaja broke the "typical" Aussie cricketer mould. (Getty Images: Jeremy Ng)

Bowled over by love

Being happy off the field goes a long way to playing well, Usman believes, and he has no greater proof of that than the period when he was dating his wife-to-be, Rachel.

Usman Khawaja says Rachel gave him the support he needed to elevate his career. (Supplied: Rachel Khawaja)

It was late 2015, Usman was back in the Test team after two years, and he was firing.

"I just could not stop scoring runs," says Usman, who notched four Test centuries that summer.

"It was 100 per cent because of Rachel. I was absolutely, head over heels, madly in love. I was so happy off the field."

They'd met in Brisbane through a mutual friend and Rachel admits she knew little about Usman's on-again off-again Test career.

"Unless you were a Warnie or a 'Haydos' or a Langer, those names that really stand out, I really wasn't across cricket," Rachel says.

Raised Catholic, she converted to Islam before their marriage in April 2018. "It was obviously a very significant moment in my life," she says. "I've become more and more grateful to Uzzy for introducing me to Islam. I see it as the gift that he's given me."

Usman says Rachel, the mother of his three daughters, is one of the greatest gifts God has given him.

Usman and Rachel Khawaja with their daughters Aisha and Ayla. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"Before Rachel, there was zero 100s for international cricket. After Rachel, I scored 18 100s for Australia at international level. She was a big part of [that] because she was the only one I could actually open up to after a tour," he says.

Usman Khawaja plays at the park with his daughter Ayla. (Australian Story: Erin Semmler)

There was much to talk about after the Test match in South Africa in March 2018: the infamous Sandpapergate tour in which Australia was sprung cheating by roughening a ball with sandpaper to make it swing abnormally.

It rocked Australian cricket and led to the suspension of Usman's mate and then-vice captain David Warner, captain Steve Smith and the man caught with the sandpaper, batsman Cameron Bancroft.

Usman says he felt sorry for the players because of the heavy penalty and worldwide disgrace they suffered but says the controversy changed Australian cricket for the better.

"Up to that point, we were playing a certain brand of cricket which wasn't in the spirit of the game a lot of the time," he says. "And I think we've actually come out of it a much better team.

"A bit of humility came back in … I think that was a silver lining for the Australian cricket team."

Teammates Usman Khawaja and David Warner have been playing cricket together since they were six years old. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

Usman Khawaja's proudest moment

Rachel remembers sitting at the SCG with their then-18-month-old daughter, Aisha, watching Usman's score tick towards 100 in the match he was never supposed to play.

Voting open for Australian Story countdown Since 1996, ABC's Australian Story has allowed people from all walks of life to tell their stories in their own words. More than 1,100 episodes and 30 years later, we are asking you to pick the most memorable.

A week before, the 35-year-old was carrying drinks, thrilled to have made it into the squad for the Ashes series of 2021/22. He hadn't played a Test for more than two years and was happy to treat his drink duties as his "swan song".

Then Travis Head got COVID — and Usman was called up for the New Year's Test.

He reached a half century. Then he made it into the 80s and Rachel recalls thinking: "No, it's too good. It's not going to happen.'"

It did. Usman made 100, adding another 37 before getting out. Come the second innings, he scored 101 not out.

"Honestly, I experienced a fairytale," Usman says. "I literally could not in my wildest dream have ever written up a script like that."

It was the start of his second wind in Test cricket. Before that SCG game, he'd played 44 Tests. That 2022 match would be the first of another 44.

"The second half, I enjoyed much more than the first," he says. "I was scoring runs, going around the world. Absolute gift."

How Usman Khawaja is changing the face of Australian cricket Trailblazer Usman Khawaja talks about racism in cricket and urges Cricket Australia to diversify for the sake of the game.

A big part of his enjoyment was the change in culture in the Australian team, with Usman thriving under captain Pat Cummins and coach Andrew McDonald.

He'd grown more confident in himself, too, and started to speak out more about racism, injustice and diversity in cricket.

"I definitely got more vocal after I came back in the team because I was like, 'I think God's given me this platform to actually speak up for people,'" he says.

Usman Khawaja with parents Fozia and Tariq Khawaja at his retirement match after playing 88 Tests for Australia. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock, Cricket Australia)

Then, the brutal attacks by Hamas on Israel happened on October 7, 2023, and days later, Usman's social media feeds were filled with more horror: Israel's devastating retaliatory attacks on Gaza and the rising death toll of Palestinians.

He believed the mainstream media was downplaying the bombing and killing in Gaza and that the deaths of Ukrainians in that country's war with Russia were given greater prominence.

"It was a racial issue," he says. "The [Ukrainian] kids were white. The Gaza kids were brown."

Usman Khawaja wrote on his shoes, "all lives are equal". (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

He decided he had to make a stand. Without telling anyone, he bought red, black and green pens, [the colours of Palestine], scrawled "All lives are equal" on his white shoes and headed out to a training session.

"I was scared because I didn't know what was going to come out of it," Usman says. "But I had to do it."

It blew up. The International Cricket Council (ICC) banned Usman from wearing the shoes during the match. Cricket Australia said it supported player's rights to express opinions but it expected the ICC's rules to be followed.

Usman copped abuse and support but the controversy went on for weeks, opening a discussion which he says needed to be aired.

"I look back on it and everything I've done in cricket, all the runs I scored and all the matches I've won, the most proudest thing I've done in cricket is probably that," Usman says.

Usman Khawaja signs a cap for a budding cricket player at a foundation community event in Brisbane. (Australian Story: Erin Semmler)

Now retired from international cricket, he continues to play Big Bash League while building the Usman Khawaja Foundation, helping kids from refugee, immigrant, Indigenous, remote and lower socioeconomic backgrounds with educational support and cricket training.

Some of them will dream of playing for the Australian cricket team and Usman hopes that his success and advocacy will make their path a little easier.

Usman Khawaja started the foundation to help foster a love of cricket. (Australian Story: Erin Semmler)

Cricket in Australia is becoming more inclusive, he says, but it's still a very "white" sport and there's a lot more work to do.

"As much as I want to think that it has fully changed, it hasn't, because if it had, there would've been another Usman Khawaja to replace me," he says.

"But there's not."

Watch Usman Khawaja's Australian Story, Unbeaten, Monday 8pm (AEST) on ABC TV and ABC iview.

World.title: Women report stalkers abusing exercise apps to harass them
World.content:
It happened on an International Women's Day ride: a group of women cyclists had stopped at a cafe in Melbourne's north-east, refuelling midway through their route.

Bianca Pickett, a 51-year-old who works in IT, was sitting opposite an 18-year-old woman, Amy*, who gasped as she checked her phone.

"Amy said, 'Oh my god, this man has been messaging me on Strava for a couple of weeks; he just said he saw me on the road, and he's going to come and say hi.'" Pickett said.

Strava is the most popular fitness app that uses GPS-based activity tracking. It is also a social networking platform, allowing people to follow and message others, and see each other's running or cycling routes.

Many runners and cyclists plan their routes on apps, and then share them. (Getty Images: Ihor Biliavskyi)

Pickett asked Amy for his name, before shuddering; he was well-known for this kind of predatory behaviour.

"He ingratiates himself to younger women," Pickett said.

"He tries to isolate them, so he sends them messages, then tries to go on a ride with you, then befriends you. I hate to think what else has happened."

Amy, she said, was "terrified" when he arrived at the cafe. Pickett reassured her she would handle the situation, and told him it was a women's only ride.

While he begrudgingly left, Pickett said the man continued to follow the women on his bike, all the way back to Melbourne.

"I kept seeing him on corners, and thought, 'what is he doing?' I just wanted an International Women's Day ride that felt safe and lovely for everyone," she said.

Pickett said she and others had complained about the man to various cycling clubs previously, to no avail. But on this occasion, and with a new, female president in charge, he was finally banned from his latest club.

Loading Instagram content

"Prior to that several male presidents had been like, 'Oh, he's a good guy, he's always down at crits helping and supporting', so I always got shut down," Pickett said.

Some women, she added, were too embarrassed to complain if they had responded to his messages before realising his intent.

While grateful that action was finally taken, Pickett is alarmed by instances of men abusing the tracking features of exercise apps to stalk women.

Apps make it 'easy' to determine someone's location

Pickett has a long list of men she blocked after they attempted to harass or stalk her online.

"Some men will ask questions like 'So what apartment block are you living in? What's your route tomorrow? What racing are you doing next? So [basically], 'how do I determine where I can stalk you?'" she said.

Pickett argued that some exercise apps make it "easy" to determine someone's location.

"If you don't have privacy settings on you can figure out exactly where someone lives," she said.

"It happens to women all the time".

Apps like Strava are widely used to record, analyse and share exercise sessions. (Getty Images: Justin Paget)

Karen Bevan, CEO of Full Stop Australia, an organisation which supports people affected by sexual, domestic or family violence, said cyber stalking was an issue developers must take responsibility for.

"Too often, staying safe on these apps depends on people finding and changing settings they may not know exist," she said.

"This puts the burden in the wrong place — the harm comes from design choices and companies are the ones who should fix them.

"Platforms need to act first; most privacy settings should be switched on at sign-up, activity start and end points hidden automatically, messages from strangers off unless a user opts-in, and [there should be] quick, meaningful responses to complaints."

In a statement, a Strava spokesperson said the platform takes the safety and privacy of its global community very seriously.

"Our fully adjustable suite of privacy controls enables people to choose what they share and with whom. Key protections are on by default, including Messaging set to 'Friends Only', and the first and last 200 metres of activity maps are automatically hidden.

"We do not tolerate harassment, similar conduct or any other violation of our Community Standards. Our Trust and Safety team proactively monitors for violations, and carefully reviews any reports made by our community, taking appropriate action as needed."

Women want to run without being tracked

Melburnian Melanie Caple, 38, said the issue was not limited to cycling, either.

Caple is an app developer, mural artist and long-time runner who revels in the freedom of hitting the track alone.

Melanie Caple designed an app that allows runners to set an estimated end time. (Supplied: Melanie Caple)

"Running is the one thing that has meant I kind of feel OK in and about the world," she said.

Growing up in country Victoria, she moved to London at the age of 20, and said she regularly ran solo without thinking about letting anyone know where she was.

As she has got older, however — and with incidents like Samantha Murphy's alleged murder on a morning run — she has felt more pressure to let her family know where she is, and that she is safe.

With a wry sense of humour, she and her sister often exchange texts before runs with the hashtag #dontgetmurdered, followed by kisses.

Caple, however, drew the line at sharing her location while running.

Like Pickett, she has heard stories of women being cyber stalked.

Caple was also previously in an abusive relationship and said using GPS tracking mimicked being stalked.

"You want your family to feel assured that you're taking responsibility for your safety, but I didn't want to feel like I had to justify my freedom and independence in the world," she said.

Caple does, however, appreciate what draws most users to exercise apps: the chance to track her progress over time, and feel pride in her achievements, such as increasing the length of her runs, or completing them in shorter times.

As a result, Caple designed her own app — called SoloRunClubxx — which allows users to track their workouts without notifying anyone of their whereabouts.

However, the app also includes a safety feature which allows the user to set an estimated end time for their run and asks them at that point in time if they have finished their run safely.

They can either respond saying they have finished, or are still running. It is only if they do not respond that a loved one is notified with their location.

Melanie Caple often texts her sister before she sets out on a run. (Supplied: Melanie Caple)

Tech companies must 'keep pace with the law'

Caple has been buoyed by community feedback to the app, citing one example where a pregnant woman fell on her route, and was taken by ambulance to hospital. Her sister was notified of her location in the emergency department after she failed to report that she was safe.

Caple said the app was designed for extraordinary instances like these, so that women and gender diverse people can otherwise feel free of surveillance.

"I wanted to work out a way that, if something was going to happen to me on a run, in that worst case scenario, someone would know without me having to sacrifice my privacy and freedom," she said.

Bevan, from Full Stop Australia, also runs regularly, and said "everyone deserves freedom" while exercising.

Women regularly run in groups for an added layer of safety. (Getty Images: standret)

"I want what every runner wants: to run in peace, to run how I want, when I want, without looking over my shoulder," she said.

"Gender-based violence is about misusing power, and restricting someone's freedom to move is part of that."

She said the law recognises tracking as stalking, and the onus is on technology companies to "keep pace with the law".

"Location technology should be designed so it can't easily be turned into a tool of surveillance and control," Bevan said.

*Amy is a pseudonym used to protect her identity.

World.title: Jillaroos hammer England 78-0 but superstar's World Cup ends in hospital
World.content:
The Jillaroos have continued a weekend of lopsided scores as they thumped England 78-0 at the Women's Rugby League World Cup, although the victory was soured by a tournament-ending broken wrist for gun centre Julia Robinson.

Eleven Australians crossed for tries in Perth, with Jaime Chapman, Jocelyn Kelleher, Isabelle Kelly and Abbi Church nabbing doubles in a 15-try rout.

Robinson also got on the board in the 16th minute, but her evening and tournament came to a painful end just a few minutes later when she got her arm trapped between teammate Shaylee Bent and England winger Amelia Brown in a tackle.

The Broncos superstar immediately came reeling out of the tackle holding her left wrist and was taken straight off the field before being taken to hospital.

Loading Instagram content

Despite missing their greatest try-scorer, the Jillaroos carried on unfazed to romp to an enormous victory that fell just short of the 90-4 win they enjoyed in their against England in Las Vegas in early 2025.

Australia entered the game second behind England in Pool A after both won their opening matches, but now tops the group as the only team with two wins and enjoying a massive 118-0 points differential.

The Australian women's win was the sixth straight drubbing in round two of the men's and women's tournaments, but fell short of being the biggest margin after the English men beat France 82-0 in the first game of the western double header.

Earlier on Saturday, Samoa thumped PNG 64-6 in the men's tournament, while Fiji's women rolled over the top of the Orchids 40-4 in Port Moresby.

Friday's games were no closer, with Fetu Samoa bagelling Wales 76-0, while the Tongan men beat Lebanon 36-0.

Looks back at all the action in our live blog below.

World.title: Former Port Adelaide AFL player Daniel Stewart dies at 37
World.content:
The Port Adelaide AFL club has said it will honour Daniel Stewart at the first home game of 2027 after the former Power forward's death at the age of 37.

Stewart, who played 36 games and kicked 31 goals for Port Adelaide between 2010 and 2013, died suddenly yesterday.

The tall key forward was drafted by the Power in the 2009 rookie draft and promoted to the senior list at the end of that season.

Originally from Victoria, Stewart was recruited from SANFL team North Adelaide after playing for the Eastern Ranges and AFL Queensland club Labrador.

His best AFL return came in the final round of 2010 at Docklands against Richmond, where Stewart kicked four goals in a 10-point win for the Power.

"On behalf of everyone at the Port Adelaide Football Club, I extend our deepest condolences to Daniel's family including his mum Donna, dad Byron, wife Laura, his two sons Bernie and Lando and his brother Leigh," Port Adelaide chief executive Matthew Richardson said in a statement.

"We also extend our thoughts to his friends, including his close friend and former teammate Matt Thomas, and to all those at North Adelaide and Labrador who knew him.

"Daniel was part of the Port Adelaide football family, and he always will be. A sudden passing like this is devastating and our thoughts are with everyone who loved him, and with the teammates, coaches and staff who shared the journey with him here at Alberton.

"The club will provide support to those affected by Daniel's passing, including his former teammates and the people who worked alongside him."

The club stated it would honour Stewart by wearing black armbands at their first home game at Adelaide Oval next season.

World.title: Former AFLW coach says likely player exodus to go 'well beyond Collingwood'
World.content:
Former AFLW player and coach Lauren Arnell has slammed the standard of Collingwood, while emphasising the responsibility of coaches to "put on a show" to grow the game.

The Magpies slumped to a new low on Friday night after failing to kick a single goal against Port Adelaide.

The 48-point defeat to the Power was the club's 10th loss this season out of 11 games. Under head coach Sam Wright, the Magpies have won just five games since the start of 2024.

"Overall, it was not the best standard of AFLW football that we would expect to see at this point of season 11," Arnell said on ABC Radio.

"Ash Centra was one of the first to walk off the ground in tears right in front of us. Totally fair. I would probably be about the same level."

Sam Wright took over as head coach at the end of 2023 and has struggled to get wins on the board since. (Getty: Mark Brake)

The pioneer of women's football and former captain of Carlton said while the AFLW continued to play 16 a side in venues open to conditions, unlike protected stadiums the MCG, Perth Stadium and Docklands in the men's game, if teams did not have high skill levels or offensive systems, they would not be able to put goals on the board.

"If you're Sam Wright, you've made some clear decisions where you want to play plus two behind the ball for a lot of the game. And my personal belief is that if you do that in AFLW, you're giving up score, and that's what we saw again tonight," Arnell said.

"And having coached against Collingwood in 2024, we beat them here at Alberton, and it was quite frustrating as a coach and someone who's been invested in women's sport and AFLW for a period of time, [as] you know that broadcast relies on high scoring.

"People who forever criticise AFLW as a sport, or a league, will always point to the lack of score and short quarters … and I'm a firm non-believer in heavy defensive systems for all of those reasons, not just because you can't score, but because we have a responsibility if you're coaching to grow the game and put on a show."

Ruby Schleicher, captain of Collingwood, will leave the Magpies at the end of the AFLW season. (Getty: Martin Keep)

Last week, Collingwood CEO Craig Kelly fronted the AFLW playing group after media reports of player unrest and concerns with the operation of the women's program.

Kelly told News Corp that when AFLW was to be introduced in 2017, Collingwood put its hand up to be an inaugural club, but now he often wondered if the Magpies would have been better off waiting to enter the women's competition at a later date.

He conceded being a foundation AFLW club might have been a mistake, while ruling out any prospect of an independent review into the women's program, which other struggling clubs have done, such as Carlton in 2023, Richmond in 2025 and St Kilda following this season.

Former player and coach Lauren Arnell slams non-offensive styles of play in the AFLW. (Getty: Russell Freeman/AFL Photos)

To Arnell, those remarks from Kelly screamed a lack of understanding between the executive and the playing cohort.

"That statement just immediately tells me you have never sat down with enough of your women's players and even asked them questions of their perspective and where they've come from," Arnell said.

"Like you've got no understanding of your playing group and potentially your coaching group."

Despite being one of the biggest sporting clubs in Victoria, Collingwood players are reported to feel behind local rivals in Melbourne, North Melbourne and Carlton, and are unhappy with multiple aspects of the program, including coaching, high performance and list management.

Collingwood is not alone down the bottom of the ladder, with St Kilda and Essendon also entering round 11 having won only one game this season.

Essendon players have looked frustrated and dejected after losses this season. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

"And I'll guarantee you, off the back of that, there's going to be a lot of movement in the trade period coming up in the next month and a half," Arnell said.

There is an expected player exodus from Collingwood at the season's end, with captain Ruby Schleicher already announcing she'll be leaving to head back to Western Australia. It is reported the West Coast Eagles offered her a four-year deal, while the Magpies' initial offer was a one-year contract extension, then upped to two.

On top of Schleicher, the high-profile players such as Tarni White, Brianna Davey, Sarah Rowe and Lauren Butler are all out of contract at season's end. Vice-captain Jordy Allen tried to exit last trade period for Brisbane but Collingwood blocked her attempts.

"I think the washout of this whole storyline will be well beyond Collingwood, and we're going to see evidence of it across the trade period coming in December, and it will be really clear which players feel like their club's not invested in the environment," Arnell said.

World.title: Aussie Picklum aglow on top of WSL standings after Portugal win
World.content:
Molly Picklum has hit peak form riding the celebrated Supertubos waves to win the Rip Curl Pro Portugal event and move back to pole position to retain her world surfing title.

"Right now I'm on top of the world … literally!" roared the 23-year-old Australian after her victory over America's former world champion Caitlin Simmers in Friday's final sent her back to the top of the World Surf League standings.

Picklum's triumph at one of surfing's most famous venues gave her the maximum 10,000-point haul to ensure she overhauled Hawaiian Carissa Moore at the top.

The win came at the perfect post-season moment with just two events left.

The Gosford star has enjoyed a shiny nickname since she referred to herself as like "a glow worm in a cave" riding inside a deep barrel wave.

So she was quick to offer a shout-out to her friends and family at home, whom she knew would be watching her first triumph of the season in the early hours.

"I just want to say thank you to all of them. I know they stayed up for this one. The glow worm absolutely did it and I love you all so much!" Picklum said.

The Australian was given a triumphant ride on a jet ski after clinching the final win before she threw herself into the water to celebrate.

"I just love it when I get to win in front of them and actually do it for them," she said.

"So many people support me and put so much energy into me. I just love winning to give back to those ones that give to me.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

"I wanted to do well here. It was a dream of mine for me. Supertubos, it's like a cross between the Brazil energy and then (Hawaiian) Pipeline and those two together are like my two favourite things.

"So, oh my God, I'm so so grateful to win here. It was literally a dream of mine, and dreams come true. It's so baffling."

Picklum was delighted to "kind of hit my stride right at the right time" as she now sits atop the leaderboard on 48,950 points to Moore's 47,065, with another Hawaiian, Gabriela Bryan, third on 44,865 with two events left, the Philippines Pro and Pipeline.

Picklum didn't have a great record against 2024 world champ Simmers, having lost six of their previous eight head-to-head contests, but she was in control of the final from the moment she delivered a superb 7.83-point effort on her third wave to build on her opening 5.50.

Simmers couldn't respond, offering Picklum's fans on the beach a belated scare when she managed a best of 6.67 on the ninth of her 11 rides, but the Australian, who only had a half-dozen rides, eventually triumphed with her combined two-wave score of 13.33 to the American's 12.84.

AAP

World.title: Wallaroos send retiring pair out with win over Scotland
World.content:
The Wallaroos have completed their three-game Scottish sweep in a spicy Canberra contest that featured biting accusations and a string of yellow cards.

Australia produced plenty of classy moments in Friday night's 38-31 win but again lacked discipline in tackles and around the ruck to keep the tourists in it.

The hosts copped four yellow cards, retiring centre Cecilia Smith earning two of those to finish her 34-Test career on a red.

Scotland had two players sin-binned and it could have been far uglier if Wallaroos centre Georgina Friedrichs's accusations of biting had been verified on review.

'You can't be what you can't see' As she prepares for her final Test appearance, Emily Chancellor reflects on the legacy she leaves in Australian women's rugby.

But the officials saw no evidence and there were no bite marks on Friedrich's forearm, so the referee waved the complaints away.

Fifty-game prop Eva Karpani was yellow-carded for a high shot in her milestone game, while impressive flyhalf Waiaria Ellis was marched for slowing down a Scottish charge late in the first half.

The win came as a relief for retiring pair Emily Chancellor and Smith, with the latter smiling as she received a standing ovation after being sent off.

"I'm really sorry about that, just wanted to go out with a bang I guess," Smith said as she embraced her daughter Ruby post-match.

"She's been there since day one [of Smith's Wallaroos career].

"Having her there at trainings, camps, on the sideline, means so much and I just want to be that role model and show you can do anything if you put your mind to it and the hard work in."

A teary Chancellor, former captain and two-time World Cup member, signed off with a win in her 42nd Test after debuting in 2018.

"It's created so much opportunity for me, so much purpose in my life. I love these girls and what we play for," she said.

"I love what this game has given us: travel the world with great people and create opportunity. You can't be what you can't see."

Victory for Australia followed wins in Sydney and Edinburgh against the same opponents, the side now out of action until the Wallaroos program transitions to a full-time operation next year under new coach Sione Fukofuka.

Piper Duck scored one of the Wallaroos' five tries in their 38-31 win over Scotland. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The hosts led 14-0 early but trailed 17-14 at half-time after a string of penalties led to three successive Scottish tries.

The Wallaroos regained the ascendancy and surged back ahead 38-24 when captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona finished a long-range effort.

But Karpani and then Smith were marched, keeping Scotland interested until the final play, but they were unable to find the match-tying converted try.

AAP

World.title: One-time minnows Tonga and Samoa now star World Cup attractions
World.content:
At Western Sydney Stadium last week, Toa Samoa had a moment of pure elation, a crushing 78-4 victory over France at the men's Rugby League World Cup.

It was capped off with an extraordinary final play that saw a penalty goal attempt from Stephen Crichton ricochet off the post.

The ball bounced towards Benaiah Ioelu who scored a try after the full-time siren had sounded, delivering Samoa's largest-ever victory.

What was more extraordinary was that a game with a kick-off time of 5:45pm on Friday, playing out what was likely and ultimately proved to be a walkover, still drew a crowd of 13,000.

It was a horror slot to play in: a workday, outside school holidays, in a busy part of Sydney where traffic was banking up across the many arterial roads that led to it.

Yet the crowd, largely comprising Western Sydney's large Samoan population, bellowed Ua fa'afetai — a traditional song of thanks and gratitude.

Fiji and the Cook Islands played each other on Sunday in Newcastle; there was a tick over 10,000 in the stands and another 1.7 million watching on television across Australia, outrating several flagship current affairs shows, news bulletins and reality programs.

These are just two examples that show this is a World Cup transformed by Pasifika passion.

Big Pasifika populations in Australia are bringing a challenge to local rugby league dominance. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The growing strength of Samoa and Tonga's men's teams has been no secret, but now more than ever the iron grip of dominance largely held by Australia on international rugby league, occasionally disrupted by New Zealand, could be under threat.

What has also been clear to those at the grounds or watching from home is that this World Cup in Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea is one where diaspora communities have breathed life into a tournament that has previously lacked the same level of excitement or prestige compared to other international sporting events.

Australia's migration story tracks with this

The shift will be most obvious on November 1, when Samoa and Tonga play each other in Sydney, in a game that was the first to sell out despite being in the third week of the tournament.

Already a series of ex-players and pundits have raised the call to move the game to the larger Stadium Australia to accommodate a crowd beyond the 30,000 that Western Sydney Stadium holds.

The interest should come as no surprise though, as the Pasifika population in Australia has been steadily increasing.

In 2011, 165,000 Australians identified as being from Pasifika communities; by 2021, that number had almost tripled to 415,033.

Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics shows outer suburban areas of Sydney and Brisbane have burgeoning communities.

It is no surprise that Tonga vs Samoa is the first game to sell out at the Rugby League World Cup. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Sierra Keung, a senior lecturer in sports leadership and management at Auckland University of Technology, said she was not surprised by the fan turnout.

"The pride for our cultures, for our people, it's more than just a jersey for our Pasifika communities," Dr Keung told ABC Sport.

She cited a distinctive moment on the field that set this explosion in motion.

In 2017, the International Rugby League changed the rules to allow players with cultural ties to multiple nations to play for the country of their choosing.

The most famous change in allegiance was Jason Taumalolo.

Jason Taumalolo's choice to change allegiance to Tonga made headlines in the rugby league world. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

That rule change is on full display at this tournament.

Of the listed starting line-up for Tonga's match against Lebanon last night at Western Sydney Stadium, none of the players were born in Tonga, but all have deep familial ties to the island nation.

Tonga beat Lebanon 36-0 to keep its campaign on track.

"This is years in the making, and it's come down to people making bold decisions, like Jason Taumalolo to be the first to say, 'I'm going to go home and represent my people,'" Dr Keung said.

Salesi Foketi is one of a number of Tongan players that chose to represent his familial roots over his country of birth, New Zealand.

"Right from when I was a boy, it was always Tonga," he said.

Winger Jojo Fifita made his debut last weekend for Tonga and it was a moment to acknowledge his forebears.

"Being able to represent my dad's side was something I'd always wanted to do when I was older and I finally got that opportunity," he said.

Extension beyond Pasifika diaspora may be the future

There is another team outside the South Pacific that is relying on heritage and cultural ties as the bind for players to represent it.

Lebanon's winger Jason Saab has potentially the most unique ties to the country.

His stepfather, whose name he took, is Lebanese, and Saab is now lining up for the Cedars.

Jason Saab says he was brought up in the Lebanese culture through his stepfather Pierre. Now he's playing for the Cedars. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Saab told ABC Sport in September of the sincere ties to Lebanese culture through his stepdad Pierre.

"That's the culture that raised me ultimately, that whole community of people. That's kind of where I found my identity to be," he said.

While all players in the Cedars squad were born in Australia, Lebanon coach Michael Cheika, who is also Lebanese Australian, said the small but dedicated rugby league community in Lebanon was driving the entire playing group, especially for those with family in Lebanon where strikes from Israel continued amid a broader conflict in the region.

"With everything that's going on over there … you've got to understand that they may not have enough petrol to get to the games, let alone field markings, fields that are available," he said.

As Samoa and Tonga have brought a genuine competitiveness to the tournament, there are other countries with large populations in Australia, such as Fiji and the Cook Islands, that could also challenge the Kangaroos, who have won 12 world titles, including six of the last seven.

Fiji and the Cook Islands, like Samoa and Tonga, have large diaspora populations in Australia. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner)

"The talent is just through the roof right now, both men's and women's," Dr Keung said.

"So I'm really excited for this World Cup, but also for future World Cups too, because it's just going to get better and better each time it comes around."

There is no doubt rugby league has cottoned on to its international life blood, and it seems the public is following suit.

On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad — whether it’s a still image, video, audio, or text — that “has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence” to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies, as well as restaurants’ ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials.

Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad was created. So you might see disclosures pop up in commercials in other states if they’re also expected to air in Pennsylvania.

The law leaves many loopholes, though. For one, what constitutes “significantly modified” is subjective. There is also a carve-out for “parody, satire, commentary or criticism,” as well as anything that is “evidently fictional.” Again, what “evidently fictional” means is unclear. The wording also suggests only content that “uses synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception” about a product or service would require a disclosure. Again, leaving questions about what qualifies as “false” under the law and who makes those decisions.

The office of State Senator Nick Pisciottano, who introduced the bill, did not immediately return a request for comment.

Tech.title: Fielded is obsessed with scammers and unhinged Japanese cyberpunk
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Lindsay Powell, who releases records under the name Fielded, has spent most of her career subverting expectations and genre conventions. According to their Bandcamp page, Fielded started as an experimental noise project before growing into something closer to R&B. But from moment one, her take on the genre was restless, relentlessly playing with what R&B even means.

Her first album, Ninety-Thirty-Thirty, includes songs heavily indebted to ’80s synth-pop and features multiple saxophone solos. Boy Angel is a quirky electronic exploration with huge saw-wave synths, jittery percussion, and sky-high vocal stacks. While 2020’s Demisexual Lovelace is a slinkier affair, released on underground hip-hop imprint Backwoodz Studioz and features contributions from Billy Woods and Elucid (Armand Hammer).

Her latest record, Some Kind of Animal, pulls from all of these various versions of Fielded, placing organ-fueled slow jams like “That Bitch” next to a cover of Nine Inch Nails’ “Closer” that has strong 2000s neo-soul vibes, as well as the industrial funk of “Heaven,” which includes a guest verse from Pink Siifu.

We wanted to know what’s behind Fielded’s genre-defying madness.

What is your most indispensable tool?

My most indispensable tool in recording is my Universal Audio Apollo Twin audio interface. I love its ease of function and I love the Universal Audio digital studio plugins. I use them on all of my records during the recording process and beyond. I can mic up and get a professional sound in no time, plus my guitars and synths sound amazing and clear.

What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?

Right now I have a pirated full-length version of the Japanese cyberpunk film 964 Pinocchio pinned to my tab bar for endless sonic and visual inspiration.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

I don’t know if it is a tech trend or a plague, but I deeply wish AI would disappear off of the face of the earth.

What creation are you most proud of?

I am most proud of my latest album Some Kind of Animal, specifically the single of the same title, and thank goddess for that; I’d be bummed if my favorite musical output was in the rearview.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

The best piece of advice I’ve ever received, throughout my whole life, is to be patient. Everything happens in perfect time; there is no reason to be jealous or envious because our journeys are completely our own and everything happens for a reason. What is meant for us will come for us, and what is not meant for us should be metabolized as a lesson that helps us grow and become exactly who we are meant to be.

What is your current obsession?

I am currently obsessed with stories about scammers. All stories about all scammers; big scams, small scams, scams that ended in minor jail time or a blow-out of incredible impact. I love scammers, and I am fascinated by their brains.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

The last piece of physical media I bought was Alissa Bennett’s compilation of essays entitled Taxidermist’s Handbook, full of — you guessed it — stories about scammers (amongst other types of criminals).

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

Freak Today, Freak Tomorrow.

Tech.title: LG’s brilliant C6 OLED TV is already $400 off ahead of Black Friday
Tech.content:
Black Friday is still over a month away, but if you’re hoping to upgrade your TV, you don’t need to wait until November. LG has already kicked off its early Black Friday sale, letting you save on the LG C6 and various soundbars through November 1st. Right now, for instance, you can snag a 55-inch C6 for an all-time low of $999.99 ($400 off), with Amazon and Best Buy matching said price. Other sizes are also discounted, including the 65-inch model, which is on sale for $1,399.99 ($300 off) from Amazon, Best Buy, and LG. If you purchase direct, you’ll also get a free Xbox Wireless Controller and a complimentary wall mount.

LG’s C6 OLED TV offers a few small but welcome upgrades over last year’s C5, including a faster Alpha 11 AI Gen3 processor designed to improve picture and sound quality, along with a brighter display. It also boasts a higher refresh rate of up to 165Hz for smoother gaming, up from 144Hz, while retaining four HDMI 2.1 ports and support for AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync, the latter of which helps reduce unwanted screen tearing while gaming.

Unsurprisingly, the C6 delivers the hallmarks of OLED technology, including inky blacks, vibrant color, and impressive contrast. Support for Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, meanwhile, helps make movies and shows appear more lifelike and immersive, while built-in access to Netflix, HBO Max, and the like lets you stream your favorite content without a dedicated streaming device. Google Cast and Apple AirPlay 2 also make it easy to share content from your phone, while Matter support lets you pair it with various smart home devices.

Solid specs aside, we’d be remiss not to mention that researchers recently raised concerns about how LG’s smart TVs collect and log user data. LG has since responded to some of the accusations, saying its TVs don’t continuously record conversations, and that features like voice recognition and interest-based advertising are optional and disabled by default. While LG hasn’t addressed all concerns, similar data-collection practices aren’t necessarily unique to LG TVs, and they don’t detract from the C6’s impressive feature set.

Tech.title: What to expect from Apple’s ‘Pro and tell’ event
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

It feels like Apple’s Welcome Home event just happened. And the iPhone Duo announcement isn’t all that far in our rearview mirror, either. Yet, the company is back with another launch, focused on the MacBook Pro, it looks like. Its “Pro and tell” event is scheduled for October 28th at 1PM ET in Los Angeles. While obviously nothing is confirmed yet, it sure seems like we’re finally going to get that long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro.

Beyond that? There could be an OLED update for the iPad Mini, plus M6 updates across other devices, following the M6 debut with the Mac Mini in August.

A touchscreen MacBook Pro

A MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen has been a fixture of the rumor mill since at least early 2023. But now, in late 2026, it may finally come to fruition. The name MacBook Ultra has been floating around, but Apple is unlikely to rebrand its flagship laptop line.

This will be the first touchscreen laptop and the first OLED laptop from Apple. It will supposedly feature an iPhone-esque Dynamic Island, but don’t expect a dramatic revamp of the macOS interface — The touchscreen MacBook isn’t going to be some sort of iPad hybrid. It may include a few flourishes, like a magnification effect when you touch the screen or new gesture controls in native apps. But that’s it.

M6 MacBook Pro

That doesn’t mean there won’t be an M6 MacBook Pro, however. The base model of the MacBook Pro could be getting a bump from the M5 after the M6 debuted in the Mac Mini earlier this year. It might also get a slight redesign, including a hole-punch style camera. Unfortunately, they’re also expected to come with a price increase as component shortages reverberate through the Apple lineup.

M6 iMac

The iMac is also expected to get an M6 update, nearly two years after its last revision. Apple’s all-in-one desktop appears like it’s going to skip right over the M5. Don’t expect any real changes beyond that, though. But at least we might get some new color options, just like we did with the M4 model.

OLED iPad Mini

Another long-rumored device that might finally be making its debut on Wednesday is the OLED iPad Mini. Other than the iPad Pro, the tablet lineup has stuck with LCDs until now. The new OLED iPad could kick off a broader transition for the product line. The screen upgrade may add $100 to the cost, though. Otherwise, it likely won’t be a significant redesign, but expect a processor upgrade from the aging A17 to the A20 that debuted with the iPhone 18.

Tech.title: I hope Apple’s touchscreen MacBook takes some lessons from this Lenovo laptop
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Like the Apple silicon in modern MacBook Pros, RTX Spark is an Arm-based processor with a beefy integrated GPU and lots of unified memory. And the Yoga is the most fun RTX Spark laptop so far because it’s a 16-inch 2-in-1 convertible with a stylus. Its Nvidia-powered compatriots also have touchscreens, like most Windows laptops, but they’re conventional clamshell designs.

The Lenovo Yoga does all your typical 2-in-1 stuff: it can be used as a clamshell laptop, and it can fold its hinge all the way back for tent mode and tablet modes. As a tablet, you can use it in either landscape or portrait orientation, and getting the keyboard out of the way is great for watching movies, playing games with a controller, or integrating your laptop into a multi-monitor desk setup with keyboard and mouse.

2-in-1s can be seen as a weird compromise between laptops and tablets. I just think they’re neat.

The Yoga 9n’s included stylus works for note-taking and drawing on its excellent OLED display, but you can also use it on the haptic trackpad for a Wacom-like experience, without blocking the screen with your hand. And the stylus is magnetic, allowing it to attach to the Yoga’s lid — either on its own, or while housed in its case. I particularly enjoy using the Yoga’s stylus for photo retouching in Lightroom Classic or Photoshop. I haven’t used a stylus for that kind of work in ages, since I gave up my old Wacom, but having one that works on either the screen or the trackpad is incredibly convenient

I expect a touchscreen MacBook Pro would have Apple Pencil support. And like on the Lenovo, it would go a long way to get me back to using a stylus for retouching. But I hope that also like the Lenovo, it works on the trackpad too — the more options, the better. And if a touch-enabled MacBook supports the Apple Pencil (which it should), I’m also hoping it attaches to the laptop, both for convenience and for wireless charging, as on the iPad Pro. Lenovo’s stylus relies on USB-C charging, which is fine, but not as convenient as always having it charged and ready to go while attached to your laptop.

Previous Next

1 / 2 The Yoga 9n’s stylus works on both the trackpad and the screen.

I don’t expect Apple to make a standard convertible laptop after all this time. Simply joining Windows manufacturers in making a 2-in-1 or swapping the MacBook Pro’s Mini LED for a touchscreen OLED and calling it a day doesn’t seem very Apple. I’m hoping for something special, like Apple’s own take on the Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio — a clever idea that brought the touchscreen forward instead of flipping it backwards — or something totally fresh. And there are hints in macOS 27 that Apple is updating to Golden Gate to make touch functions feel more natural than just poking and prodding at things designed for a mouse cursor. As fun as I find 2-in-1 Windows laptops and Chromebooks, using those desktop operating systems with a finger or a stylus can get clunky.

My hopes are high for Apple to wow us, because this MacBook Pro with touch is sure to be expensive. And Apple’s recent design decisions aren’t faultless. The HomeView’s lack of apps is perplexing. The iPhone Duo is a little messy. Current MacBooks are so great, it’s easy to forget the butterfly keyboard fiasco wasn’t all that long ago. After all this time of holding out on adding a touchscreen to the MacBook, Apple has to make it worth it.

Tech.title: Lee Chang Dong ponders the ethics of the camera
Tech.content:
Lee Chang Dong’s seventh feature film, Possible Love, is inspired by true events from 2009, when a Korean conglomerate fired a third of its staff – 2,600 employees – after which many died by suicide. Possible Love is the latest in a long line of Lee movies that engage with themes of class or labor or religion or compressed modernity, that uniquely Korean affliction, without feeling didactic.

A different kind of movie would have captured the heat of that labor struggle. Possible Love picks up with the characters in the aftermath, a murkier time that defies easy understanding. The film opens with an epigraph: “Thou shall not covet.” What follows is a movie about characters who covet. They covet each other’s job, designer clothes, spouses, and positionality. Mi-ok (Jeon Do-Yeon) is the long-suffering wife of Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), her laid-off husband. At a funeral of a colleague who died by suicide, Mi-ok and Ho-seok meet another couple, documentary filmmaker Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong) and her rich husband, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). And off we go.

The Verge spoke with Lee during his trip to New York about how he arrived at his politics, porousness between people, the properties of the camera, and what it is like to work with Netflix. The interview was conducted in Korean and translated into English.

I am also from Daegu. I wonder how this fact shaped you? And more broadly, to whom or what do you owe your political education?

As you know well, Daegu is referred to as the heartland of conservatism in Korea. I went to school there, all the way through university, so I grew up steeped in that conservative disposition and was influenced by it. But until I graduated from college, in the spring of 1980, I didn’t realize how politically conservative Daegu citizens were.

That spring, in May of 1980, I participated in protests against the Chun Doo-hwan regime as a university student. It was on the streets that I met them, the citizens, and experienced their hardline sentiments in a visceral way. It was shocking to me. Afterwards, I thought a lot about how come the people in Daegu were so politically conservative. In light of all that, the thoughts of a person I perceive as myself, that person’s attitude towards the world, could only be bound with a certain kind of tension.

I was interested in how different directors respond to similar social forces in different ways – like Bong Joon Ho’s Parasite and Park Chan Wook’s No Other Choice. I imagine you know them both personally. What is the conversation between you all when working on your various projects?

We do know each other personally, but we seldom talk about our work. It might be the result of coincidence. Though of course, there might be a certain inevitability hidden within them. We lived through the same modern Korean history, and you cannot call that coincidence.

One thing does come to mind. A long time ago, I think before he made Mother, Bong Joon Ho told me over drinks that he had almost finished writing a script and wanted to show it to me. It was a story about a mother, and he was wrestling with how he could portray that person’s pain, whether he even had the right to. He said he wanted to show me the script. But once he sobered up, maybe he forgot, because he never showed it to me. Later, when I saw the film, I felt I might understand what he had been talking about.

Possible Love is concerned with similar questions: How can I portray another person’s story, another person’s pain? What position am I in? How much distance should I keep from them? You could say that these questions around the ethics of the camera are connected to the worry Bong Joon Ho had back then.

Like Ye-ji, I come from the so-called margins, and now report on that terrain, which is perhaps why watching her character pursue a near-vampiric level of access, I felt something close to repulsion. How were you able to represent the filmmaker–participant dynamic so accurately?

I can’t say how accurate it is. I don’t think Ye-ji’s attitude can be generalized. Not every documentary filmmaker has a rich husband. Nevertheless you can say Ye-Ji captures something universal about filmmakers, or those who deal in other people’s stories, directors such as myself, or reporters, in that they aren’t exactly the people they portray. Even if they came from a lower class, they are no longer of it. Their position in life has changed. And yet, in order to do their work, what do they do? When someone else’s suffering unfolds dramatically in front of them, are they to capture the moment on tape, or should they step away from the camera? Or maybe it isn’t unfolding dramatically in front of them, in which case, do they create a certain effect by producing the moment, by staging it?

What does it mean to capture someone on film? NYFF

I think those are basically properties of the camera. The moment you hold a camera you have power, and the camera operates according to that power.

It’s not so much that I portrayed it so precisely, but these properties of the camera are something worth thinking through together.

For us filmmakers, we don’t belong to the world of our subjects, nor are we on the side of capital either. We are in the middle where we are, it can be said, in a neutral, or perhaps cowardly position. Despite that, those who make movies, those who tell stories of others, in the end, can, through their efforts, bring about some small change.

In this film, Ho-seok ends up pouring out what’s inside of him in front of the camera, which functions as a kind of treatment, even if that isn’t what Ye-ji intended.

Possible Love is a collaboration between you and screenwriter Oh Jung-mi. How did you two come to work together, and what does that collaboration look like?

She is a student I met at Korea National University of Arts. You could say it’s a school that draws the most talented and ambitious students, and she was special even among them. By special I mean she was creative and wrote well, of course, but she also has a perspective, and the ability to take a step back and regard something, and find meaning in things.

As I get older, I grow duller and numb, and set in my ways, and she is a friend who reliably jolts me out of it, which is very precious to me.

I think I’m lucky. Not just with Oh Jung-mi but everyone around me that I work with is very precious to me, and I feel lucky to have met them.

The problem with Oh Jung-mi, though, is that while working together, I kept scrapping projects. So she suffered. But she never left. She stayed beside me, and even though she herself is someone who makes and develops films, she has given me a lot of help up to now.

Ye-ji documents in service of higher purpose. Mi-ok’s character snaps photos of the table spread for no purpose at all. The footage from the helicopter captures a moment of police brutality. How does the function of cinema compare to all the other instances in which we hit record?

Ye-ji has a desire to capture in her camera vanishing laborers [and] the value of their labor — not unlike her dry cleaner father. And yet, it is undeniable that she also regards their lives as source material for her own movie. As narrative filmmakers, stories of others in pain often is nothing but material for a commercial movie.

As for Mi-ok, she knows about the properties of the camera, but she, too, has a desire: to broadcast her pain, and her problems. She has a secondary desire, which is that she wonders if her husband’s traumas may not be healed through the camera, because she believes that his biggest issue is keeping all his problems, his despair and his anger, hidden.

So each has their own desires regarding the camera.

As a filmmaker, firstly, I had the goal of conveying the contents of the documentary Ye-ji was making, of capturing the sufferings of the laid-off laborers. I believed what Ye-ji tried to show, I had to show through my own film.

The group therapy session scene, for example, could be very long and tedious, and for some viewers it might be something that they cannot emotionally relate to, because they came to see a narrative film, not documentary. Despite that, I felt I had to convey it.

Regarding the crackdown scene, some of it appears through archival footage shot from a distance. But as someone making a fiction film, I also have a responsibility to convey Ho-seok’s subjective memory cinematically. So you could say within the narrative structure of Ye-ji’s documentary, multiple layers of roles and goals co-exist.

What are some notes you received from your American movie executives that felt unique to working in the American system versus Korean?

I didn’t feel that at all. From pre-production through post-production, Netflix, as the investor, never once interfered or offered unsolicited notes. Of course, I can’t generalize from that. I haven’t asked everyone else. But I had none of that. In that sense they absolutely guaranteed my independence and freedom as a director.

Now the film is finished and we are promoting it, and in particular part of what we call the Oscar campaign. I probably wouldn’t have gotten this kind of help without Netflix, that’s clear.

Possible Love was released in select US theaters October 23rd and will be available on Netflix globally on November 6th.

Tech.title: Laika has spent 20 years building up to Wildwood
Tech.content:
Across several decades in Hollywood, Caleb Deschanel has seen a lot. He served as cinematographer on films like The Passion of the Christ and The Patriot, worked on sequences in The Godfather and Titanic, and directed a few episodes of Twin Peaks. Even still, nothing could quite prepare him for his first stop-motion project: working as the cinematographer on Wildwood, the latest release from Coraline studio Laika. While he knew that stop-motion was a long and involved process, he was still surprised by just how much work went into these movies. “When I started I thought it was one thing, and then I quickly found out that it was another thing,” Deschanel says. “It was much more complicated than I expected.”

Wildwood has been a long time coming. Laika CEO Travis Knight originally optioned the rights for the book of the same name, written by Decemberists frontman Colin Meloy, in 2011. But production didn’t begin until a decade later. “I’ve been working on it in some form or another for 16 years,” Knight, who also directed Wildwood, says. “The reason why I stuck with it, the reason why I had to make this movie no matter what, is because of what it meant to me personally. Underneath it all, it’s a story about love and loss and grief, it’s about the impossible things that love asks of us, and that meant something to me personally in a very profound way.”

It’s also the biggest production Laika has ever undertaken. Wildwood tells the story of a young girl named Prue who has to venture into the “impassable wilderness” that surrounds Portland in order to find her baby brother. When she enters the forest she discovers a fantasy realm reminiscent of Narnia, with magical spells, talking animals, and warring factions. It required nearly 50 animators and more than 200 puppets to pull it off, and the film is full of ambitious sequences, like a 12-minute battle with dozens of soldiers and a chase scene through a bustling Portland, where Prue’s brother is carried away by a gigantic murder of crows.

Image: Laika

Image: Laika

According to head of animation Brad Schiff, the studio’s ethos involves mixing “old-school craft with modern technology.” With each project, he says, Laika develops new techniques. If something works well, they then push the idea even further on the next project. For instance, on Laika’s previous film, Missing Link, the main character was outfitted with a diaphragm so that when an animator turned a screw on the puppet’s back, the diaphragm could expand or contract, creating the illusion that it was breathing. This has since become the standard for puppets in Laika’s films.

These may sound like small details, but over the years they add up. For costume designer Deb Cook, there wasn’t a single innovation on Wildwood that stood out to her, but rather the sheer number of tools she had at her disposal. “Over time we’ve gathered together a library of techniques that we’ve been able to put into practice on this movie,” she says. This was especially important on Wildwood, which features a huge range of costumes; in the city sequences everyone is dressed in modern clothing, whereas in the forest characters have more fantastical looks.

“It was much more complicated than I expected.”

For Wildwood, many of the advancements came down to materials. The costumes made use of more flexible fabrics, for example, and the team also engineered a new process for creating silicone that’s lighter and more durable than what they previously used. “We’ve done this so we can wean ourselves off of foam latex, which is stinky and it shrinks over time, and five years later it kind of just crumbles,” says Oliver Jones, head of characters and practical effects. “There are advantages to rethinking a lot of these materials that were our go-to probably since King Kong.”

The scale of Wildwood has also forced the studio to adopt another seemingly much more boring practice: being better organized. “They’ve been misplaced,” Cook says, when asked if she’s ever lost a puppet. “There’s now a very sophisticated tracking system because there are so many moving parts, and so many stages around the studio.”

And while much has been said about the large and elaborate sequences in the film — Knight says the epic battle scene is “probably the most technically challenging thing that we’ve ever done” — all of these techniques are designed to imbue more humanity into characters that are portrayed by puppets. In that regard, small details like the flow of fabric or the impression of breathing are vitally important.

Image: Laika

Image: Laika

“We also have really subtle and intimate scenes, quiet scenes that don’t have a lot of flash, that have virtually no sound design or music, where the only thing that you’re experiencing is the grief of a father talking about a secret that he’s been holding on to for 15 years, or a quiet moment of a woman grieving the loss of her son,” Knight explains. “These are moments where you have nowhere to hide and the performances of these little puppets — these little assemblages of steel and silicon and fabric that have no life of their own — completely spring to life because of the hand and the artistry of the human behind it. Those are the moments that I’m most proud of.”

In this way, the long road to Wildwood hitting theaters makes a lot of sense. Laika has been around for just over 20 years, and over the course of each film the studio has innovated to steadily push its craft forward. Knight may have been thinking about the film for 16 years, but creating the version that is coming out in 2026 wouldn’t have been possible without all of the learnings spread across films like ParaNorman and Kubo and the Two Strings.

For Knight, it’s been especially gratifying to bring it to life with a team of both Laika veterans and newcomers, including not only Deschanel but also a handful of young animators for whom Wildwood was their first feature film project. Some were young enough that Coraline, Laika’s very first film, was what inspired them to get into the field in the first place. “I was really moved by that,” says Knight. “It also made me feel old as shit.”

Wildwood is in theaters now.
